headline: A Russian scientist travels to the West to conduct research with colleagues – risking everything in the process. Our reporter accompanied her.
lead: Vera Petrow travels to Western Europe to continue her research projects: What was recently perfectly normal now involves high personal risks for her. A recounting of her week-long research trip to a German-speaking city.
body:
# A Russian scientist travels to the West to conduct research with colleagues – risking everything in the process. Our reporter accompanied her.

*Vera Petrow travels to Western Europe to continue her research projects: What was recently perfectly normal now involves high personal risks for her. A recounting of her week-long research trip to a German-speaking city.*

**Andrew Müller (text), Florian Generotzky (images)** · Wissenschaft · 2024-09-17 · 2373 words · [ld.1844050](https://www.nzz.ch/wissenschaft/der-eiserne-vorhang-im-labor-wie-russische-wissenschafter-die-sanktionen-umgehen-ld.1844050)

![Vera Petrow is in her mid-30s and a passionate arthropod researcher.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/09/01/b122559e-febf-4f3c-bb66-b1f0c240a03d.jpeg?crop=2251,3376,x181,y0)
*Vera Petrow is in her mid-30s and a passionate arthropod researcher.*

_Russian biologist Vera Petrov simply wants to do her work, but since the war in Ukraine, she has had to operate almost like a secret agent. She smuggles money and hides research materials. She cannot reveal in this text exactly what she is researching. It is not drugs or even nuclear weapons, but small invertebrates from the phylum Arthropoda, which includes insects, crustaceans, and millipedes. Completely harmless. But if Petrov says something «wrong,» she risks being imprisoned by her own government. The new iron curtain runs not only along the border between Russia and Ukraine, but also right through the laboratories of the world._

The aquarium in the corner of the room babbles softly, as if nothing were amiss. Its sound mingles with the concentration in the air as the two young biologists lean over their microscopes. Around them are shallow plastic sample containers and wooden collection boxes filled with cardboard boxes of prepared arthropods. Vera Petrov sits with her back straight, looking through the microscope eyepiece, her hands resting beside the brightly lit stage.

She carefully holds small specimens up to the light. Every now and then she hums. When Petrow is examining arthropods she particularly likes, or when she's on the trail of something new, she rubs her hands together enthusiastically and smiles.

She's been fascinated by these little creatures since her youth. In the early 1990s, when many people in Russia didn't have enough to eat, her parents moved to the countryside. They grew fruits and vegetables and gathered mushrooms and berries in the forest. There, instead of listening to the crude jokes of her schoolmates, Petrov took long walks, searching for animal tracks. She never saw the large mammals, which frustrated her. Then one day, lying in the grass, she observed the many small arthropods around her and understood: This is my mission!

## Even during the Cold War there was more cooperation

Petrov and her Western colleague Philip Blum have selected several genera of these small animals for revision. This means checking whether species have been recorded twice or whether specimens with the same scientific name actually belong to different species. They might even discover entirely new species in Blum's collection. This is fundamental taxonomic research, then, to catalog life on the planet – a cornerstone of biology.

The collaboration between Blum and Petrov almost failed. Western countries like Switzerland, Germany, and the USA largely severed all cooperation with Russian scientific institutions in order to isolate the Putin regime internationally; research funds and findings were not to benefit it. Even during the Cold War, Western and Soviet researchers collaborated more closely than they do today.

The sanctions apply to all disciplines, whether weapons research or climate science, military geography or biodiversity research. They are supported by broad alliances of major scientific institutions. However, discussions sometimes arise: Isn't science a bridge to diplomacy? Do the sanctions do more harm than good?

## She thought she would no longer be able to practice her profession

Ultimately, science itself decides whether further collaboration is possible in a given case. Direct exchange with Russian researchers is even considered desirable. Thus, no one knows exactly how many smaller collaborations are taking place under the radar.

Petrov and Blum had connected via Facebook and had never met in person before. Blum had sent her prepared arthropods for identification, and they were considering joint publications. Originally, Philipp Blum, somewhat younger than Petrov, was supposed to travel to Russia for his doctoral research and visit her at her institute. But when the Russian army invaded Ukraine, that was no longer possible. Vera Petrov was shocked. «I thought I would no longer be able to practice my profession,» she says.

For Petrov, the collaboration with Blum is crucial. She would benefit from joint publications; each article not only enhances her reputation in the scientific community but also boosts her meager salary. For many years, she has visited museums and institutes outside of Russia, conducting research and exchanging ideas with colleagues. Blum has access to promising collection material and performs genetic analyses that are extremely useful to Petrov in her work. For her institute in Russia, the method is too expensive.

Blum also relies on this cooperation. Without Petrow's expertise, it would be difficult for him to produce a good doctoral thesis. She is one of only a handful of leading experts worldwide on arthropods, the subject of Blum's research.

## Please, no ardent Putin supporters

Petrov, who still had a valid Schengen visa, was planning to travel to Western Europe soon anyway to collaborate with colleagues. Perhaps, Blum's doctoral advisor suggested, an exception could be made in this case. After all, the collaboration had begun before the war, and it concerned a dissertation with a rapidly approaching deadline. Exceptions are most readily granted to junior researchers. However, Blum's advisor added, one couldn't simply invite Russian colleagues. One had to be certain, he said, that one wasn't inadvertently inviting a fervent Putin supporter.

Ideological vetting is generally considered undemocratic and incompatible with academic freedom. But Philipp Blum saw no other way out and wrote an email to Petrov: «I'm a little embarrassed to ask you this, and I hope you don't misunderstand.» He asked her to sign a resolution against the war. «I didn't mean to offend her,» Blum says. «But I wanted to get it out of the way.»

When Petrov read the email, she found Blum's question both understandable and silly. She believes politics and work should be kept separate. In Russia, it's forbidden to even speak of a war. Those who speak out against it rarely do so via email. Even if you're only researching arthropods, you never know who might be reading along.

## «Of course I am against the war.»

Nevertheless, Petrov replied the very next morning. «Of course I am against the war,» she wrote. However, she was a single mother and had to be extremely careful. If she spoke out publicly against the war, she could be imprisoned. Indeed, the Putin regime has already imprisoned several scientists critical of the government.

Philipp Blum understood the situation, and Petrov's email was sufficient for his doctoral advisor as well. However, it still needed to be clarified that no money would change hands that could prop up the Russian state. This is a core element of the sanctions. Previously, Blum's research institution would have covered Petrov's travel expenses. «When I learned that they were paying for the flight themselves,» says Blum's doctoral advisor, «I was incredibly relieved.»

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/09/01/edeea771-a21b-4f42-9576-c7ae639c473f.jpeg?width=1024)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/09/01/0bf39d30-0bfd-4f9c-92c2-504a4b572948.jpeg?width=1024)

Petrov's journey lasts several weeks, with stops in four countries. Her first stop is Philipp Blum, who picks her up from the airport. From then on, they meet every morning at 9 a.m. in his laboratory. Blum and Petrov aim to produce at least two publications, and they don't have much time.

A week after her arrival, Petrov is deep in work. With one hand on her forehead, she pores over arthropods and colorful lists on which she makes notes. Her gaze scans the specimens under the microscope. Petrov searches for differences between the specimens: a slightly shorter antenna, a smooth spot on the underside of the body, or indentations that are only visible at many times the magnification.

## She is constantly discovering new species

Blum sits at the table diagonally next to Petrov. Using needle-like instruments, he prepares more specimens and hands them to her. Every now and then, the two joke, toss Latin species names back and forth, or discuss new observations.

Petrov soon discovers a new species. «Just like that,» says Blum. For Petrov, this is nothing special anymore, but he has never described a species before. In the next few days, he will name one after his mother, as a birthday present for her.

One afternoon, the two researchers took a short walk together and bought some food at the supermarket. At the checkout, Petrov was amused by the brand name of the small vodka bottles on display: «Gorbachev,» like the last president of the Soviet Union.

## «Come on, they're just arthropods.»

It's not a given that Petrov pays for her shopping by credit card. To get one, she had to travel abroad. Russian banks have been excluded from the international SWIFT system, so her cards are worthless elsewhere. The new Iron Curtain manifests itself in many such everyday things.

To pay the publishing fees of Western journals, Petrov also had to spend a whole week in a neighboring country of Russia, telling authorities and bank employees that she lived there, presenting documents, and paying the equivalent of around one hundred euros. «I'm a very persistent person,» she says, laughing. She often enjoys finding creative solutions to such problems. Then again, it all becomes too much, and she just wishes she could work in peace.

Vera Petrov finds the sanctions «understandable, but not right.» After all, she researches biodiversity, not nuclear technology, she says. «Come on, we're comparing apples and oranges,» Blum agrees. «That's hardly going to influence the war.»

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/09/01/30914a50-cb1e-480e-abd2-887a23454dd7.jpeg?width=1024)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/09/01/56b575bf-6dbe-440c-87b2-a912bac045df.jpeg?crop=2377,3565,x123,y122)

In the early afternoon, Petrov and Blum are sitting in the break room of his research institute, chatting. Blum asks if it's true that Putin is primarily conscripting men in the country's provinces for military service. «They just grab them off the street,» Petrov says. And anyone who, like her, doesn't just watch state television, is also familiar with the horrific images from Ukraine: dead bodies, destruction, and screaming children.

Then Petrov wants to change the subject. She reports that at her institute in Russia, they don't talk about politics either, but focus on work.

Blum's doctoral advisor is familiar with this from other Russian biologists. They had cultivated this practice of staying out of sensitive matters even during Soviet times. «But that's no longer possible,» he says.

Those in favor of the sanctions share a similar view, considering them the only option as long as the invasion of Ukraine continues. «Russia's war of aggression violates international law and betrays the rules and values ​​of international cooperation on which our science is also based,» says Christoph Hilgert, spokesperson for the German Rectors' Conference.

## It is naive to invoke scientific neutrality

The militarization and indoctrination of Russian society doesn't stop at the universities – therefore, it's naive to invoke academic neutrality. «For example, Russian propaganda uses joint publications to deny its own isolation and make the West appear divided,» says Hilgert. «They like to portray it as if the sanctions aren't even being enforced.»

Critics of the sanctions, however, warn that Western isolationism primarily affects Russian researchers, who are mostly blameless for Putin's delusions. Or they point to the climate crisis. Just as data on the thawing of Siberian permafrost is now lacking, biodiversity can only truly be viewed globally. A few days before Petrov's departure, she and Blum had already discovered several new species.

Often it's quiet for an hour; only the aquarium and the whirring of the microscopes as they focus the image can be heard. Once, Petrov receives a call from a colleague in Russia who asks if she can bring him some zoological material. Obtaining permits is difficult due to the sanctions, and postal service between the West and Russia is also disrupted. She gives him the address of the institute from where she will be returning.

Sometimes Petrov considers emigrating. She says all her friends and most of her colleagues are against the war. «Many have already left Russia.» She had actually saved money to buy an apartment – ​​but now she's keeping it so she can leave at any time if the situation worsens.

## Russian science once had a good reputation

The emigration of skilled workers is considered a threat to the Russian scientific system, which for a long time enjoyed a good reputation. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union built large institutes that were also highly regarded in the West. Systemic rivalry often had a positive impact on funding. However, with the fall of communism, the decline of Russian research began, and this decline is now intensifying.

Putin invests very little in areas not relevant to the war effort. Due to sanctions, Western research material is scarce, and access to databases and networks is blocked. While Western states welcome fleeing Russian researchers, some observers say that this isolation is driving them into the arms of other autocratic regimes like China.

So far, Petrov has remained in Russia primarily because of her parents, who look after her child while she travels. Another reason is her love for her work. Although she could conduct research elsewhere, she helped build the collection at her institute. Despite having far less space and inferior equipment compared to Blum's laboratory, Petrov feels comfortable there.

## Ukrainian researchers in a dilemma

«Other researchers have it harder than I do,» says Petrov – thinking of a colleague from Kyiv whom she had actually planned to visit. He has been an expert for decades in a field dominated by Russian researchers. Ukraine tries to prevent such collaborations. But if he doesn't publish with Russians, he can't practice his profession, Petrov explains. And if he continues to collaborate with Russians, he will lose his job in Ukraine.

On the last day of her stay with Blum, Petrov packs her belongings, including some arthropods from his collection. She plans to take the animals back to Russia, compare them with specimens from her own collection, and identify them. Hundreds more will be added during her trip. She hopes she won't be checked on the flight home _._

Philipp Blum accompanies Petrow to the bus station and waves goodbye to her. _ _ She travels to three other locations in Europe to conduct research with colleagues there as well. Because of the sanctions, there are no longer any direct flights to Russia, and the circuitous journey back takes almost 24 hours. Petrov smuggles dollar and euro bills, which she is not allowed to take with her due to the sanctions, into her bra.

The cardboard boxes containing over six hundred arthropods, which Petrov had hidden in her checked luggage, passed through customs without any problems. But Petrov doesn't yet know how she'll return Blum's specimens. Perhaps she'll take the animals with her to a conference in South Korea a year later and send them to him from there. Or perhaps she'll return soon – either for a visit or as a refugee.

_Note: Petrov and Blum's names have been changed. Images: Laif_
author: Andrew Müller (text), Florian Generotzky (images)

headline: Young, angry, and fiercely determined: activists are fighting alongside the Sudanese army against the rebel militia – and the greatest humanitarian catastrophe of our time
lead: Once crushed by the Sudanese army, volunteer groups like the «Ghadiboon» are now working alongside it to win the civil war. They are on the front lines with young fighters who will never give up on the dream of democracy.
body:
# Young, angry, and fiercely determined: activists are fighting alongside the Sudanese army against the rebel militia – and the greatest humanitarian catastrophe of our time

*Once crushed by the Sudanese army, volunteer groups like the «Ghadiboon» are now working alongside it to win the civil war. They are on the front lines with young fighters who will never give up on the dream of democracy.*

**Christian Putsch (text and images), Omdurman** · International · 2025-01-04 · 1965 words · [ld.1864526](https://www.nzz.ch/international/jung-wuetend-und-wild-entschlossen-aktivisten-kaempfen-mit-der-sudanesischen-armee-gegen-die-rebellen-miliz-und-die-groesste-humanitaere-katastrophe-dieser-welt-ld.1864526)

The young man was a professional football player in a previous life; now he sits on a plastic chair on the side of the road in the city of Omdurman, with a rifle leaning against his right leg.

The same leg with which the striker once scored goals has since been pierced by shrapnel. The wound has healed just well enough for him to fight again. He sits side by side with his comrades, who are taking a short break from the war on this December day.

They drink tea while explosions shake the buildings. Smoke hangs over the rooftops of Omdurman; the front line is only four kilometers away. Soon they will set off again to the other side of the Nile, into deserted streets, past burned-out cars and bullet-riddled houses, to the cemetery where one of their comrades is buried. And soon this brief respite will end with the last drops of tea in their glasses.

Adam Daffala Dama, 29 years old, tall, with a fine beard, has had wrinkles etched into his youthful face by the war. He belongs to the «Ghadiboon,» who call themselves «the angry ones» in Arabic and form a volunteer army of around 200 democracy activists. They joined the army to support it in the civil war against the paramilitary militia Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

![Once a professional football player, now a volunteer in the army: Adam Daffala Dama, 29 years old.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/01/02/245b5240-7599-4193-8dac-8d6a43d9feaa.jpeg?width=1024)
*Once a professional football player, now a volunteer in the army: Adam Daffala Dama, 29 years old.*

There are many such volunteer groups. Here, not far from the capital Khartoum, where the White and Blue Nile rivers meet, they are often seen jogging through the dusty streets. They are being trained in record time for this conflict, which has now raged for almost 21 months and, in the shadow of Ukraine, Gaza, and Syria, has become the world's largest humanitarian catastrophe. Given their sometimes meager equipment, they are often referred to as cannon fodder. But Dama refuses to accept this. «We are patriots,» he says. «We are fighting for survival, for our people and our families.»

In essence, his campaign began long before the war: five years ago, he was still fighting against the army, to which he now belongs. As one of hundreds of thousands of demonstrators who forced the overthrow of dictator Omar al-Bashir, who had bled the country dry for decades. Dama, an activist from the very beginning, dreamed of a new Sudan, a just Sudan, a modern Sudan. Thus, even after the end of the Bashir regime, he continued to protest against the ongoing military rule, against corruption, and against a justice system that never truly functioned as one.

## narrowly escaped death

Even back then, they called themselves Ghadiboon. Dama and his friends, who had become a close-knit community fighting for their lives. Osman and Mudathir, two of his closest comrades, had already lost their lives, Dama recounts. On June 6, 2019, when the army crushed the protests against the new military rulers. «I, too, only narrowly escaped,» he says.

Dama, who as a promising professional earned the equivalent of 400 Swiss francs a month, left the football field behind, as well as his family plans, to fight for democracy. Both forearms bear the scars of gunshot wounds inflicted by Sudanese security forces long before the outbreak of this war – his current allies.

![«The Angry Ones» were already fighting during the 2019 revolution.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/01/02/34dd5b99-f134-4b76-a16f-04071ed8dea4.jpeg?width=1024)
*«The Angry Ones» were already fighting during the 2019 revolution.* (Private)

## First enemy, then friend

How is it possible that he is now fighting for the army that was once his enemy? Why did he switch sides?

Dama sips his tea, pauses for a moment, and then presents his version of events: The 2019 massacre, in which his friends also lost their lives, was perpetrated primarily by RSF fighters, not members of the army, he says. At the time, they were supposedly on the same side. Bashir himself had established the militia as a security force, out of fear of an army coup.

In April 2019, security forces and militias finally overthrew the dictator together. The transitional government suffered the same fate two years later. From then on, Sudan's army chief, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the RSF leader, Mohamed Hamdan «Hemeti» Dagalo, shared power. But this fragile balance, too, was short-lived: when the militias refused to integrate into the armed forces in April 2023, it collapsed. The war began. A country was thrown into disarray. And with it, the perceptions of the enemy.

In the first few weeks, Dama tried to help as a civilian. The thousands of resistance committees that had formed decentrally during the revolution became «emergency centers» where citizens organized aid, cared for the wounded, and distributed food. They have just been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, because 25 million Sudanese – every second citizen – are threatened by hunger.

Dama initially joined one of these civic groups. He risked his life delivering medical supplies. When videos circulated on social media showing RSF fighters humiliating captured soldiers crawling on the ground, he decided to take up arms. And with him, thousands followed the army's call to the hastily set up camps. Dama received only two months of training before going to war.

The RSF have become his enemy. Refugees from areas controlled by the militia also report their murders, rapes, and brazen looting. Even corpses have been exhumed, they say, in search of gold fillings in their teeth.

The extent of the violence was also evident here in Omdurman four days before the encounter with Dama, when the RSF fired dozens of artillery shells into a residential area. A bus was hit, and at least 17 civilians were killed. Dozens of civilians are also reported to have been killed in army airstrikes in the Darfur region, which is largely controlled by the RSF.

## War of Propaganda

The West regards the Sudanese generals, who see themselves as representatives of a legitimate institution, with a similar degree of mistrust as it regards the RSF war criminals. This is because the generals are blocking American mediation attempts. Moreover, they receive support from Iran and Russia. In addition, the Muslim Brotherhood is gaining increasing influence. And wasn't it the army that controlled and oppressed Sudan for decades, both economically and politically?

«Even back then, the security apparatus was far more complex than it was perceived abroad,» says Adam Daffala Dama, who has also prepared an answer to this. His anger was directed less at the army than at the General Intelligence Service. The secret service was responsible for the suppression of regime opponents at the time. «There were soldiers sitting next to us who supported us in our struggle.»

It's hard to say how freely Dama can speak. Just a few meters away sits a high-ranking soldier, seemingly lost in thought as he stares at his cell phone. Even though the army has been allowing a few journalists back into its areas in the northeast and center of the country for several months, it is the army that tries to control the narrative by monitoring and approving interviews—including the one with Dama. The RSF militia, financed by gold smuggling and reportedly hired by a Canadian PR firm, ignored a request from the «NZZ am Sonntag» for an investigation in its territories.

On both sides, this war is also a propaganda exercise. A planned interview with a family, who are part of the army's civilian program but also have relatives on the RSF side, is not permitted. Instead, captured mercenaries from Chad and South Sudan are offered as interview partners.

«Right now we are fighting for our country, for peace, for stability,» Dama says, a little too quietly to sound emphatic. His Facebook profile, however, suggests that he voluntarily joined the army. Where Dama once documented his protests against Bashir, he now posts triumphant pictures from the front.

«When the war is over, we will see what differences we have with the intelligence service and the army,» he says. And: He has «confidence» that after a victory over the RSF, the army will hand over power to civilians within «two to three» years, even though he can’t think of any politician he would like to see at the head of state.

## In the hail of bullets

The teacup is empty, Dama has to leave. Away from his visions for the country, back to the front. He and the Ghadiboon climb into a pickup truck and drive off. The first stop is a cemetery in the middle of nowhere, where Taha has been buried since September 29th. Together they had once protested against the dictatorship and taken up arms after the war began. With Taha, they had also ridden motorcycles to the town of Bahri, where they were ambushed by RSF snipers.

Some Ghadiboon managed to turn back in the hail of bullets. Taha didn't. For days his body rotted in the road; finally, they were able to recover and bury him. «He had no chance,» says Dama, running his hand over the stones piled on his friend's grave. Taha was the sixth Ghadiboon he had buried.

What must be going through the mind of a man who sees his friends die and continues to fight – as a foot soldier, as a helper to those who once fought him? Does Dama believe what he's saying? Or is he trying to twist the horrific reality to suit his own purposes, not only for the army interviewer, but also for himself?

The operation also involved soldiers who remained in armored vehicles. Dama, however, doesn't see this as unequal treatment. «The soldiers don't always stay in bulletproof vehicles,» he says. Why didn't any of them wear bulletproof vests? «That was our decision; we feel more mobile without them.» And are two months of training sufficient for such an operation? «We already had over a year of combat experience.»

![After 20 months of war, not much remains of the Sudanese city of Bahri.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/01/02/84d9a6f7-5790-46e4-b4eb-f5b78be579af.jpeg?width=1024)
*After 20 months of war, not much remains of the Sudanese city of Bahri.*

Onward they go, past plumes of smoke toward the front line in Bahri. Shortly before the Al-Halfaya Bridge, soldiers in off-road vehicles approach them. They wave the Sudanese flag and fire celebratory shots into the air to mark their recent successes. Soon, however, an ominous silence descends once more. The area is considered «liberated» from the RSF in army parlance, but the threat of sniper attacks remains.

A picture of destruction unfolds, as is evident everywhere in Sudan. Survival seems impossible in this apocalypse. Estimates range up to 150,000 dead and 14 million displaced. And there is no end in sight. Dama and the others may dream of a united Sudan, but the country is fracturing into numerous power centers, many of them ethnically defined, that extend beyond the command structure of RSF and the army. At least Darfur in the west of the country—a region larger than Germany—is likely to remain in RSF hands for a long time. «When we're finished here, we'll continue in Darfur,» says one of Dama's comrades. According to many observers, the Libyan scenario is more probable: the disintegration of the country.

One of the soldiers in the convoy now wants to take a detour. This story should end on a hopeful note, in a side street, at the home of an old woman with henna-red hair and deep wrinkles in her face: Bahir Kambal. Here she survives in the house where she was born. Here she also gave birth to and raised her son – fleeing is out of the question for her. Many say, not without pride, that older Sudanese people are particularly stubborn. Kambal is living proof.

She refused to leave when the RSF occupied her neighborhood just days after the war began. She hasn't left her house in 20 months. Sometimes the few remaining neighbors brought her soup, sometimes relatives sent money from abroad. «I didn't sleep a wink at night,» she says, «I stayed awake, afraid of looters.» Even after she was flogged by the militias, she didn't consider fleeing.

![Samira Bashir Kambal will stay, come what may.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/01/02/2144138e-ba41-41ae-ba5c-d4bc5c478908.jpeg?width=1024)
*Samira Bashir Kambal will stay, come what may.*

Adam Daffala Dama, the former professional footballer, sits at the edge of the courtyard, listening to the old woman's stories. His gaze is empty, but without anger. He knows what it feels like to lose one's homeland. Of his old life, his old dreams, little more than a faded jersey of his club remains. It lies in a drawer at the Ghadiboon accommodation in Omdurman. He hasn't worn it in a long time. But he keeps it.
author: Christian Putsch (text and images), Omdurman

headline: Unique as an athlete and as a person – Mikaela Shiffrin breaks all boundaries with her 100th World Cup victory
lead: The American ski racer achieved a historic milestone in the Sestriere slalom, setting new standards. But Mikaela Shiffrin is far more than just an athlete. A chronicle of many encounters off the slopes.
body:
# Unique as an athlete and as a person – Mikaela Shiffrin breaks all boundaries with her 100th World Cup victory

*The American ski racer achieved a historic milestone in the Sestriere slalom, setting new standards. But Mikaela Shiffrin is far more than just an athlete. A chronicle of many encounters off the slopes.*

**Remo Geisser** · Sport · 2025-02-23 · 1751 words · [ld.1860022](https://www.nzz.ch/sport/ski/ski-phaenomen-mikaela-shiffrin-100-siege-und-persoenliche-einblicke-ld.1860022)

![«I am not a prodigy»: Mikaela Shiffrin in Are in 2012, where she won her first World Cup race at the age of 17.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/11/29/4ea12d47-292d-4cc1-848b-3d1b091a039e.jpeg?width=1024)
*«I am not a prodigy»: Mikaela Shiffrin in Are in 2012, where she won her first World Cup race at the age of 17.* (Jonathan Nacktstrand / AFP)

Mikaela Shiffrin has now amassed 100 victories in the Ski World Cup, having won the slalom in Sestriere on Sunday. The record of 86 wins held by Sweden's Ingemar Stenmark, which stood for 34 years, almost seems ordinary in comparison.

Shiffrin is the best female ski racer ever to hurtle down the icy slopes of the World Cup, but that's not what this text is about. I've had the privilege, over twelve years and in countless encounters, of witnessing how this American stands out from the rest as a person and personality, just as much as she does as an outstanding athlete. That's what makes her unique.

It's late November 2012 in Beaver Creek. Beat Feuz is in the hospital with a damaged knee, and the Swiss ski crisis is beginning. It's a welcome relief to be invited to a dinner by a pasta company. The hostess is Mikaela Shiffrin, who lives down in the valley, then 17 years old with only one podium finish to her name. She stands at the entrance to the ballroom in an evening gown, flanked by her brother Taylor in a tuxedo, and shakes hands with each guest, saying, «Nice to meet you.»

Before the main course, Shiffrin stands in the middle of the room and talks about herself, her experiences, her goals. I'm astonished. There stands a teenager, the tables are full of older men, journalists with hundreds of World Cup races under their belts, and Shiffrin speaks completely unfazed, without hesitation or faltering. She's in this role just as she was back then on the slopes: far ahead of her age.

Three weeks later, she won her first World Cup race; in February 2013, Shiffrin became World Champion, and a year later, Olympic Champion. She was the outstanding slalom skier, captivating audiences with her effortless grace. At 18, Shiffrin had already won nine World Cup races, two season slalom titles, and the two most important global championships. That's more than many others achieve in an entire career. She was called a prodigy, the Mozart of skiing.

## When Shiffrin executes a perfect run, she feels like she's dancing

That was a topic when we first sat down for an interview in October 2013. She chatted away nonstop, laughed out loud at some of the questions, and gave such thoughtful and nuanced answers as if I had sent her the list of questions days in advance so she could prepare.

Over the years, it became clear that Shiffrin was always like that. Even when, as at the 2022 Winter Games, she spoke into the microphones with tears in her eyes after a string of disappointments, it sounded as if she had analyzed every point the night before and clearly formulated her thoughts on it.

We talked in 2014 about Mozart, whom she knew from classical concerts she had attended with her father. Shiffrin described how she puts on headphones when she visualizes a slalom course; the music then sets the rhythm of her mental run. And when she manages a perfect run on the slope, it actually feels like dancing. But no: «I'm not a prodigy.» What she has achieved is the product of a lot of hard work and support.

A few years later, I was sitting with her mother on a bench in the sun in Austria, talking about our children and parenthood. Eileen Shiffrin told me how she fostered her children's natural love of sports. Her son Taylor wanted to play soccer but didn't make the school team, so she bought small goals and spent hours playing with her children during the summer holidays.

Taylor also raced skis, and his little sister followed in his footsteps. She did it with such dedication that she would even ski lap after lap in the rain, completely focused. Their mother had the idea of ​​buying her a unicycle to improve her balance, and later she gave her juggling balls. And so Mikaela Shiffrin cruised around the neighborhood on her unicycle, juggling balls. «The neighbors must have thought we were completely crazy,» said Eileen.

The conversation revolves around the question of why outstanding athletes often work closely with their parents, such as Marcel Hirscher, Lara Gut-Behrami, and Mikaela Shiffrin, who always shared a room with her mother when traveling for World Cup events. It's about a deep trust, Eileen said. «Do you think Lara needs her father? Pauli is there for her because the two of them have a great relationship. The same is true for Marcel Hirscher and his father.»

After her first World Championship victory, the then 17-year-old Mikaela Shiffrin said at the press conference: «I need my mom.» The American Ski Federation refused to acknowledge this for a long time, and the family had to pay all travel and hotel expenses out of their own pockets. This reportedly cost half a million dollars in total.

Later, the mother was accepted as part of the small Shiffrin team within the federation. With her keen eye, she immediately recognized her daughter's slightest weaknesses. And Eileen sometimes played the role of the merciless critic. Many coaches didn't dare to address mistakes bluntly, she says. «I can do that because our relationship can withstand it.»

For years, Eileen Shiffrin was part of a success machine that seemed unstoppable in the skiing world. As Mikaela had already said in that 2014 interview, the engine was hard work, hard work, hard work. Her father, Jeff, once said that his daughter never skied simply for fun; every single turn involved a task – even the few meters from the lift to the starting gate.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 94c15a6eadd659eb977086455e9777e2]

## «This is Emma, ​​she has leukemia.»

But the athlete never isolated herself in this professional world, and she understood early on that while sport is important, there are other things in life. More important things. We talked about this in Méribel in 2015; Shiffrin had just won the slalom discipline title for the third time in a row. A week earlier in Åre, she had met Emma Lundell again, whom she had met in 2012 during her first victory. Lundell was a little girl back then who approached Shiffrin at the end of an autograph session. The child's mother said, «This is Emma; she has leukemia.»

That's when she, Shiffrin, started to cry, the ski racer recounted in 2015. She was tired and just wanted to go to bed. «And the little girl waited the whole time, just to be able to shake the winner's hand.» In January 2015, two young American skiers also died in an avalanche; one of them had gone to school with Shiffrin. All of this showed her how fleeting happiness can be.

In 2019, Shiffrin became world champion in slalom for the fourth time in Åre. At the press conference, she brought Emma Lundell onto the stage. No journalist had asked her about it, but it was important to her: «Emma, ​​you are my angel, my inspiration.» Lundell, then 17, had beaten cancer and become a competitive cross-country skier herself.

A year later, tragedy struck Shiffrin as well. Her father fell from the roof of their house while shoveling snow. The athlete had just won a race in Bansko when she received the news. She traveled home with her mother and lay down next to her father in the hospital bed. He died in her arms. The loss devastated her; it took Shiffrin almost two years to recover, both personally and athletically.

In an interview just over a year ago, she spoke about loss and grief, about the trauma she suffered, and about the mental emptiness it all triggered. In 2022, she began seeing a clinical psychologist. She said her primary goal wasn't to regain her full athletic performance. «We all have to learn when work takes priority, but also when life and love should be at the center,» she said. Shiffrin wanted to find her balance with the help of a professional.

The following winter, she won 14 races, surpassing Stenmark's record. She achieved this in Åre, Stenmark's hometown and the place where she first won, where she met Emma Lundell. It's fascinating how fate keeps intervening in this unusual career. Åre became a kind of emotional center for Shiffrin. Soon she'll return there with her 100th victory under her belt. The next race Shiffrin will enter is in Åre in just over two weeks.

The red carpet had already been rolled out in her homeland at the end of November for her 100th victory: on the East Coast of the USA, where she had lived since the age of eight and laid the foundation for all her successes on icy slopes. A triumph there would have had a special radiance. Shiffrin was leading in Killington after the first run of the giant slalom, but she crashed in the final and suffered a deep stab wound to her abdomen.

It took Shiffrin two months before she could return to the slopes. Impaling herself on her own ski pole triggered a trauma that still haunts her in giant slalom. On Saturday in Sestriere, Shiffrin missed qualifying for the second run.

## It has long since become a brand

Ultimately, Killington's injury was perhaps the decisive dramatic twist that transformed what seemed like an effortless string of victories into an existential struggle. This is likely to bring Shiffrin even more attention, especially back home, than she already enjoys. She already mentioned in our first extended conversation that she wants to establish herself as a brand. That's why she sometimes forgoes a summer vacation if it means, for example, a photoshoot with a major magazine.

The now 29-year-old therefore makes consistent use of social media. She posts pictures from the ski circuit, of her love for Norwegian ski racer Aleksander Kilde, of glamorous appearances, or of the Northern Lights in Levi.

But even on these platforms, she doesn't just remain a figurehead. She has campaigned for stricter gun laws in the US, and above all, she has shared her grieving process after her father's death with her followers. Many people who had also suffered tragedies thanked her for it. They told their own stories and wrote that, thanks to the athlete, they no longer felt alone in their grief.

Shiffrin seems to have found the perfect balance between work and life. This is evident in the way she overcame her injury and secured her 100th victory. With this achievement, a significant milestone has been reached, allowing the athlete to look to the future without any pressure. Where will the counter stand when she eventually retires? At 110? At 120? It will be a mark for the ages.
author: Remo Geisser

teaserImage.caption: The American ski racer achieved a historic milestone in the Sestriere slalom, setting new standards. But Mikaela Shiffrin is far more than just an athlete. A chronicle of many encounters off the slopes.

headline: Not keen on military service? Europe's defense has a recruitment problem. The big picture.
lead: European countries are debating the reintroduction of conscription. Where does it apply? Where doesn't it? And what do Europe's youth think?
body:
# Not keen on military service? Europe's defense has a recruitment problem. The big picture.

*European countries are debating the reintroduction of conscription. Where does it apply? Where doesn't it? And what do Europe's youth think?*

**Julia Monn** · International · 2025-04-02 · 1345 words · [ld.1876768](https://www.nzz.ch/international/wehrpflicht-in-europa-zahlen-fakten-und-aktuelle-umfragen-im-ueberblick-ld.1876768)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/01/b9957397-acaf-4337-9ada-cf62e5c3692b.png?width=1024)
**

Europe plans to prepare for a more uncertain world by investing billions in new tanks, aircraft, and missile defense systems. But while the debate rages over where all this money will come from, the next, and potentially even bigger, problem is already emerging: Who will operate all this equipment? There is a shortage of soldiers, and a significant one at that, say experts, including Cameron Abadi in an interview with the NZZ.

## How many soldiers does Europe have, and where is military service compulsory?

If war were to break out today, the more than thirty countries of Europe could together mobilize just under two million active soldiers. That is only slightly more than the USA alone can provide. This refers to professional soldiers who would be ready for immediate deployment. Additional forces, i.e., reservists, would first have to be mobilized and equipped.

> [embed: datawrapper chart ]

It is striking that among the ten countries with the most active soldiers, only Turkey and Greece rely on conscription. Both countries are also using military means to wage their dispute over islands and resources in the eastern Mediterranean.

Otherwise, conscription is maintained primarily in countries bordering Russia—such as those in Scandinavia and the Baltic states—or in the neutral states of Switzerland and Austria. In the Balkans , Croatia and Serbia are reintroducing conscription this year. Furthermore, Denmark, as the second European country after Norway, is extending compulsory military service to women.

However, the length of service, the age at which soldiers are drafted, and whether there are alternatives such as civilian service are regulated differently everywhere.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 345456dee30e23ccd832188381b3195b]

Here are three examples: In Turkey, men between the ages of 20 and 41 are required to perform 6 to 12 months of military service. However, it is possible to pay a fee to be exempt from this service . Furthermore, those who are studying or work in certain professions in research, the arts, or elite sports are allowed to postpone their service.

Finland has a different system. Men aged 18 and over complete 5.5 to 12 months of military, border guard, or civilian service. After that, they belong to the reserves and can be called up in an emergency until the age of 50, or until the age of 60 for non-commissioned officers or officers.

Switzerland also pursues its own approach with its militia system. Every Swiss citizen is obligated to perform military service or civilian service. The majority complete their service over several years following a short basic training course, with refresher courses. Military service lasts at least 245 days, civilian service 368 days. Service is generally completed between the ages of 18 and 30. Afterward, one belongs to the reserves; the length of service depends on rank.

## How have troop strengths changed?

Despite different models, European countries with conscription have one thing in common: they have thousands of soldiers in reserve who must be ready for deployment in case of emergency.

> [embed: datawrapper chart ]

Over the past decade, many countries have significantly reduced their armed forces – and not only in countries with conscription. Large all-volunteer armies like those of Great Britain, France, and Italy also saw substantial personnel reductions between 2015 and 2025. In Germany and Spain, troop strength increased only minimally. And the situation is no better with reserves: even in large NATO countries, they remain manageable, often numbering only a few tens of thousands of soldiers.

> [embed: datawrapper chart ]

The abolition of conscription marked the beginning of the decline in army numbers. Great Britain started the process in 1960, followed by France in 1997, Spain in 2001, and Italy in 2005. Germany was the last to take this step, suspending conscription there only in 2011.

The restructuring of the armed forces was the result of shifts in security and socio-political contexts. With the end of the Cold War, traditional national defense and conventional warfare lost importance. They were replaced by deployments abroad in crisis regions and disaster relief. Full-time soldiers were considered better suited for these tasks than conscripts.

Governments and experts assumed that professional armies were not only more efficient in handling increasingly complex weapons systems, but also cheaper than massive mass armies. This was because the latter were expensive not only in terms of recruitment, but also in terms of housing, equipment, and training. At the same time, the willingness to perform military service declined in many societies. Military service was considered outdated, whether for pacifist reasons or because of a lack of financial and social incentives.

The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine has changed the security landscape since 2022. Yet only one large all-volunteer army has responded: Poland . Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine alone, its armed forces have grown by approximately 50,000 soldiers and are set to expand further. While the Polish government does not intend to reinstate conscription, it is planning voluntary military training for all adult men to ensure a broader troop pool in case of emergency.

## What does the population think about a reintroduction?

Poland's continued reliance on voluntary military service, despite its direct proximity to the war in Ukraine, is drawing criticism within the country itself. Conservative politicians and high-ranking military officials are calling for a return to conscription. They believe the population supports them. According to recent polls, 55 percent of the population favors the reintroduction of military service.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc65fa8b5]

However, there is a clear difference between the generations: While the 18- to 29-year-olds – i.e., potential recruits – are mostly against conscription, those over 30 are clearly in favor of it.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc6410660]

Even the idea of ​​voluntary military training divides the generations in Poland. While a majority of the population supports it, many under 30 reject the idea. Nevertheless, Poland's compromise between volunteering and conscription is likely to be closely watched in Western European capitals. From Paris to Berlin to Madrid, the question of mandatory service is once again resurfacing in public debate.

However, only in France and Germany is there currently a clear majority of the population in favor of reintroducing compulsory military service. The situation is different in Italy, Great Britain, and Spain, where a majority opposes its reintroduction. This is shown by a survey conducted in March by the YouGov polling institute for these countries.

> [embed: datawrapper chart ]

The results also reflect other national surveys. However, as in Poland, it shows that even in France and Germany, young people have little support for compulsory military service. It is the 35- to 40-year-olds who overwhelmingly favor it.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) ff42fc9dffbfb98a85c0a482801befae]

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) ff42fc9dffbfb98a85c0a48280674f61]

In Italy and Spain, even among older generations, there is a lack of clear support for conscription. However, support is lowest among potential recruits, where only about a third would be in favor of mandatory service.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc60fbbd9]

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc641a983]

The situation is quite different in Switzerland, where conscription is still in place. According to the latest study by the army, only 31 percent of those surveyed want to abolish the system. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, the figure is higher at 39 percent – ​​but this represents a significant decline: in 2023, almost half of young people were in favor of ending conscription.

## How high is the willingness to fight in an emergency?

While the debate about military service is often conducted theoretically, in a real emergency a completely different question comes to the fore: Who would actually be willing to fight for their country in a crisis?

A year ago, a survey in Great Britain caused a stir in this context. It showed that not only do many Britons oppose conscription; around a third of those under 40 even stated that they would refuse military service if their country were threatened with invasion.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc65962d1]

The willingness to fight for one's country in a crisis is, in recent times, about as moderate among the British as in other major European countries. According to a Gallup poll conducted every ten years, in 2024 less than half of respondents in most European countries would take up arms to defend their country in a crisis.

In Great Britain and Spain, around a third of the population would still fight. In Germany and Austria, this figure drops to 20 percent. Italy brings up the rear: only 14 percent of the population would be prepared to defend the country in a crisis. Compared to the 2014 survey, this willingness has declined even further.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 50f5f9f48c3ba32070a3a08cc63f89f2]

The situation is different in Finland. Ten years ago, two-thirds of Finns declared their willingness to fight for their country in a crisis – even though Russia had not yet attacked Ukraine and Finland was not yet a NATO member. Both of these things have changed since then.
author: Julia Monn

headline: «Asians are no longer intimidated by the arrogance of Europeans.»
lead: Political scientist Kishore Mahbubani says the West is overwhelmed. The Americans are clinging to the illusion that they can still prevent China's rise. And the EU is completely disoriented. A discussion about the state of the world.
body:
# «Asians are no longer intimidated by the arrogance of Europeans.»

*Political scientist Kishore Mahbubani says the West is overwhelmed. The Americans are clinging to the illusion that they can still prevent China's rise. And the EU is completely disoriented. A discussion about the state of the world.*

**Katrin Büchenbacher, Benedict Neff (text), Maurice Haas (images)** · International · 2025-04-16 · 2856 words · [ld.1879569](https://www.nzz.ch/international/kishore-mahbubani-warnt-europa-china-zu-verprellen-sei-gefaehrlich-ld.1879569)

![Kishore Mahbubani believes the West shares some responsibility for the war in Ukraine.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/15/7d8471a2-3bd9-4649-b7cb-22d6b5a4c222.jpeg?width=1024)
*Kishore Mahbubani believes the West shares some responsibility for the war in Ukraine.*

He was a UN ambassador, president of the Security Council, dean of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy – ​​and thinks like a philosopher. Kishore Mahbubani is one of Asia's most distinguished geopolitical intellectuals. He was born in India in 1948; his family later emigrated to Singapore. Mahbubani studied philosophy and, after graduating, began his diplomatic career. For over a decade, he served as Singapore's ambassador to the UN in New York.

In the interview, he challenges Europe. He speaks of a changing world order – and of the fact that the West still doesn't understand what's really going on. The greatest threat to Europe is not China, but its own self-righteousness.

**Mr. Mahbubani, the trade war between the US and China has escalated rapidly. Both sides are signaling maximum force. Who will back down first – Trump or Xi?**

The question is, who is better able to endure pain in the long run? I suspect it's the Chinese. The government in Beijing doesn't have to face any elections. The Republican Party, on the other hand, faces midterm elections in two years. And the worst-case scenario for Donald Trump is if the Republicans lose in 2026. This situation weakens Trump's position.

**So you consider democracy a disadvantage in a trade war?**

Not only that. China is a huge country and largely self-sufficient in many areas. That's why it can withstand enormous pressure.

**At the same time, China's government is also under pressure because the economy is already in crisis.**

When it comes to China's economy, the West thinks in terms of one, two, or three years. The Chinese, on the other hand, think in terms of decades. If we had conducted this interview ten years ago and I had said, «Give China another ten years, and it will seriously compete with Mercedes, BMW, or Toyota»—you would have laughed at me. And what happened?

**Electric cars from China have become so good that even the EU has imposed import tariffs on them to protect European car companies. Are you suggesting that China's economy is only facing temporary difficulties?**

Yes. Currently, the mood among Chinese entrepreneurs and consumers is subdued. But that can change quickly. Whether it's solar panels, wind turbines, battery technologies, electric vehicles, or robotics: China invests more in future-oriented industries than any other leading economy. The fruits of these investments will come.

**When historians look back on this moment in history in the future, will they mark Trump as a turning point in the decline of the West and the rise of Asia?**

The rise of Asia and the relative decline of the West are not short-term phenomena. They are driven by major historical forces. We are returning to the normality of world history. The last two hundred years of Western dominance appear to the West as a matter of course. In reality, they were the exception. For almost two millennia – from the year 1 until around 1800 – China and India were consistently the two largest economies in the world. The West then gained ground with the Enlightenment, the Renaissance, and the Industrial Revolution. But it was always only a matter of time before Asia caught up – and that is precisely what is happening now.

**When will Asia overtake the West?**

By 2050, China and India could once again be the world's number one and two economies. And this will happen regardless of whether Trump or Biden is in the White House. These tectonic shifts are like an approaching wave: unstoppable.

**You speak of a «relative loss of importance» of the West. What exactly do you mean by that?**

Relatively speaking, because Western countries can also be successful in the Asian century, provided they understand that geopolitical conditions are changing and adapt accordingly. So far, the record is sobering. America and the European Union are geopolitically overwhelmed in different ways. America is clinging to the illusion that it can still prevent China's rise. The European Union seems genuinely disoriented. The continent needs a complete strategic reboot.

**What leads you to that conclusion?**

Europe baffles me. The most obvious example is the war in Ukraine: it could entirely have been avoided, from the very beginning. Europe simply had to seriously address Russia's deep-seated security interests. When NATO declared in 2008 that Ukraine should join the defense alliance, it was an enormous provocation for Russia. Why do they do such a thing? It demonstrates a complete lack of common sense. In October 2022, I spoke with Henry Kissinger, and he told me he could hardly comprehend what had happened to Europe. A hundred years ago, Europe ruled the world—today, it isn't even capable of governing itself.

**They imply that Europe provoked this war.**

If you go into a bear's den and poke it in the eyes, you shouldn't be surprised if it strikes back. But the European stands there astonished and asks: Why did the bear hurt me?

**From a European perspective, Russia is the aggressor.**

This shows how naive Europe has become. Anyone who still doesn't recognize that the West bears some responsibility for this chaos is deluding themselves. Of course, the Russian invasion of Ukraine is illegal, a clear violation of international law. But when the West imposed sanctions on Russia, they were supported by only about 15 percent of the world's population. 85 percent didn't. This demonstrates how isolated and out of touch the European perspective is.

**How should Europe react when confronted with a country like Russia that pursues imperialist goals and attacks neighboring countries?**

I say this as a friend of Europe: Europe should ask itself how to live with difficult neighbors. Why don't you try to understand that Russia sees the world completely differently? It's different in Asia. We are extremely diverse, but we get along – precisely because we know how different we are. We don't expect others to become like us. Europe, on the other hand, has this idealistic zeal that everyone should become like them.

**You're turning a war into a diversity debate. Ukraine didn't want to change Russia, it simply wanted independence.**

I stand by my point: the real question is this: Can you handle diversity – in a world where you are a minority? Europeans now make up only 6 to 7 percent of the world's population. And even if you count the entire Western world, it's barely more than 12 percent. 88 percent live outside the West – and it is precisely these 88 percent who are now beginning to wake up. The question is: Do you want to adapt to this new world – or do you really expect it to adapt to you?

**The Asian countries get along far less well with each other than you suggest.**

We are not at war.

**China has had border disputes with India for years. In the South China Sea, China claims territories that near-neighboring states also claim. There are also tensions with Japan and South Korea.**

You mentioned India: Do you know who India's most important trading partner is? It's China. Of course, there are tensions, yes – but they manage, they find solutions, they maintain perfectly normal economic relations. When will Europe resume normal trade relations with Russia?

**They accuse Europeans of being naive. What do you see as the cause?**

Europe boasts excellent universities and renowned think tanks – and yet it seems stuck in a 19th- and 20th-century way of thinking. This isn't just about colonial patterns of thought, but about a deeply ingrained sense of superiority. And many Europeans still carry this arrogance with them today.

**Do you experience this feeling of superiority primarily in political action or also in everyday life?**

There too, but the crucial point is: Asians are no longer intimidated by this. It used to be different. In my memoirs, I describe growing up in a British colony—I was born in 1948, and Singapore remained under British rule until 1963. For the first fifteen years of my life, I genuinely believed that as an Asian with brown skin, I was inferior to the white man—that he was more intelligent, more capable, simply better. For me, that was the natural order of things. It took me a long time to realize: That's not true.

**When did you begin to question this worldview?**

This was a slow process – fueled by the rise of Asia. Let me give you a simple figure to illustrate how much the world has changed: in 1980, the EU's gross domestic product was ten times that of China. Today, they are roughly equal. And by 2050, the EU will be only half the size of China. So, if you shrink from ten times to half the size – and yet continue to talk down to China – the problem isn't with China, it's with yourself.

**Do you think history could reverse itself – and Asians could feel superior in the future?**

No, I don't think so. But they will no longer feel inferior either. Europeans often speak condescendingly about the rest of the world—without realizing it. They make demands, impose sanctions, and take it upon themselves to judge others. But that old power of interpretation is gone.

![The relative decline in the West's importance is not a short-term phenomenon, says political scientist Kishore Mahbubani.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/15/a0264541-89cc-4699-9116-6503d9582fcd.jpeg?width=1024)
*The relative decline in the West's importance is not a short-term phenomenon, says political scientist Kishore Mahbubani.*

**If you are right, and China becomes the largest economy and India the second largest by 2050: What would this mean for the world?**

When a major power rises, the question arises: Do you want to provoke it – or work with it? Understanding China doesn't mean submitting to it. The Vietnamese have a clever saying for this: Whoever wants to lead Vietnam must simultaneously be able to stand up to China – and get along with China. This requires geopolitical skill and strategic finesse. And that, I fear, is precisely what Europe has lost.

**They advise Europe to play a more independent role – including vis-à-vis the United States. Do you believe that this is truly in Europe's interest? Or does it ultimately serve primarily China?**

Experienced European statesmen once said: States have neither lasting friends nor lasting enemies – they only have lasting interests. During the Cold War, the interests of Europe and the USA coincided because they faced a common adversary: ​​the Soviet Union. But in twenty or thirty years, Europe's greatest challenge will no longer come from Russia.

**But rather?**

Africa's demographic development is Europe's biggest future issue. In 1950, Europe had twice as many inhabitants as Africa. Today, Africa's population is two and a half times that of Europe. By 2100, it will be ten times larger. If Africa doesn't develop, its people will migrate to Europe. And we are already seeing the political consequences of a few thousand refugees: far-right parties are gaining strength, the AfD is becoming increasingly influential, and the extreme right is in power in Italy. Therefore, Europe's strategic goal should be to enable as much economic development as possible in Africa. China is currently investing the most in Africa. It's understandable that the US wants to contain China. But why should it be in Europe's interest to simply follow suit?

**China's close ties to Russia do not exactly inspire confidence in Europe. Why doesn't China use its influence on Russia to persuade Putin to stop his war?**

The Chinese are intelligent and strategically astute. China doesn't want to dominate the world – governing its own country is challenge enough. So why would China voluntarily entangle itself in conflicts abroad? In the 15th century, the Chinese fleet was far superior to the Spanish and Portuguese. China could have conquered the world back then. But it didn't, because that's not part of its cultural DNA.

**China is indeed deeply involved in the war in Ukraine as a supplier of war-related goods to Russia. The country is massively rearming. Chinese companies operate a global port network with over a hundred locations – on almost every continent. And with the Belt and Road Initiative, China has a presence in numerous countries. All with peaceful intentions?**

China's global influence will continue to grow. That's a reality. But will China therefore conquer other countries? Certainly not. Although it would be capable of doing so. Western great-power thinking is alien to China. China doesn't behave like the United States. Imagine if China behaved like Donald Trump – and simply demanded: Give us back Greenland.

**What about Taiwan? China's intention to annex the country sooner or later is obvious.**

The best way to secure peace in Taiwan is quite simple: don't change the status quo. As long as Taiwan doesn't declare independence, there will be no war. It's that simple. Those who want to change this status quo are the troublemakers. For example, the visit of influential US politician Nancy Pelosi to Taiwan in 2022 was completely unnecessary. The US officially adheres to the policy that Taiwan belongs to China, the so-called One-China policy. Then they should act accordingly.

**Many people in the West view China through the same lens they once used to view the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union was clearly expansionist; that was part of its communist ideology. You, on the other hand, believe that China has completely abandoned this goal—why are you so certain of that?**

Let me ask a very simple question: When Xi Jinping goes to bed at night, do you seriously believe he dreams of Marx and Lenin? Chinese civilization has existed for five thousand years. And what did Chinese emperors dream of for centuries? Stability and prosperity for their civilization. Xi Jinping wants to make Chinese civilization great again. And if you think he wants to make communism great again, then you've clearly read too much American propaganda.

**Why are all party documents still full of Marxist-Leninist vocabulary? Is it just folklore?**

In geopolitics, one must learn a crucial lesson: Don't take things literally—take them seriously. Try to understand people's thinking. You have to delve deeper, into their psyche, into their history. I encourage Europeans: Learn! Strive to improve! Even if China were truly terrible, a genuine threat to its neighbors, the question remains: What European interests are being served today by antagonizing China? That's what I'd like to understand.

**China is simultaneously a partner, competitor, and systemic rival for Europe – democracy on the one hand, autocracy on the other. The threat lies in the fact that an authoritarian regime is in power in China, and that this regime is gaining influence worldwide.**

Are you seriously telling me that it is Europe's job as a democracy to export democracy?

**It's not about exporting – it's about preserving democracy.**

Nobody will take your democracy away from you – certainly not the Chinese.

******What will China's political system look like in 2050? Do you see any trends towards democracy?**

The idea that Europe can teach China democracy – anyone who truly believes that is utterly naive. Do you seriously think Europe can teach China anything? Ultimately, everything lies in the hands of the Chinese people. A country's cultural DNA doesn't change overnight. If China has a bad ruler, it loses its Mandate of Heaven. If it has a good ruler, the people are content. That's how it's been for millennia – and that's how it will continue. And I urge you on one point: never underestimate the complexity of Chinese thought. In many ways, it's more nuanced and sophisticated than European thought – which often gets stuck in black-and-white categories: democracy or autocracy, friend or foe.

**Give an example.**

You only have to look at what China is doing. When China launched the Belt and Road Initiative, the US started a global counter-campaign. They urged countries not to participate. 193 countries had the choice – 150 countries joined. Isn't that a remarkable achievement by the Chinese? Do you think it just happened by chance – or perhaps it's the result of a highly complex strategy?

**The rise of Asia – and especially China – was only possible because it was integrated by the West.**

Yes, of course – China has benefited enormously from the Western-dominated global trading system. And that is precisely why China wants to preserve the rules-based world order of 1945. While the US is withdrawing from the World Trade Organization, China remains firmly entrenched within it. In fact, China's commitment to globalization is deeper today than that of any other country in the world.

**How do you see the future of globalization – against the backdrop of the current trade war?**

The good news is that almost all Asian countries are pushing globalization forward – and we hope that Europe will follow suit. This is an opportunity for Europe and Asia to stand together for globalization and actively defend it.

******Do you see no danger that a trade war between the US and China could ultimately escalate into a real war?**

No, I don't believe that. All the major players are aware of the danger and are acting accordingly. Of course, many in Asia are worried about Trump and his tariffs – but nobody believes that this will change the long-term direction of world history.

**They remain calm.**

You know, I came from extreme poverty – from rock bottom, literally. When I was six, I was put on a nutrition program because I was malnourished. We lived without a flush toilet, debt collectors came to the door, my father went to prison. I've experienced real Third World poverty. And you want to tell me that something even worse could happen? No way.__ If you don't understand where Asian countries come from, you will never understand their resilience.
