headline: How the police brought down the world's most feared hacker: a reconstruction of the end of Lockbit
lead: A year ago, investigators arrested members of the Lockbit ransomware gang, seized bitcoins, and shut down servers. "Operation Cronos" showed the world how to punish hackers who hide from prosecution in Russia.
body:
# How the police brought down the world's most feared hacker: a reconstruction of the end of Lockbit

*A year ago, investigators arrested members of the Lockbit ransomware gang, seized bitcoins, and shut down servers. "Operation Cronos" showed the world how to punish hackers who hide from prosecution in Russia.*

**Gioia da Silva, Lukas Mäder** · Technologie · 2025-05-07 · 3075 words · [ld.1880992](https://www.nzz.ch/technologie/lockbit-wie-die-polizei-den-gefuerchtetsten-hacker-der-welt-zu-fall-brachte-eine-rekonstruktion-des-endes-von-lockbit-ld.1880992)

![A $10 million bounty has been placed on his head: Dmitri Choroshev aka LockbitSupp.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/07/e154c6e1-57be-4672-870c-af626748be32.jpeg?width=1024)
*A $10 million bounty has been placed on his head: Dmitri Choroshev aka LockbitSupp.* (Illustration by Olivia Meyer / NZZ)

Robert McArdle's pulse quickens. It's May 7, 2024, just before 3 p.m. The countdown is about to end, and the police will release the name of the head of the Lockbit hacker gang. One of the world's most successful cybercriminals will be dragged into the public eye. And McArdle will finally learn who is hiding behind the pseudonym LockbitSupp.

McArdle heads cybercrime research at the IT security company Trend Micro. He has been investigating Lockbit's criminal activities for years. In the preceding months, he repeatedly provided law enforcement agencies with small clues about the gang upon request: a username here, an IP address there.

An international consortium of investigators pursued these leads for years, piecing together the information into a comprehensive picture. In 2024, they struck. The investigators called the police operation, which was successfully concluded a year ago, «Operation Cronos.»

And indeed, McArdle is not disappointed. The FBI publishes the name of the man believed to be the head of the Lockbit gang. It is the Russian Dmitri Khoroshev.

Khoroshev cultivated the image of a brilliant hacker: brutal, arrogant, and more intelligent than the police. He is a ruthless criminal, responsible for attacks on thousands of companies, including hospitals and schools, encrypting their data and extorting hundreds of millions of dollars. At times, almost half of all ransomware attacks originated from his group.

«For us, who had fought against Lockbit for years, it was a moment of triumph,» says McArdle, who saw the arrest warrant in the first few minutes after it was published. «With Khoroshev, we were able to unmask one of the most successful cybercriminals of all time.»

Combating hacker groups is extremely difficult for the police. Their trails are hard to trace. And not all countries cooperate with investigators. This is especially true for Russia, where many of the masterminds behind ransomware gangs are based.

The success of «Operation Cronos» proves, however, that law enforcement is not powerless – even when hackers hide in Russia. Using psychological methods, investigators were able to destroy something that is also essential for criminal activity: mutual trust.

The rise and fall of the world's most notorious hacker group is a lesson in how the fight against cybercriminals can work. Based on conversations with investigators and interviews with cybersecurity experts, we recount the story of Lockbits.

## Lockbit perfects the system of division of labor

Lockbit emerged in 2020 in the cybercriminal underworld. In January, the group began advertising its ransomware on a Russian-language hacker forum. They particularly emphasized the technical capabilities of their malware: it encrypted victims' servers faster and required less computing power.

Back then, Lockbit had one main goal: growth. The core group around Dmitri Choroshev wanted to acquire business partners, so-called affiliates. These affiliates independently carried out attacks using Lockbit's encryption software. In return, they paid the core group 20 percent of the extorted ransom. This model was called «Ransomware as a Service.»

The system has a crucial advantage: the number of attacks can be increased easily and quickly. Even less technically skilled criminals can carry out the actual ransomware attacks on companies. The core group around Dmitri Choroshev is responsible for the further development of the malware. It's a criminal division of labor.

The model leads to Lockbit's success. In July 2020 , a wave of attacks against medium-sized companies sweeps across the Americas. Around the same time, the first companies in Switzerland also fall victim to Lockbit. However, there are no major cases yet.

## Lockbit becomes the most successful hacker gang

Lockbit's first major success came a year later, in the summer of 2021. The hackers attacked the consulting firm Accenture, stole confidential data, and rendered the company's IT systems unusable by encrypting them. Lockbit demanded $50 million in cryptocurrencies to decrypt the systems.

However, Accenture was able to restore the encrypted data from a backup and refused to give in to the extortion demands. Lockbit then resorted to a tactic known as «double extortion.» The hackers threatened to publish the stolen data, thereby increasing the pressure on their victims: the public exposure was intended to force them to pay up.

Accenture continues to refuse payment. Lockbit then publishes the stolen data, including internal presentations and working papers. The case makes headlines. Accenture, a company that sells cybersecurity services to its clients, suffers a reputational loss.

For the extortionists, the boom began. In 2022, Lockbit was the most widely used ransomware variant worldwide. In Canada, 22 percent of all attacks originated from Lockbit. In the US alone, the FBI recorded around 1,700 attacks since 2020. The victims are said to have paid ransoms totaling approximately $91 million.

## Absurd popularity: $1,000 for a Lockbit tattoo

There are several reasons why Lockbit has been able to grow so large. A key factor is the malware's technical power: the core group around Dmitri Choroshev has continuously improved it. Now it cleverly hides itself within the victims' IT systems to avoid detection. It gathers information about the company and, after the attack, erases its traces to hinder the work of investigators.

An improved version includes a tool that allows affiliates to quickly siphon off large amounts of data undetected. Criminals hardly need any IT expertise anymore. Thanks to a simple user interface, a few mouse clicks are all it takes to copy and then encrypt the data. Ransomware attacks become incredibly easy.

Perhaps the most important factor in Lockbit's success is its payment model. Normally, victims pay the ransom to the core group, which then pays the affiliates. Lockbit does things differently: Affiliates receive their share of the ransom directly from the victims. The advantage: The core group can't cheat its affiliates out of their share. This builds trust and increases the incentive for affiliates to work with Lockbit.

Besides its excellent product, Lockbit is also working on its image. In 2022, the company's leader launched a major PR campaign: anyone who got the Lockbit logo tattooed and posted pictures of it on social media would receive $1,000. Photos of Lockbit tattoos did indeed appear.

> [embed: oembed ]

The success of the appeal demonstrates the absurd popularity and respect that Lockbit has cultivated. In 2022, the group is no longer just a gang of criminals. Lockbit is a brand, loved by insiders, hated by outsiders.

## Police worldwide are investigating Lockbit

Lockbit's success attracted the attention of the police. As early as 2021, Europol formed a task force. This task force included representatives from many countries investigating Lockbit, including Germany, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. France led the investigation. Thus began «Operation Cronos.»

Europol is now compiling the evidence from various countries. This includes, for example, the IP addresses of the servers from which the criminals accessed the victims' IT systems. It also includes the email addresses that the hackers provided to rent these servers, and the addresses of crypto wallets that Lockbit gave the victims for transferring the ransom. Europol analysts are comparing this information and forwarding it to the national police forces.

For example, if German investigators are looking into an attack originating from an IP address in the Netherlands, Europol might inform them that their Dutch counterparts are already monitoring that server and can provide further information. The criminals may be using the same cryptocurrency wallet to rent multiple servers. In this way, the police gradually uncover the gang's infrastructure.

However, one of Lockbit's strengths becomes a disadvantage. Because the malware is so easy to use, criminals no longer need a solid technical understanding. And beginners are more likely to leave traces, says one investigator. This can help the police.

For example, an attacker only needs to forget to activate the VPN service that anonymizes their internet connection just once. And suddenly, investigators have an unmasked IP address at their fingertips, giving them clues to the hacker's location. Even criminals make mistakes.

Besides the police, IT security experts like Robert McArdle and John DiMaggio are also investigating Lockbit. DiMaggio, chief strategist at the IT security company Analyst 1, caused a stir with his research on the ringleader, then known only by his pseudonym LockbitSupp.

DiMaggio interacted directly with LockbitSupp on several occasions. He describes him as an arrogant criminal who nevertheless communicated professionally and objectively – except that he repeatedly sent a cat meme, i.e., a picture of a cat. This detail would later prove crucial.

## The beginning of the end: The police strike

Sometime in mid- to late 2023, the international investigators of «Operation Cronos» had gathered enough information. After several postponements, the participating countries agreed to launch their operation in February. The FBI from the USA and the NCA from Great Britain took the lead.

Details of the so-called «Action Day» are strictly confidential. A participating investigator said there was great fear that someone would warn the criminals, rendering the operation unsuccessful.

But the operation succeeds. On February 19, 2024, investigators post a message on Lockbit's darknet site: «This site is under the control of law enforcement.» It's a clear signal to the affiliates and the public. And it marks the beginning of the criminal gang's downfall.

![The police published this announcement on the Lockbit darknet site.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/22/ca07c3b2-88ed-4db6-94af-0104787e5bbe.jpeg?width=1024)
*The police published this announcement on the Lockbit darknet site.* (Analyst 1 , screenshot from the darknet)

Investigators may have been in Lockbit's systems for an extended period, spying on the hackers. They haven't revealed what the crucial step was that allowed them to penetrate Lockbit's systems. One investigator involved even says that authorities only received confirmation that Lockbit's central servers had actually been identified on the «Action Day.»

Investigators succeeded in arresting three affiliates. In Ukraine, a father and his son were arrested, and in Poland, a 38-year-old man. Polish police released a video of the arrest, accompanied by dramatic music. The video shows police officers leading away a man in jeans and a blue jacket; his cell phones and laptop were sealed.

> [embed: youtube ]

Furthermore, the police have identified two Russian hackers and published their names: Ivan Kondratiev, known in the hacker scene under his pseudonyms Bassterlord and Fisheye, who has written two textbooks on ransomware attacks, and Artur Sungatov. Because Russia, unlike Ukraine and Poland, is not cooperating with Western investigators, these two hackers are still at large. However, they are wanted in the US and are on the sanctions list.

## Psychological warfare against unreachable criminals

Following the police operation in February, it is initially difficult to assess the true extent of the authorities' investigative success. At that time, Lockbit had 190 affiliates, some of whom were likely behind multiple individuals. To the public, three arrests and three public identifications may seem like a small number.

But the police employ a strategy that dismantles the group's network: they use methods to psychologically unsettle the criminals.

This is evident in the arrest video from Poland: In one scene, stuffed animals and crayons appear, seemingly lying on the floor of the perpetrator's apartment. Such scenes are intended to deter other hackers. The message the investigators are sending to criminals is: Look, we've got him, and you're not safe anywhere, not even in your own homes.

## Hello! We have your Bitcoins

To deter those criminals from Lockbit whom they cannot arrest or identify, the police create a script for the remainder of «Operation Cronos.» This is intended to undermine trust between the criminals and Lockbit's central organization.

Perhaps the most effective tactic is personal contact. The police send affiliates private messages via the internal Lockbit system. Upon their first login after the police operation, the criminals receive a message stating that investigators now possess their usernames, the addresses of their crypto wallets, their IP addresses, and the transcripts of their chats with victims and with Lockbit support. From there, some affiliates likely reasoned, the path to public identification is short.

Further pinpricks followed: The day after the takeover of the leak site on the darknet, the police redirected visitors to the URL to another site. There, they published arrest warrants and announcements of sanctions against the hackers.

From a psychological perspective, two things are interesting here: First, the investigators are adopting the branding and structure of the original Lockbit leak site for the new site: same colors, same font, and the Lockbit logo is still present in the upper left corner. However, unlike usual, the police site doesn't list the hacked companies as «victims,» ​​but rather the criminals themselves.

Secondly, the police are refraining from communicating all the investigation results at once. According to a log from Analyst 1, the authorities are publishing arrest warrants and announcements of sanctions over a five-day period. Robert McArdle, the cybercrime expert at Trend Micro, says: «This strategy is clever because it intimidates the affiliates a little more each day.»

Just before the police take their modified Lockbit leak site offline, they launch their final major attack – against the gang's leader. They publish a statement claiming to know the name behind LockbitSupp. Along with this, they release a cat meme, thus also employing the criminal's visual language. McArdle interprets this as follows: «The police have shown Lockbit affiliates that they actually have access to Lockbit's core infrastructure. How else would they know about LockbitSupp's love of cat memes?»

![The Cat meme showed affiliates that their leader had actually been investigated by the police.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/22/14399b97-a7ac-4422-920a-985d6efd3e5b.jpeg?width=1024)
*The Cat meme showed affiliates that their leader had actually been investigated by the police.* (Analyst 1 , screenshot from the dark web)

## Dmitri Khoroshev strikes back

But Dmitri Khoroshev, one of the most successful cybercriminals of all time, launched a counterattack. Less than a week after the successful police operation, he launched a new Lockbit leak site on the dark web. It looked exactly like the old site, but listed fewer victims. However, the victim list included one prominent entry: the FBI.

Of course, the FBI wasn't actually hacked. However, LockbitSupp uses the FBI entry to explain the takedown from his perspective: Among other things, he admits that the police gained access to his IT infrastructure «because of his personal negligence and irresponsibility.» He writes: «Because I've been swimming in money for five years, I got very lazy and continued cruising on my yacht with busty girls.» That's why he didn't install an update that would have been necessary to fend off the investigators.

While Khoroshev admits his own mistakes, he immediately tries to regain the trust of his affiliates. He writes that the hack didn't just affect him; other hacker groups and forums had suffered the same fate, they just hadn't noticed. As a counterattack, Khoroshev threatens to attack American government agencies.

In the two weeks that followed, Khoroshev published several posts on his new leak site about companies that had allegedly been victims of new hacking attacks. For a moment, it looked to outsiders as if Lockbit was back. However, it soon became clear that most of the alleged attacks had taken place before the investigators took the site down, and Lockbit was simply publishing old data. In other cases, Khoroshev was bluffing—in reality, he hadn't even obtained their data.

His blatant lying had only one goal: Khorashev wanted to save his image. «He was putting on a brave face, hoping not to lose his business partners and his reputation as a high-flying criminal,» says McArdle. But the plan backfired. In the following months, the authorities gained increasingly deeper insights into the Lockbit network.

## The finale: the unmasking of the Lockbit boss

The final step in the police operation takes place in early May. The authorities reactivate the original Lockbit leak site and publish an announcement that they will reveal the identity of LockbitSupp. «Coming soon,» on May 7, 2024.

This announcement, too, serves the purpose of unsettling criminals, Jon DiMaggio writes in a post. «LockbitSupp had mocked the FBI for years, claiming they were too stupid to catch him. It seems they were smarter than he thought.»

On May 7, 2024, the American government published an arrest warrant for Dmitri Khoroshev. It offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.

![Dmitri Choroshev aka LockbitSupp in a billiard hall, most likely in Russia. Image by Analyst 1.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/22/d10fe37e-b798-4954-a156-4c339e1436a4.jpeg?width=1024)
*Dmitri Choroshev aka LockbitSupp in a billiard hall, most likely in Russia. Image by Analyst 1.* (Analyst 1)

Shortly thereafter, John DiMaggio of Analyst 1 published further information about Khoroshev. He was born in 1993 and lives in the Voronezh region of Russia, not far from the Ukrainian border. He also owns several businesses that appear legitimate at first glance, including a textile shop. DiMaggio also believes he has obtained the hacker's email addresses, phone numbers, and home address. He publishes this information as well.

This «dox,» as the publication of personal information is called, along with the other psychological components of «Operation Cronos,» is causing many affiliates to turn away from Lockbit. Their fear is too great that the police are still within the Lockbit network and will identify them as well.

Because one thing is clear: being publicly identified is unpleasant for Russian hackers. Khoroshev, aka LockbitSupp, Kondratiew, aka Bassterlord, and Sungatov won't be honeymooning in Paris or taking city breaks in Dubai. They'll never even see New York with their own eyes. They have to assume they'll be arrested immediately if they ever show up at a Western airport.

While they can certainly lead a comfortable life on Russian territory, life in Russia is also better when one's neighbors are unaware of the criminal and damaging nature of one's source of income. Lockbit hackers, in particular, who are likely to possess substantial wealth, now have to worry about becoming victims of other crimes. For example, their children could be kidnapped. Furthermore, they must assume that Western intelligence agencies or other hackers are after them.

These publicly available identifications allow Western law enforcement to restrict the lives of Russian hackers, at least to some extent. This is despite Russia protecting its hackers by ignoring international requests for legal assistance.

## Conclusion: Cybercrime can be combated

Today, a year after the police raid, Lockbit is active again. But the large organization with dozens of affiliates no longer exists.

«Lockbit is just a shadow of its former self,» says McArdle. «The group no longer has the power or dominance it once did.» An investigator involved in «Operation Cronos» is convinced that the gang will never regain its former strength.

Operation Cronos demonstrates that law enforcement agencies can successfully combat cybercriminals. They dismantled the most notorious ransomware gang, thereby preventing numerous cyberattacks.

Investigators have likely succeeded in identifying several members of the group. While they have so far only been able to arrest a small portion of the criminals, the message is clear: anyone active in Lockbit must now expect arrest, at least if they travel to a Western country. Lockbit affiliates will no longer be able to travel to Italy, Thailand, or Turkey without fear. The myth of the untouchable Russian hacker has been shattered.

But «Operation Cronos» is also a message to politicians: If the police receive enough resources to combat cybercrime, they can be successful. This is not yet the case. Crimes on the internet are often prosecuted less vigorously than extortion or fraud. The Lockbit story shows that it could be worthwhile to change this.

_Contributors: Simon Huwiler, Forrest Rogers_

---

headline: He says he's not a gangster. The US government says he's lying. How a deported immigrant became the face of Donald Trump's immigration policy
lead: The complicated story of Kilmar Ábrego García from El Salvador.
body:
# He says he's not a gangster. The US government says he's lying. How a deported immigrant became the face of Donald Trump's immigration policy

*The complicated story of Kilmar Ábrego García from El Salvador.*

**Flurin Clalüna** · Gesellschaft · 2025-05-09 · 1816 words · [ld.1882781](https://www.nzz.ch/gesellschaft/von-trumps-usa-bis-el-salvador-wer-ist-kilmar-abrego-garcia-ld.1882781)

![Kilmar Ábrego García has lived in the USA for 13 years. In March he will be deported back to El Salvador.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/05/11dc5f54-aceb-4351-95c4-3bb82f0b4fc0.jpeg?crop=3024,2016,x0,y501)
*Kilmar Ábrego García has lived in the USA for 13 years. In March he will be deported back to El Salvador.* (Ábrego García Family via Reuters)

On the afternoon of March 12, 2025, Kilmar Ábrego García was driving home from work. His five-year-old son, whom he had picked up from his grandparents' house, was in the back seat. In College Park, a small town in Maryland a few miles from his home, a police officer pulled García over. He assumed it was a traffic stop and pulled into the parking lot of an IKEA store. Then he called his wife, Jennifer.

This is what they agreed upon: Because English isn't his native language, García would use speakerphone in such situations. Jennifer hears the police officer tell her husband to turn off the engine and get out of the car. García says his son is in the back; he's disabled, doesn't speak, and is autistic. Then Jennifer hears the police officer take her husband's cell phone and hang up.

Jennifer immediately notices that something is wrong. But she has no idea yet how much her husband's life is about to change: Kilmar Ábrego García, a 29-year-old metalworker born in El Salvador, will become the most famous face of Donald Trump's immigration policy.

Shortly after ending the call, the police officer called Jennifer back on Kilmar's cell phone. He said he was from the Department of Homeland Security. Jennifer had ten minutes to pick up her son. When she arrived, her husband was sitting on the curb in the Ikea parking lot. He was barefoot and beltless, but handcuffed. «They claimed Kilmar's immigration status had changed and that they were taking him away.»

As the police officers take him away, Kilmar is crying. Jennifer tells him: «You will come home again. You haven't done anything wrong.»

## Two truths

We know exactly what happened on March 12th because Kilmar García's wife, Jennifer Vásquez, made it public in a sworn affidavit . The subsequent course of the story can be followed in American newspapers: how a small life becomes entangled in high politics; how García becomes more important than his case; and how his name is used to manipulate public opinion: as a criminal immigrant or as an innocent deportee.

Three days after García's arrest, three deportation planes bound for El Salvador were parked on the tarmac at Harlingen Airport in Texas. Along with more than 260 undocumented immigrants and suspected gang members, García was flown back to his homeland.

First, he is taken to a maximum-security prison an hour outside the capital, San Salvador. With space for 40,000 prisoners, it is the largest prison in Latin America. Human rights experts compare it to Guantanamo.

A few days later, García was transferred to another city – to a prison with better conditions. He is still there.

The Foreign Ministry says García is in «excellent health» at the new institution. His family says this is not true.

![Kilmar Ábrego García (bottom row, fifth from the left) in the high-security prison Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo in El Salvador. His relatives recognize him by his tattoos.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/08/de92c83e-e7b0-4a41-ab07-057d455aac90.jpeg?crop=7124,4752,x891,y594)
*Kilmar Ábrego García (bottom row, fifth from the left) in the high-security prison Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo in El Salvador. His relatives recognize him by his tattoos.* (Secretaría De Prensa De La Presi via Reuters)

## «Wonderful gentleman from Maryland»

What is true and what isn't in the García case? And who is this man that all of America and half the world have been talking about for weeks? Depending on whom you believe and which documents you read, a different picture emerges. Almost as if García had lived two lives.

According to documents released by the government about García, he is a member of MS-13, a criminal street gang with roots in El Salvador, which the government designated a terrorist organization in February. There are also reports describing him as an abusive husband. Trump mockingly calls him «a wonderful gentleman from Maryland.»

According to his wife, the activists, and the union members who have been demonstrating for him for weeks, García has nothing to do with gangs. He is an upstanding father who works hard and lovingly cares for his disabled children.

Who is right, who is wrong?

This case has long ceased to be about truth. It's about who can better convince the public of their version of the truth: The government needs the image of the dangerous criminal to justify its harsh immigration policy; the family's lawyers portray García as a victim of a system that persecutes innocent people. Even a Democratic senator is advocating for him and has visited him in El Salvador.

García is a man caught between two narratives: either he should be immediately brought back from El Salvador to the USA because he has done nothing wrong, or he should stay where he is because he deserves nothing better. These narratives are like tools: whoever controls the interpretation of García's life controls how people think about him.

More important than the interpretation of his life story is its legal classification: Kilmar Ábrego García was never convicted of a crime and should never have been deported to El Salvador. The US Supreme Court ruled the deportation illegal. The government called it «an administrative error.»

To understand why García ended up in this situation, one has to go far back in his life, read old court rulings, and talk to family members. This is exactly what reporters from the «New York Times» and CNN did, delving into García's past.

![Demonstrations in support of Kilmar Ábrego García in front of the White House in Washington.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/05/e72e458e-994a-40da-ad63-d805cc17dfd2.jpeg?width=1024)
*Demonstrations in support of Kilmar Ábrego García in front of the White House in Washington.* (Astrid Riecken/The Washington Post via Getty)

## Escape to the USA

Kilmar Ábrego García grew up in the mid-1990s in a working-class neighborhood on the outskirts of San Salvador. His father was a police officer and soldier who later drove a taxi; his mother sold tortillas and flatbreads from the garage of their house. This was a time when gang crime was on the rise in El Salvador after the end of the civil war.

The Barrio 18 gang also extorted money from the García family at that time. The gang demanded protection money and tried to recruit the two brothers. Out of fear, the Garcías first sent the older brother, Cesar, to the USA, and later Kilmar as well.

In 2012, Kilmar, aged 16, began his journey through the desert and crossed the border near the small town of McAllen in Texas.

García moved to the East Coast, to Maryland, and lived as inconspicuously as possible—like many of the roughly one million undocumented immigrants from El Salvador in the US. He worked in construction, sometimes he had a job, sometimes he was a day laborer, sometimes unemployed. In 2018, García met his future wife, Jennifer Vásquez, an American woman who brought two disabled children into the relationship.

The problems began in 2019, seven years after the immigration. This is where the narrative of the criminal immigrant began. After that, nothing was ever the same again.

On March 27, 2019, García was standing with three men in the parking lot of a hardware store in the small town of Hyattsville, Maryland. The police report states that the men were «loitering.» The police officers believed them to be members of the MS-13 gang.

The report states regarding García: «Officers observed that he was wearing a Chicago Bulls cap and a hoodie depicting banknotes.» The basketball cap and the banknotes—with the eyes, ears, and mouths of the US presidents obscured—were, in the officers' view, typical of Hispanic gang culture. When an anonymous informant confirmed García's identity as a gang member and also revealed his gang nickname («Chele»), they were certain: García must belong to MS-13.

García tells the police his whole story, from childhood to his escape. Everything is recorded in the interrogation transcript. But it also states that he is a gang member. He will never shake that reputation.

## Marriage in prison

García remains in custody for several months and is sent to a deportation center. Because no one knows if he will be deported, Jennifer and Kilmar decide to get married. Jennifer is pregnant; she is expecting her third child. In June 2019, a priest comes to the prison to perform the wedding ceremony.

Jennifer Vásquez writes in her statement: «We were separated by a glass partition and were not allowed any physical contact. An official had to hand over the rings. It was unbearable not being able to hug him.»

![García's wife, Jennifer Vásquez: «It was unbearable not being able to hug him.»](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/04/24/ae13b062-84ac-4366-80be-9d07aae7ca7a.jpeg?width=1024)
*García's wife, Jennifer Vásquez: «It was unbearable not being able to hug him.»* (Carol Guzy / Imago)

Four months after the wedding, an immigration judge ruled that García's fear of the gangs in El Salvador that had threatened him and his family years before was justified. He was released and granted protected status, known as «withholding of removal,» which means García cannot be deported to his home country. He can stay and work in the US, but he doesn't know for how long.

After his release, García is doing an apprenticeship at a building technology company and attending further training courses.

In December 2022, he ran into trouble with the authorities again: the highway patrol stopped him for speeding. When the officers checked the car, they discovered eight people inside. In the report, they suspected García of being involved in human trafficking. But because there was no evidence, nothing happened. García only received a fine because his driver's license had expired.

Family life is also difficult. Not only do Jennifer's two children from her previous relationship suffer from autism and epilepsy, but their son is also autistic. Vásquez writes in her statement: «Although raising three young children with special needs is challenging, Kilmar and I love our children. Having Kilmar as my life partner is the greatest blessing for our family.»

## Hidden violence

Vásquez doesn't tell everything about her husband. What she omits is contained in a statement published by the Ministry of Internal Security in April 2025: Vásquez has filed several complaints against García. She claims her husband beat, kicked, and pushed her; once, he dragged her by the hair from the car and left her standing in the street; furthermore, he locked the children in the bedroom and smashed doors, tablets, televisions, and phones.

When asked about the incidents, Vásquez told the media that she and her husband had gone through a «difficult time» after his first imprisonment, but had overcome it through therapy. She has withdrawn the charges against her husband.

Is Kilmar Ábrego García a good person? And does that even matter? Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland says: «I'm not defending the man, but his right to a fair trial.» To make it clear that he will not advocate for García's repatriation from El Salvador, Donald Trump simultaneously releases a photo of García's knuckles. The letters MS-13 are written on them, with symbols tattooed below.

![Senator Chris Van Hollen is visiting Kilmar Ábrego García in El Salvador. The meeting is taking place at Van Hollen's hotel.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/08/bb3853a2-dfe5-4e6b-8a52-6477c09e1d5c.jpeg?width=1024)
*Senator Chris Van Hollen is visiting Kilmar Ábrego García in El Salvador. The meeting is taking place at Van Hollen's hotel.* (Press Office Senator Van Hollen, via AP)

Experts have been arguing about the tattoos ever since. Some say they are proof of García's gang membership. Others say they prove nothing at all.

What remains is a man whose story tells more about a divided America than about himself.

headline: In Artemisia Gentileschi's paintings, the eyes tell the whole story
lead: The Rome-born painter is one of the most important artists of the Baroque period. A comprehensive exhibition of her work is now on display in Paris, including previously unseen paintings.
body:
# In Artemisia Gentileschi's paintings, the eyes tell the whole story

*The Rome-born painter is one of the most important artists of the Baroque period. A comprehensive exhibition of her work is now on display in Paris, including previously unseen paintings.*

**Roman Bucheli** · Feuilleton · 2025-05-17 · 1442 words · [ld.1884009](https://www.nzz.ch/feuilleton/artemisia-gentileschi-ld.1884009)

![Artemisia Gentileschi: «Susanna and the Elders», 1610, oil on canvas (170×119 cm).](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/15/c94c6915-958b-4ec4-8b8b-88b7ee13b534.jpeg?width=1024)
*Artemisia Gentileschi: «Susanna and the Elders», 1610, oil on canvas (170×119 cm).* (PD)

No one painted eyes like hers. They offer a glimpse into the psyche, reflecting the highest drama. While Artemisia Gentileschi painted emblematic stories from the Bible, as was then considered the canon of visual art, she achieved what many at the time did not dare: she brought forth individuals, her biblical stories depicting scenes that resonate with everyday life.

Among these works is the spectacular painting «Susanna and the Elders» from 1610. She was 17 years old when she painted it. It took courage to depict the woman's nudity in the bath so explicitly—all the more so since Gentileschi likely used himself as a model in the mirror—and the fear she conveys in the young woman's face is also fundamental; disgust and despair scream from her eyes. These are the antithesis of the lust of the two elderly people who assail her from beyond the wall.

«Susanna and the Elders» is the centerpiece of the major exhibition currently on display at the Musée Jacquemart-André in Paris. It was the first painting that Artemisia Gentileschi, born in Rome in 1593, signed with her full name. Her name was practically carved in stone beneath the painting: as an inscription in the brickwork on which Susanna sits bathing.

One could call the painting prophetic, but Gentileschi likely only depicted what women of his time could expect, based on the biblical account of Susanna's slander. Less than a year later, Artemisia Gentileschi was raped by a painter in her father's and teacher's workshop. Only the promise that he would soon marry her prevented her from stabbing the perpetrator. When he later broke his promise, Artemisia's father ensured that he was tried and exiled.

## The young Artemisia paints a masterpiece

Susanna at her Bath is a popular subject in painting of the time and frequently requested by patrons. It is presumed that Artemisia's father, Orazio, suggested the motif to her. It was intended to be her journeyman's piece, with which he planned to introduce her to the art world.

Radiological examinations have revealed that the preliminary drawing most likely originated with the father, while Artemisia was responsible for the painting itself. The authorship, prominently attested to by her signature, is the exclamation mark with which the artist is released into independence from her father. Of course, all of this would have been for naught if the painting had not demonstrated the artist's extraordinary talent and if the young woman had not already practiced her art with great mastery.

Two years later, Orazio wrote a letter of recommendation to Christine of Lorraine, the wife of Ferdinando I de' Medici. It seems to support the assumption that the father had long suspected how far his daughter would surpass him: «Besides three sons, I also have a daughter, and this daughter, as was God's will, I trained as a painter in three years, so that today she is so skilled that I dare say she is unparalleled (...), as I will show Your Highness in due time and place.»

Artemisia Gentileschi painted the Susanna motif several more times later, but no version achieved the expressiveness and directness with which the viewer was drawn in as a witness to the assault, nor the urgency of the 1610 painting. Even though Susanna was a victim in this painting, and her eyes betrayed the greatest fear, she was not defenseless. Gentileschi had painted a self-assurance on her face and body in the face of danger, a quality that would reappear in her later work and in many variations.

## Seductress and murderer in one

The curators of the Paris exhibition are particularly careful not to portray the artist as a victim who sought to process the humiliation of the assault in her work. This simplistic interpretation is tempting, given that Artemisia Gentileschi later frequently and masterfully varied the Old Testament story of Holofernes' murder by Judith . However, one should be wary of interpreting this as a form of revenge sublimated in art against her former rapist.

Here, too, one must look into Judith's eyes and read her body language in the different treatments of the subject. Resolute and serious at the same time, she beheads Holofernes with the sword; defiantly triumphant, she carries the sword on her shoulder after the deed is done; and Gentileschi regularly bathes Judith's face in harsh light, sharply dividing it into a light and a dark half. She is not an avenger, but the savior of the Jewish people, and she is both seductress and murderer. Only one thing is she not: a victim.

The theme of self-empowerment reaches its climax in Gentileschi's work with Cleopatra 's suicide. She painted several versions of this story, recounted by Plutarch, at different times. Perhaps the most striking is a painting created in the first half of the 1620s.

Gentileschi paints the Egyptian ruler naked, using his own model, and depicts her at the moment of death, as she brings an asp viper to her breast to receive its fatal bite. Cleopatra's face is divided. While her dying eyes gaze heavenward, her gaze already half-faded but still fully sane and alert, her mouth is slightly open. Her lips emerge from her softly shadowed face, provocatively full and luminous red. The hour of death is transformed here into an act of supreme sensuality.

Artemisia Gentileschi often bestows her own features upon her heroines—unless, as with the «Lute Player» of 1614/15, she is painting an explicit self-portrait. However, these are not egocentric self-dramatizations when she adorns Susanna, Judith, Cleopatra, or even a reclining Venus with her own attributes. Rather, she places the biblical narratives and even the ancient goddess within the backdrop of her own life.

![Artemisia Gentileschi: «The Lute Player», 1615–1617.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/15/69a643eb-4893-4b44-a9d8-2b46dd29c7d0.jpeg?width=1024)
*Artemisia Gentileschi: «The Lute Player», 1615–1617.* (PD)

Nothing human is alien to art, she seems to be saying. Above all, she also suggests that wherever ultimate questions are addressed—be it tyrannicide, love, or death—Gentileschi brings human beings to the canvas, not stereotypes. Every painting speaks directly to the viewer: You are the one being addressed; your story is being told here.

This is especially true for those images that depict humanity at its most human: as sinners. Artemisia Gentileschi painted a «Repentant Magdalene» several times. In Gentileschi's work, the iconic sinner of the New Testament becomes a woman who, while melancholic, is nevertheless self-aware and confident in her physical allure.

Nothing about her suggests any particular remorse, neither guilt nor repentance is evident; she bares her breast carelessly, not provocatively, and the fullness of her garments paradoxically suggests lust rather than chastity. This Magdalene may be aware of her sins, but she feels no guilt. For that seems to be what she wants to tell the observers: I am a human being, a sinner indeed, but a human being nonetheless.

## Caravaggio was the true teacher

One must imagine Artemisia Gentileschi as a self-assured woman. She knew that she painted better than most painters of her generation. And as bold as her pictorial inventions were, so too was her life. She traveled extensively, in Italy from Naples through Rome and Florence to Venice; in 1638 she visited her father in London and stayed there for two years.

She became pregnant five times, but only two children survived. Early on, she had a lover besides her husband, with his consent. To this emotional intelligence was added literary knowledge: she only learned to read and write as an adult, read Petrarch and Ovid, and wrote her own poetry.

And yet, at the end of her life, her trail goes cold: she likely died of the plague in Naples in 1656. Only gradually, in recent decades, has it become possible to reconstruct her life's work; many paintings are lost, others have been rediscovered. Some of her paintings are being exhibited in Paris for the first time.

Artemisia Gentileschi had learned her craft from her father. But even in her earliest works, she was far ahead of him. Recognizing this, alongside his determined support of his daughter, was perhaps Orazio Gentileschi's greatest achievement.

Meanwhile, Orazio belonged to a different generation, and his daughter had a new art before her. She found it in the paintings of Caravaggio, the revolutionary of the Baroque era; he, with the works accessible to Artemisia in Rome, was her true teacher. Before his paintings, she learned to look into the soul of people and fearlessly paint what she found there: human imperfection, which she united with the perfection of her painting.

_Artemisia. Heroine of art. Musée Jacquemart-André, Paris, until August 3rd._

- Influenced by Caravaggio, Gentileschi depicted human imperfections and self-empowerment in her works, making her a unique voice of her time.

headline: Germany's welfare state is threatened with financial collapse
lead: Demographic trends and medical advances are causing social security contributions in Germany to rise rapidly. This jeopardizes jobs and slows growth. The welfare state is in danger of destroying its own foundations.
body:
# Germany's welfare state is threatened with financial collapse

*Demographic trends and medical advances are causing social security contributions in Germany to rise rapidly. This jeopardizes jobs and slows growth. The welfare state is in danger of destroying its own foundations.*

**Malte Fischer, Düsseldorf** · Wirtschaft · 2025-05-29 · 1779 words · [ld.1886544](https://www.nzz.ch/wirtschaft/deutschlands-wohlfahrtsstaat-droht-der-finanzielle-kollaps-ld.1886544)

![People in Germany are living longer but having fewer children. This is causing social security expenditures to rise faster than revenues.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/28/5f036e99-4dd0-4030-aa17-74a41c169088.jpeg?crop=3627,2720,x279,y352)
*People in Germany are living longer but having fewer children. This is causing social security expenditures to rise faster than revenues.* (Michael Nguyen / Imago)

Lars Klingbeil has just under four weeks left to deliver his final project. On June 25, the Federal Cabinet is scheduled to approve the 2025 budget, for which Klingbeil, as Finance Minister, is responsible. The projected gap between revenues and expenditures is expected to be larger than it has been in a long time. According to sources within the CDU/CSU, expenditures could exceed revenues by up to €100 billion. This would make the deficit almost twice as large as the one projected by the previous coalition government before it collapsed over the budget dispute .

One reason for the deep deficit is the rapidly rising expenditure in social security, particularly in health and long-term care insurance. To prevent social security contributions from rising even faster, the government intends to provide financial support from the federal budget. A €10 billion injection of funds for statutory health insurance and €6 billion for long-term care insurance is under discussion.

The government has just transferred an early federal subsidy of €800 million to the health fund, from which statutory health insurance funds receive their money, to secure the fund's liquidity. Further funds are needed, says Health Minister Nina Warken. The financial situation of the statutory health insurance system, which incurred a deficit of €6 billion in 2024, is «more dramatic than previously assumed.» The system is «deep in the red.»

Doris Pfeiffer, the chairwoman of the board of the National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV), is therefore calling for immediate action. «Otherwise, health insurance premiums will skyrocket at the next turn of the year,» she warns. Pfeiffer advocates a spending moratorium for all areas of healthcare. «No more price or fee increases that exceed current revenues,» she says, until reforms bring revenues and expenditures back into balance.

## Subsidies from the federal budget

The financial situation of Germany's social security system is precarious. This isn't limited to health and long-term care. In the pension and unemployment insurance systems, too, expenditures are threatening to outpace revenues. Meanwhile, employees and their employers are already paying more money into the system than at any time since World War II. Nearly 42 percent of gross income currently flows into social security in the form of contributions.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) d9221e68a3421f75e0b3e564fad80261]

Without sweeping reforms, contributions will continue to rise rapidly in the coming years due to demographic trends. They drive up non-wage labor costs, jeopardize jobs, reduce workers' purchasing power, and stifle growth. The welfare state risks destroying its own foundations.

But instead of tackling the problems through structural reforms, the federal government is papering them over with subsidies from the federal budget, thus driving national debt even higher.

## Expansion of the welfare state

The massive expansion of the welfare state in Germany began in the early 1970s under the Social Democratic Chancellor Willy Brandt. At that time, employees and employers together only had to pay 26.5 percent of gross income into social security. The rapid expansion of social benefits caused contributions to rise sharply in the following years. By the early 1980s, the total contribution had already reached 32.4 percent.

The upward trend in contributions was initially driven by health and unemployment insurance. Long-term care insurance was added in 1995. While unemployment insurance contributions declined again from 2006 onwards as a result of the employment boom, health and long-term care insurance contributions continued their unabated climb.

Currently, employees and employers, who share the contribution burden, must pay an average of 17.1 percent of gross income to the statutory health insurance (GKV). The contribution rate consists of a general rate of 14.6 percent plus an additional contribution of an average of 2.5 percent, set by the individual health insurance funds. The general contribution rate for long-term care insurance is currently 3.6 percent. Childless individuals pay a surcharge of 0.6 percent, while parents with more than one child benefit from discounts. The contribution rate for unemployment insurance is currently 2.6 percent, and for pension insurance, it is 18.6 percent.

## Real net wages are shrinking

Calculations by the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Halle (IWH) illustrate the extent to which contributions reduce employees' purchasing power, using the most recent collective bargaining agreement in the public sector as an example. This agreement provides for a 3.0 percent wage increase for federal and municipal employees as of April this year, with a minimum increase of €110 per month. Wages will be raised again in May 2026, this time by 2.8 percent.

Taking into account special adjustments under collective bargaining agreements and the elimination of the inflation bonus, the gross salary of an employee in the middle service will rise by 3.2 percent this year compared to the previous year, according to calculations by IWH economists. The increase is projected to be 3.1 percent in 2026.

![Due to rising social security contributions and inflation, people have less and less money in their pockets. This is slowing down consumption.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/27/108e3664-3d2c-4487-8bd4-fd8de46527d6.jpeg?width=1024)
*Due to rising social security contributions and inflation, people have less and less money in their pockets. This is slowing down consumption.* (Andreas Franke / Imago)

Because the additional contributions to statutory health insurance and the contribution rate to long-term care insurance rose sharply at the beginning of this year, only 1.9 percent of the gross wage increase of 3.2 percent remains as net income.

After accounting for inflation – which the IWH economists estimate at slightly more than 2 percent for this year and next – the net collectively agreed wage of a mid-level employee will shrink by 0.4 percent in real terms this year. Next year, the decrease will be 0.1 percent. Although gross wages in the federal and municipal public sector have risen significantly faster than consumer prices, the IWH economists conclude that, due to rising social security contributions, «nothing will remain» after taxes.

## Brake on private consumption

The situation is similar in the private sector. In many industries, negotiated wages are rising less sharply than in the public sector due to the crisis. For example, in their latest spring report, economic research institutes are forecasting a meager increase in net wages across the economy this year of only 1.3 percent. This is insufficient to offset the rise in consumer prices of just over 2 percent.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 0a48765495a834ac06e6622f3a877f60]

Even disposable incomes, which include government transfer payments, barely increase after accounting for inflation. This year and next, the institute's economists expect only a meager real increase of 0.2 percent and 0.6 percent, respectively. Therefore, it is hardly surprising that consumption, which accounts for roughly 75 percent of economic output, is failing to gain momentum.

Without sweeping reforms to the social security systems, the gap between gross and net wages is likely to widen further in the coming years. This is because the aging population and advances in medical technology are driving up expenditures in pension, health, and long-term care insurance.

## Contribution rates soon to be 50 percent

A scenario analysis by the Iges Institute, an analysis and consulting firm specializing in the health and social insurance sectors, illustrates the potential consequences. In the baseline scenario without reforms, Iges projects that the contribution rate for health insurance will climb to 20 percent by 2035. For long-term care insurance, it will rise to 4.5 percent, and for pension insurance to 21.2 percent.

If the CDU/CSU and SPD implement their pension plans (mothers' pension and fixing the pension level) as agreed in the coalition agreement , the contribution rate for pension insurance will even climb to 22.1 percent, predict the Iges experts. For unemployment insurance, they anticipate an increase in the contribution rate to 3.1 percent.

If the demographic trend and the development of income and expenditure continue, «the total burden of social security contributions will amount to almost 49 percent in ten years,» says Martin Albrecht, Managing Director and Head of Health Policy at Iges. In a worst-case scenario, the total contribution could even rise to 53 percent.

## The pressure for reforms is growing

Under these conditions, it is unlikely to be worthwhile for companies and employees to create or accept jobs in Germany.

![Federal Health Minister Nina Warken (CDU) wants to stabilize the finances of health insurance funds through subsidies from the federal budget.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/28/2204ae40-4c81-4fa4-956c-b9ac441a0a07.jpeg?width=1024)
*Federal Health Minister Nina Warken (CDU) wants to stabilize the finances of health insurance funds through subsidies from the federal budget.* (Juliane Sonntag / Imago)

Pressure is mounting on the federal government to subject the social security system to a comprehensive overhaul. But instead of quickly setting a new course, the CDU/CSU and SPD coalition plans to first task a commission with developing reform proposals. While there seems to be a growing realization within the government that faster reforms are needed, Health Minister Warken says the commission is not bound to submit proposals only in 2027. «We will tackle things sooner,» she promises.

But how far this promise will go remains to be seen. Government members like Family Minister Karin Prien are still calling for more, not less, social spending. Prien recently pushed ahead with a proposal to introduce a care allowance as wage replacement for family caregivers. She did not specify how this would be financed.

## Longer working hours are possible

Over the past few years , countless studies by scientists have detailed what needs to be done to prepare the social security system for demographic challenges. Instead of expanding the mothers' pension and fixing the pension level in relation to earned income, they recommend raising the retirement age in line with increasing life expectancy.

A recent study by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) , the Ifo Institute, and Stanford University shows that older employees can also hold their own in the workplace. Based on a representative sample of adults in Germany, the researchers concluded that basic cognitive skills such as reading, writing, and arithmetic reach their peak for most people between the ages of 40 and 45.

If these skills continue to be used intensively in the workplace in subsequent years, they remain at a high level well beyond the age of 60. «Overall, the results refute the common assumption that cognitive abilities inevitably decline with age,» the researchers write. Therefore, it is crucial for individuals and society to maintain skills by using them frequently.

## Cost reduction through more market economy

While longer working lives can improve the revenue side of the welfare state, market-based reforms can counteract the expansion of spending. In healthcare, for example, a patient co-payment for treatment and medication costs, tiered according to income and severity of illness, could lead to more economical access to medical services without restricting the free choice of doctor.

![Older employees can maintain their cognitive abilities in their daily work and thus work longer.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/05/07/e3472c80-872b-4553-8af7-f57c3e0b0e3e.jpeg?width=1024)
*Older employees can maintain their cognitive abilities in their daily work and thus work longer.* (Xavier Lorenzo / Imago)

Potential savings also lie in the administrative costs of social security, which, according to calculations by the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), amount to almost 25 billion euros annually. This is more than the government spends in total on parental allowance, housing allowance, and student loans, says employers' association president Rainer Dulger.

According to calculations by the BDA (Confederation of German Employers' Associations), administrative costs absorb 1.3 percentage points of the total social security contribution of almost 42 percent. If it were possible to reduce administrative costs, for example through leaner structures in self-governance and better cooperation between social security institutions, employees and employers would benefit from lower contributions. Germany needs «a social security system that operates efficiently, digitally, and cost-consciously,» says Dulger.

The federal government still lacks the courage to implement the necessary reforms. If nothing changes, the holes in the social security system and the state budget are likely to grow even larger in the future. A balanced budget – the crowning achievement of any finance minister – will then become an unattainable dream for Lars Klingbeil.

- Experts advocate for longer working lives, cost reductions, and market-based reforms to avert the looming financial crisis.

headline: No more boozing to boost a career? Why alcohol consumption in China is tumbling
lead: Business in China has long been associated with marathon drinking sessions. Younger people now want different options. Even the government has declared war on traditional Chinese spirits – but not out of concern for public health.
author: Katrin Büchenbacher
summaryBullets: Alcohol consumption patterns in China are shifting, with younger people drinking less and shifting to lighter beverages like beer instead of spirits.

headline: The old world order has collapsed. Europe must adapt to chaos in order to survive.
lead: For over three decades, Europe believed that war was a thing of the past. Now it's back, and it's clear: rules only apply as long as an authority is willing to enforce them.
body:
# The old world order has collapsed. Europe must adapt to chaos in order to survive.

*For over three decades, Europe believed that war was a thing of the past. Now it's back, and it's clear: rules only apply as long as an authority is willing to enforce them.*

**Herfried Münkler** · Feuilleton · 2025-07-02 · 1396 words · [ld.1891521](https://www.nzz.ch/feuilleton/welt-im-chaos-warum-die-regelbasierte-ordnung-gescheitert-ist-ld.1891521)

![With the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the expectation of living in a peaceful world has also vanished in Europe: rockets from Gaza fly towards Israel in May 2021.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2024/06/12/580e91c2-a7f5-422a-9c36-2b4bf590df6b.jpeg?width=1024)
*With the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the expectation of living in a peaceful world has also vanished in Europe: rockets from Gaza fly towards Israel in May 2021.* (Mohammed Saber / EPA)

The world order now appears somewhat less chaotic than it did two or three weeks ago: Israel and Iran have a ceasefire, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo have signed a peace agreement, and US President Trump reaffirmed American security guarantees for Europe at the NATO summit in Brussels.

Some wars and conflicts that recently filled us with fear and terror have been temporarily halted. But this is by no means the case for all wars and conflicts: Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine continues unabated, and no one can say when or how it will end; the war in the Gaza Strip is also not over, and the civil wars in Libya and Sudan persist. These receive little attention in Europe, even though they are one of the causes of migration.

That the Iranian nuclear program has actually been set back by years seems questionable after the statements made by US intelligence agencies. Donald Trump's initial grand pronouncements were clearly exaggerated. He has since indirectly admitted this himself when he threatened to order further airstrikes if the Iranian regime did not definitively abandon the development of nuclear weapons and delivery systems. The recent lull in the chaos of world politics is therefore likely to be little more than a temporary reprieve. That is, if it is indeed a reprieve at all, and not a respite before the next exchange of blows.

## Sanctions instead of bombs

But why has there been such a recent increase in wars? In Europe, for over three decades, we had held the expectation that interstate war was a thing of the past, that military force would be replaced by economic power as the mode of steering international politics. We believed that armed force would increasingly be replaced by economic sanctions when it came to bringing a rule-breaker and disruptor of order to heel, and that international arbitration tribunals would take over the role of military strikes and resolve conflicts peacefully.

We were convinced that interstate wars would then cease to exist, and that in the case of intra-societal wars, the international community's responsibility to protect would come into play, bringing an end to civil wars fought in the form of massacres. Europeans saw themselves on the path to a world in which it would be possible to «create peace with fewer and fewer weapons.»

What has replaced this is not only an increase in wars, but also the need to secure peace through the provision of an ever-growing quantity of weapons. The prospect of a stable and cost-effective peace has vanished and will not return in the foreseeable future.

## Power in the service of order

What went wrong? Yes, there are a number of decisions that, in hindsight, could have been made differently. But whether that would truly have led to us continuing to live in a peaceful world, to the Russians not attacking Ukraine, and to Hamas not invading Israel, is doubtful.

It wasn't contingent decisions, but rather structural problems within the rules-based order that led to its erosion. The US has lost political authority: The US president had to use B-2 bombers against Iran to persuade both sides in Tehran (and Tel Aviv) to agree to a ceasefire. It took military force to establish authority. And it is highly questionable whether authority gained in this way will last long, or whether it will require – again and again – a demonstration of military superiority.

The authority of a guardian of the world order is the prerequisite for political actors to comply with the rules without having to resort to force. The fundamental conditions for peace without the use of force have never been sufficiently clarified; therefore, the rules-based order has always been subject to the proviso that there must be an irresistible actor who places their power at the service of this order. Where this was not the case, the order stood on shaky ground and threatened to collapse as soon as someone intervened with great force. This was the case at the end of February 2022 with Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine.

## Magical thinking

But who was the guardian of this order—or at least could have been? Many Europeans placed their trust in the United Nations, which was legitimately positioned to guarantee the rules. But the UN was almost always blocked by the veto of the permanent members of the Security Council whenever existential questions were at stake for a veto-wielding power. The world organization was and is a weak guardian when things get serious. Other Europeans trusted the USA, which had sufficient power to enforce compliance against rule-breakers—except in the case of the nuclear powers Russia and China.

However, the US had a fatal tendency to confuse the role of guardian with that of master, prioritizing its own interests over the rules. This led to the formation of an anti-American coalition led by Russia and China, which included virtually the entire Global South.

This became relevant when the UN General Assembly was to condemn Russia for its attack on Ukraine and impose sanctions, and those mentioned voted against it or abstained. It was, in effect, half of humanity that abstained or voted against imposing sanctions on the rule-breaker. With that, the rules-based order was finished, even if some politicians refuse to acknowledge it and believe they can salvage the rule-based structure with incantations. But that's magical thinking, which has never helped.

## No silver lining on the horizon

Furthermore, the US withdrew from its role as guardian of global peace, first gradually and then dramatically, for entirely understandable reasons. Global compliance with the rules and the peace built upon it are a collective good from which no one can be excluded, even if that individual contributes absolutely nothing to its availability.

The US, in its role as guardian, had to contribute the lion's share, leading both its elites and its voters to question whether this wasn't ultimately an unfair disadvantage. Donald Trump's «America First» policy represented a resounding abandonment of the guardian role and a decisive shift towards its own national interests—even if one sometimes gets the impression that Trump isn't entirely sure what those interests are. For the global order, however, the only relevant point is that he isn't interested in the well-being of others and disregards the rules when they prevent him from pursuing his own interests.

This gave the rule-breakers carte blanche, and the USA firmly established itself among them. From the cosmos of rules-based order thus arose the chaos of international politics in which we currently find ourselves. There is no silver lining on the horizon heralding the arrival of a new order. Europeans, in particular, will have to adapt to a chaotic order in order to assert themselves. If they fail to do so, they will suffer structural disadvantages.

## A lesson in power politics

The implications of this were recently demonstrated by efforts to persuade Iran to negotiate the end of its nuclear program. The Europeans lacked the coercive measures to motivate the Iranian regime to negotiate, and thus were stalled and unable to achieve anything. Israel and the US, on the other hand, possess these measures and used them decisively.

In a power-based order, superior air strikes are an alternative to merely offering negotiations, at least as a means of forcing them. This was a lesson in power politics, demonstrating to Europeans how to end fighting and compel negotiations.

We must prepare ourselves for the fact that this kind of behavior will set a precedent and that those who merely point to the rules will politically lose out. Where chaos reigns, one needs the means to assert oneself within it and to enforce a minimum of adherence to rules. The current moment of respite gives us the opportunity to reflect on the new circumstances and reposition ourselves. However, this «moment of respite» means that we don't have unlimited time. Europe must act quickly.

_**Herfried Münkler** is Professor Emeritus of Political Theory at Humboldt University in Berlin._
