headline: The redefinition of photography - a studio visit with Dayanita Singh in Delhi
lead: The Indian photographic artist Dayanita Singh teaches us to see the old in a new light. An encounter
body:
# The redefinition of photography - a studio visit with Dayanita Singh in Delhi

*The Indian photographic artist Dayanita Singh teaches us to see the old in a new light. An encounter*

**Susanna Koeberle** · NZZ am Sonntag Magazin · 2025-10-11 · 2259 words · [ld.1906052](https://www.nzz.ch/nzz-am-sonntag-magazin/die-neudefinition-der-fotografie-ein-atelierbesuch-bei-dayanita-singh-in-delhi-ld.1906052)

![Dayanita Singh's paintings always show traces of relationships.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/e982c935-8615-45a3-856e-c2a3e6abbd5e.jpg?crop=4893,4891,x1673,y613)
*Dayanita Singh's paintings always show traces of relationships.* (Mark Henley / Panos Pictures)

Everything happens very quickly. Shortly after my interview request via email, Dayanita Singh wants to FaceTime. Her cheerful face appears on the screen, and the unapproachable image I had of the internationally renowned photographic artist immediately dissolves. This warm exchange continues until our meeting.

One of the first terms that comes up in conversation with Dayanita Singh is «dissemination.» «Dissemination,» that's what she's aiming for, she says. Although the German word doesn't fully capture the meaning. Dayanita Singh wants to make art accessible to as many people as possible, for example through books.

The book is a democratic means of disseminating art – a book is more affordable than a painting or a sculpture. Singh's sales events are also significant in this context. Each book is signed by her and lovingly wrapped in fabric. Anyone who buys one is simultaneously treated to an encounter with her and ennobled as a curator. Anyone who owns such a work can easily put together their own Dayanita Singh exhibition. The artist's ideas spread.

But «dissemination» also includes the idea of ​​germination; the word derives from the Latin verb «disseminare,» meaning to sow. It originates from the world of plants. By spreading an idea, one changes one's environment.

I first met Dayanita Singh a few weeks later in Italy, more precisely in Bologna. There, the Indian-born artist held a small ceremony at the State Archives. She presented the «Archivio di Stato di Bologna» with one of her «pillars»—as she calls them: stacked wooden structures covered with her photographs, resembling columns.

With this gift, she expresses her gratitude for being allowed to photograph in the archives of the capital of Emilia-Romagna. The small-scale gift ceremony has the feel of a performance. With an almost dance-like movement, the artist removes the plastic covering that concealed the artwork.

She seems delighted, and everyone present applauds. But shortly afterward, her critical gaze reveals that she wants to change something about the composition of the pictures. Two friends restack the heavy wooden pieces until it looks right to her.

## Study in New York

Dayanita Singh is internationally renowned for her artist's books, which she conceives of as portable museums. A distinctive feature of her work is how she presents photography, thereby expanding the boundaries of the medium. She typically displays her black-and-white photographs of people—friends, family, musicians, or dancers—archives, or buildings in mobile, self-designed wooden structures.

There are two distinct schools of thought on how to approach an artist's work: either starting with her biography or with her work itself. In Dayanita Singh's case, both approaches are equally insightful. Her very first publication, from 1986, was formative for her life and work. The book was titled «Zakir Hussain,» after the legendary tabla player and composer (1951–2024) who played a central role in Dayanita's development.

The tabla is an Indian percussion instrument whose rhythmic sounds possess a trance-like quality. Singh translated this musical technique into a book by collaged the grid-like image sequences of contact prints and combining them with handwritten notes. The book was published while she was still studying at the National Institute of Design (NID) in Ahmedabad, where she studied visual communication.

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/9404de39-66d8-4f44-9bbf-3afb8f03265f.jpg?width=1024)
** (Dayanita Singh studio)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/cd959ea6-2ccf-4c0b-9b66-175a5c9cd9b2.jpg?width=1024)
** (Dayanita Singh studio)

![«Zakir Hussain Maquette» (Steidl, 2019) is a new edition of the book that Singh published in 1986 as a student. It is about her mentor, the Indian tabla player.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/11/a9a8e44a-581d-4068-9bc3-47567031895a.jpg?width=1024)
*«Zakir Hussain Maquette» (Steidl, 2019) is a new edition of the book that Singh published in 1986 as a student. It is about her mentor, the Indian tabla player.* (Dayanita Singh studio)

For six winters, the young woman accompanied Hussain's troupe and toured India with the musicians. Although the group played traditional Indian music for a wide audience, they had come into contact with Western music at an early stage.

As a teenager, Hussain met Beatles member George Harrison, who had traveled to India to study with sitar master Ravi Shankar. During their tour with Hussain, Singh not only photographed his performances but also the musicians' daily lives.

Focusing on a single figure and documenting their life was unusual in photography at the time. Later, she decided to train as a photojournalist and documentary photographer in New York. She learned to focus from Zakir Hussain – because when playing, a musician must be completely present with their instrument and able to block everything else out. Focus isn't just important in photography, she says; it's also central to her life as an artist. His concept of dissemination also influenced her. After all, that's precisely what the musician did: he disseminated classical Indian music.

Singh grew up as the eldest of four sisters in a well-to-do environment marked by transformations in several respects: After the partition of India in 1947, her parents had to move from Lahore to Delhi. Her father, she tells us during our second meeting in her Delhi studio, was obsessed with constantly rearranging their apartment. When guests came, he would transform the living room into a bedroom. He was also constantly rearranging furniture.

Her father's constant reconfiguration of the home greatly displeased her mother. By nature, she was an archivist, a woman who craved order. However, one thing the parents did share was a sense of curation.

While Kanwar Mahinderpal Singh curated the living spaces, Nony Singh, the mother, used the glass table as a display case for her photographs. Or she compiled extensive photo albums. And who was her absolute favorite subject?

Exactly, Dayanita Singh, how could it be otherwise? And what became of this daughter? An artist who constantly rearranges her own photographs.

Dayanita Singh likes to compare photography to raw vegetables. Photography, too, is raw material that needs to be transformed. She doesn't simply photograph beautiful things. Her images, whether of people or inanimate objects, are always traces of relationships. She captures moments of togetherness.

Singh speaks of photography as a form of friendship. One of the questions she poses is: How can photography become a physical and emotional experience? In this context, the Indian artist also speaks of photography as a hyperlink.

![Singh's photo collection «Museum of Dance (Mother Loves to Dance)» in the Gropius Bau in Berlin, 2022.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/7a63727e-877d-478a-a38b-f254d4ec810b.jpg?crop=2121,1591,x253,y0)
*Singh's photo collection «Museum of Dance (Mother Loves to Dance)» in the Gropius Bau in Berlin, 2022.* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

![Singh's jacket with nine pockets turns the wearer into a mobile museum (Museum Bhavan, Steidl 2017).](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/56916e3c-275b-4f40-963a-5d6e7758ae8a.jpg?crop=3307,4195,x0,y714)
*Singh's jacket with nine pockets turns the wearer into a mobile museum (Museum Bhavan, Steidl 2017).* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

Singh's paintings are rarely intended to be hung on walls. They are either published in books or arranged in groups within wooden structures for exhibitions. Sometimes these structures resemble shipping crates on wheels, sometimes oversized screens, and occasionally almost houses.

![One of the nine leporellos in the Bhavan Museum. The book transforms into an exhibition in front of the Taj Mahal.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/11/085ea835-134b-4788-85d2-b824989bc36e.jpg?width=1024)
*One of the nine leporellos in the Bhavan Museum. The book transforms into an exhibition in front of the Taj Mahal.* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

This type of presentation is significant in several respects. Firstly, it recalls the father's activity as a «family architect.» A family friend was a well-known architect and designer and had his furniture made by the same carpenter who also worked for Singh's family.

Singh still has her precisely crafted displays made of dark teak wood produced in this family workshop. Furthermore, these spatial structures challenge the classical form of photography by bringing it closer to installations, as seen in contemporary art since the 1970s.

![Dayanita Singh is bringing a mobile exhibition of her book «Museum of Chance» to the India Art Fair 2015.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/e3b01753-4857-4a37-aa75-3b94c507bd93.jpg?crop=2825,2976,x0,y0)
*Dayanita Singh is bringing a mobile exhibition of her book «Museum of Chance» to the India Art Fair 2015.* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

A short time later, Dayanita Singh and I met again in India. Following the itinerary of several exhibitions initiated by the artist, I traveled from Mumbai to Ahmedabad and from there to Vadodara.

It is, as it were, the artist's eyes that guide my journey through «her» country. I visit many impressive temples and buildings. Even more significant, however, are the encounters with local people that she facilitates for me. I am not simply a tourist, but a visitor. Through the artist, I become part of her network.

## The «third breast»

Arriving in Delhi, the journey takes less time than expected because it's Sunday. I'm on my way to the artist's studio. Delhi is a city with around 34.7 million inhabitants, and navigating this behemoth is an unpredictable undertaking.

![Self-portrait by the photographic artist Dayanita Singh («Museum of Chance», Steidl, 2013).](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/8e02f7fd-5dd0-4c3f-ab40-c2f3c521ae12.jpg?crop=2865,3407,x0,y0)
*Self-portrait by the photographic artist Dayanita Singh («Museum of Chance», Steidl, 2013).* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

I arrive a little early, and the artist is still in her daily yoga session. In India, yoga isn't a lifestyle activity for stress management, but rather a part of everyday life. Similarly, photography is Singh's everyday way of seeing the world. It's fitting, then, that she refers to her camera, which she often carries at waist level, as her third breast. Perhaps this also explains her grounded demeanor and open nature.

Before Singh shows me her studio, which is located above her apartment, she makes an unusual suggestion: would we like to spontaneously curate a mini-exhibition together?

She takes out a box containing 16 objects designed by a friend who is an architect: a kind of nut, a bird, coins – and unusually – a totem with a human head – all painted gold.

The collection is embedded in a layer of material reminiscent of earth. When you pick up the artifacts, an imprint remains. Less than twenty minutes later, Singh looks at the result with satisfaction: the resulting arrangement could serve as a model for a future exhibition. This is definitely an unusual way to begin an interview. And it offers insight into the artist's working method.

Dayanita Singh's studio is a magical place: a paradise of books and a museum in one. Over the course of her career, Singh has created various «mobile museums» dedicated to different themes: archives, architecture, music, or portraits of people. Nine of these series were brought together in the 2017 book «Museum Bhavan.» The artist's museums continue to grow to this day.

Through her practice, she turns the Western concept of the museum as a lofty temple of art on its head. And sometimes Singh herself becomes a walking museum: In «My Life as Museum» (2018), she wore a jacket with nine pockets in Venice, each containing one of her «Museum Bhavan» leporellos. Everything is in motion, just as it was when she toured India with Zakir Hussain.

Several stacks of photographs lie on a table. Dayanita picks up a few pictures, and suddenly a detail catches her eye. She holds two pictures side by side: «What's going on here? I know something's happening,» she says.

As the archivist of her own archive, she can respond to existing material in new ways, creating new lines and narratives. Archives as places of hidden and silenced knowledge have long fascinated Singh; she has been photographing these spaces for many years in both India and Italy. Next year, in mid-April, a major exhibition will open at the «Archivio di Stato» in Venice, showcasing her 25-year engagement with Italian archives.

Her own photographic archive is becoming increasingly important to her. She has been working intensively with it since the pandemic. The first «Montages,» in which she reconfigures old and newer images, were created starting in 2019.

She cuts her photographs herself, overlays multiple images, and creates something new by layering widely separated eras and places: echo chambers that bridge time and space. As a viewer, one senses that different worlds are meeting here, yet the eye accepts these fictional places as third spaces.

In doing so, Singh also exposes the constructed nature of every photograph – a highly topical issue, keyword AI-manipulated images. She says that these superimpositions have made her a «photo-architect.»

![Mona Ahmed, dancing in the center, lived in a cemetery in Delhi. Singh shared a deep friendship with her. The photo is from «Museum of Dance (Mother Loves to Dance)».](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/11/b9270424-a2a8-43c3-9443-5fcf20f16a5c.jpg?width=1024)
*Mona Ahmed, dancing in the center, lived in a cemetery in Delhi. Singh shared a deep friendship with her. The photo is from «Museum of Dance (Mother Loves to Dance)».* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

## Singh's Paths to Switzerland

She repeatedly mentions mentors who significantly changed her life. Zakir Hussain was one such person. Another figure is Mona Ahmed, a transgender person. Singh met Ahmed in 1989 while working as a photojournalist; she was tasked with portraying a eunuch community in Delhi.

The pictures were not initially published; instead, a close friendship developed from this encounter. And this is where Zurich comes into play, or rather, the publisher Walter Keller (1953–2014). Singh first met him in 1992 at the bookstore of his publishing house, Scalo, located on Weinbergstrasse.

He looked at the portfolio of the then 31-year-old photographer and recommended that she not make books initially, but instead focus on building an archive. Dayanita Singh followed this advice.

In 1997, she received a grant from the foundation established by Swiss photographer Robert Frank, which allowed her to continue her career as a photographer. At that time, Singh worked primarily as a family photographer; she gave the portraits to the families as gifts. When Walter Keller agreed to publish her photographs, the next surprise followed.

He wanted to show Dayanita's pictures of Mona. Of course, not without her consent. The book launch took place at the Mehendyan Cemetery in Delhi, where Mona lived until her death in 2017. Even the Swiss ambassador attended. The video of the book launch was shown this year in the exhibition «Mona and Myself» at the Gallery White in Vadodara.

I looked at them. Even after her death, Mona haunts several of the artist's photomontages, almost as a ghost. In one video, Mona can be seen reciting old poems in Urdu.

As soon as I stepped out of the air-conditioned gallery space in Delhi, I was enveloped by the Indian heat. This sensation mingled with what I had seen and heard. Photography is also about feeling. That is the gift Dayanita Singh gives us.

![The artist's early work from the eighties, collected in the book «Let's See» (Steidl 2022).](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/10/08/f684976b-dcdf-4016-ad4f-627a1b3e2d9f.jpg?width=1024)
*The artist's early work from the eighties, collected in the book «Let's See» (Steidl 2022).* (Dayanita Singh Studio)

headline: In Rio's favelas, killing becomes a ritual
lead: Following the bloodiest police raid in Brazilian history, relatives speak of executions. While many citizens of Rio de Janeiro celebrate the police, the drug gangs continue as usual.
body:
# In Rio's favelas, killing becomes a ritual

*Following the bloodiest police raid in Brazilian history, relatives speak of executions. While many citizens of Rio de Janeiro celebrate the police, the drug gangs continue as usual.*

**Thomas Milz (text), Francisco Proner (images), Rio de Janeiro** · International · 2025-11-05 · 1922 words · [ld.1909890](https://www.nzz.ch/international/in-rios-favelas-wird-das-toeten-zum-ritual-ld.1909890)

At the entrance to the Bairro 13 slum stands a burned-out car wreck. Next to it lie steel beams that, three days earlier, had served as a barricade against the police. The police had arrived to arrest Doca, who runs the operations of the Comando Vermelho (CV) drug gang in Rio de Janeiro's North Zone. After bloody clashes, the police later reported sixty dead drug criminals and four dead police officers that day. But this number quickly proved to be too low.

Behind the barricades lies a football pitch, the heart of the favela, as such slums are called in Rio. The morning after the police raid, the bodies found by residents in a forest further up the mountain were brought here. Fifty-seven dead, whose deaths the police had previously concealed. The bodies lay shoulder to shoulder on the street, their grieving relatives bent over them.

![Barricades made of burning cars were intended to halt the police advance in the Bairro 13 slum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/ea947f4c-1cf7-4bca-8bf9-906d4ca0fa2c.jpg?width=1024)

![Relatives are trying to identify the bodies found in a wooded area above the impoverished settlement. A total of 57 bodies were discovered there.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/1d6f536c-94bc-49eb-a1c0-2edc2f402fad.jpg?width=1024)

Now, two days later, the pools of blood have vanished. So has the police. The enraged locals would lynch any police officer who showed up here, says Adriana Odara of the Movimento Negro Unificado, a human rights organization representing the interests of the Afro-Brazilian population. She plans to show a group of journalists the wooded area on the mountain where the bodies were found today. But she's still waiting for permission. We'll see who's in charge up there hours later.

So, people wait at the community center next to the soccer field. Here, Fabiana Silva is explaining to relatives how they can gain access to the bodies. She works for a government agency that provides free legal aid. She says that the fact that the forensic medicine department is keeping the bodies sealed for so long is not standard procedure.

Relatives claim that the police executed the «boys,» as the rank-and-file fighters of the Comando Vermelho are called, in the forest, even though they had surrendered. «We don't deny that they belonged to the CV,» says one woman. «But executions are unacceptable.»

Activist Odara says they found many bodies with their hands bound behind their backs and gunshot wounds to the forehead and neck. Some had burn marks, indicating torture. Others had their torsos slashed open and their limbs severed; one body was also decapitated. Odara shows a photo of a police officer with a sword. Rio's police chief, however, claims the bodies were mutilated afterward to incriminate the police.

![Human rights activist Adriana Odara says many bodies were found with hands tied behind the back and gunshot wounds to the forehead and neck.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/8e77177b-7a5e-4b7b-b532-6f0d9880e6d1.jpg?width=1024)

![A resident of the slum shows cartridge cases he has collected in front of his house.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/cbbb61e7-491e-4f11-b576-a35a8e53bd21.jpg?width=1024)

They are demanding an independent autopsy, as they don't trust the state medical examiners, says Odara. They also doubt the official figures – 117 dead and 113 arrested criminals. Local residents estimate the total number of dead to be 200, Odara says. There are still many missing persons, confirms legal advisor Fabiana Silva, without wanting to give exact figures.

## «Operation Containment»

Last Tuesday morning around 4:30 a.m., «Operation Containment» was launched with 2,500 officers. Police advanced into Complexo da Penha, a cluster of favelas named after the baroque Penha Church perched atop a hill, from several directions. Bairro 13 is part of this complex. Meanwhile, other units advanced into Complexo do Alemão on the opposite side of the hill.

According to police, the two favela complexes near the international airport are the CV headquarters in Rio and a training center for CV members from across Brazil. Up to ten tons of cocaine and at least fifty assault rifles are reportedly delivered here monthly and then distributed from here to other favelas controlled by the CV.

In the late 1970s, the Comando Vermelho (Red Command) was founded in a prison by drug criminals and left-wing opponents of the then-military dictatorship. This gave rise to a criminal gang that justified its actions as a fight for social justice. This explains the Robin Hood image that some members of the Red Command still have today. The CV supports imprisoned members and their families with drug money. Like Márcio Santos Nepomuceno, who has led the CV from prison for almost thirty years. His family considers him a political prisoner of the corrupt state.

![A street in the Penha favela complex. For over eighteen hours, police engaged in firefights here with fighters from the Comando Vermelho gang.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/dd0c82e2-ed0c-4308-b270-bbaa70593707.jpg?width=1024)

![Traces of the fighting can be seen at the entrance to the street known as Cabaré.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/6e5bde47-63d2-433b-8e5d-786f7fbb8f5f.jpg?width=1024)

In reality, Comando Vermelho runs a ruthless business. They are locked in a bitter struggle with the gangs Terceiro Comando and Amigos dos Amigos for control of Rio's favelas. For example, the day before the police raid, CV attacked a favela belonging to Terceiro Comando, killing two innocent civilians. However, Comando Vermelho's main adversaries are now militias formed by corrupt police officers and soldiers. Founded in the 1960s as vigilante groups, these militias are now also involved in drug trafficking, extortion, and, more recently, investing in the real estate market.

## Unmistakable fronts

The many rival gangs make Rio a patchwork of organized crime. Rio's newspapers are almost daily filled with reports about politicians with ties to the gangs, and dozens of police officers have been dismissed in recent years because of their connections to the militias. This chaotic situation fuels speculation among the Cariocas, the residents of Rio. Is the far-right governor Cláudio Castro fighting the Comando Vermelho on behalf of the militias? And is the left-wing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva protecting the drug cartels?

In Rio, favela residents are always blamed for all the city's problems, says a local woman who wants to accompany us up the mountain. For her safety, we'll call her M. But the real masterminds of organized crime are outside the favelas. «How do the weapons and drugs get across borders and through checkpoints before being delivered here?» The guys here from Bairro 13 certainly couldn't handle such logistics.

Naming these masterminds would be dangerous, she says. They must have access to internal police information, in any case. «On the eve of the raid, everyone here in Bairro 13 knew the police were coming,» says M. That explains why the CV boss, Doca, was able to escape.

## Armed men are waiting on the mountain

After two hours, the visit to the mountain is permitted. The journey continues by motorcycle, past roadblocks, and two kilometers up the road. «You have nothing to fear when God is on your side,» is written on a house wall. At an intersection, two horses stand in a pile of garbage. In the houses above the intersection, the «boys» put up fierce resistance that day. Now, three days later, armed youths are standing here again. «Please don't photograph them,» says M. The air smells of marijuana.

![On October 29, local residents recovered dozens of bodies from a forest above the slums.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/161bf409-a3eb-440b-89e6-87dd27e23524.jpg?width=1024)

![Traces of the firefights can be seen in the street known as Cabaré.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/b06dd3f6-a7d1-4837-9d4c-6c43df2df5aa.jpg?width=1024)

Videos circulating on social media show police storming the street known as Cabaré that morning. In the comments under the videos, they are hailed as heroes. «Only dead bandits are good bandits,» «The vagrants must die.» According to polls, two-thirds of Rio's residents support the police action; in the slums, approval is even higher.

Many yearn for a hardline policy like that practiced by El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, even though Bukele has suspended fundamental rights and carried out mass arrests in his country. «Direitos humanos,» or human rights, are merely an excuse used by left-wing politicians to protect bandits, one hears people say, even in Rio's slums.

The narrow streets of Cabaré are roofed with corrugated iron. But now the rain is dripping through everywhere. Police riddled the roofs with bullets from helicopters, says a gaunt figure collecting spent cartridges. All numbered, so by the police, he says, pointing to the bullet holes in his house: «God protected me.»

![«Penha belongs to Christ»: a religious message amidst a war zone. From helicopters, police riddled the corrugated iron roof of the Cabaré street with rifle bullets.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/fb36c3e9-3852-42f5-851d-4642024272db.jpg?width=1024)

![Residents are trying to remove the traces of the firefights.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/2779ece4-4d14-4f35-896b-a623ea06b3cb.jpg?width=1024)

Across the street, three bullet holes are visible in the front door of an elderly woman's house. The police had been searching for bandits in a corner building, but that wasn't their area. She had known the «boys» since she was a child, and they had always respected her. The recent press reports that they demanded protection money from them were untrue. On the contrary, the woman says, the «boys» were always there for her when she needed help. Unlike the state, which sends the police to kill people here, M. adds.

The corner house the police were looking for is located one street over. Thirty armed men climbed in through a window and barricaded themselves in her living room, a 36-year-old woman recounts. «War will be met with war,» the police officers who surrounded the house shouted. She negotiated with the police for the «guys» to surrender. «Otherwise, the police would have stormed our house and killed them all,» she says.

Her house and the small restaurant next door were riddled with bullets. She didn't know if the refrigerators and ovens still worked. The police officers had stuffed their bags with drinks from her refrigerators and moved on.

## The forest

Above Cabaré Street, a concrete staircase built into the hillside leads into the forest. Police drone footage shows the uniformed «boys,» armed with automatic rifles, fleeing down it that day. Straight into a deadly trap. Special forces approaching from the other side of the mountain had long since cut off the route into the Complexo do Alemão. Now the «boys» were surrounded.

![Residents recovered another body from the forest separating the Penha favela complex from the Complexo do Alemão. Fighters from the Comando Vermelho had resisted police here for hours.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/e6b66613-3666-4eb3-9b90-5da4c4f476c6.jpg?width=1024)

![Local residents are combing the forest in search of more bodies. Dozens of people are still considered missing.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/64805f01-e053-4679-996c-ae44e770566f.jpg?width=1024)

Residents later found the 57 bodies in the forest. A few camouflage uniforms, shoes, and backpacks lying on the forest floor bear witness to the carnage. Bloodstains are visible on rocks, and bandages are scattered about.

«We couldn't go any further up the mountain,» M. said. Why remained unclear. There's a quarry up there, rumored to be a hideout for the Comando Vermelho. Locals said the police had dumped more bodies in a nearby ravine. But the area was inaccessible without mountaineering equipment. So we had to turn back. On the way down, we passed young men with machine guns and radios.

## The protest

A protest march has gathered on the football field down in Bairro 13. Left-wing politicians and human rights activists are giving interviews. Flags bearing the names of Karl Marx and Che Guevara are visible, as are demonstrators wearing Palestinian scarves and Islamic Jihad T-shirts. Chants against the governor ring out repeatedly: «Cláudio Castro is a murderer!»

A TV helicopter circles overhead. In a restaurant around the corner, the patrons are glued to the television, which shows an aerial view of their neighborhood. The program displays images of the protest alongside videos of the fighting from three days ago. Bandits who made life hell for honest citizens were killed, the presenter rants. A group of young men, undisturbed by this, are having their lunch. They have propped their rifles against the wall next to the table.

![Residents protested against the police raid in Bairro 13 on October 31st. According to official figures, 117 members of the Comando Vermelho and four police officers died in the operation.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/b564cdc7-6d2a-46a7-9b34-40ae096444d0.jpg?width=1024)

![Hundreds of people are taking part in the protest in Bairro 13. In the background, the baroque Penha Church, which gave the region its name, can be seen.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/62673d56-1b72-4a03-9399-2f268e30d0f4.jpg?width=1024)

While the protest march moves through Bairro 13, shots are fired a few kilometers away in another favela, where the Comando Vermelho and the Terceiro Comando are fighting. On a city highway, an innocent 28-year-old woman in the back seat of her taxi is fatally struck in the head by a stray bullet. Three days after Rio de Janeiro made history with Brazil's bloodiest police raid, the city has returned to normal.

![One of fifteen barricades with which the Comando Vermelho had sealed off the slum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/11/04/849e090a-8aca-43f2-bade-b23c5a48e65a.jpg?width=1024)
*One of fifteen barricades with which the Comando Vermelho had sealed off the slum.*

---

- A police raid in Rio's favelas resulted in at least 117 deaths and 113 arrests, though locals claim there were up to 200 deaths and accuse the police of executions and torture.
- The raid targeted Comando Vermelho, one of Brazil's most powerful drug cartels, known for drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and violent conflicts with rival groups and militias.
- The situation remains tense, with residents demanding independent investigations as debates over violence, corruption, and the state's role persist.
author: Thomas Milz (text), Francisco Proner (images), Rio de Janeiro

headline: Swimming in the crater that killed the dinosaurs: What extinguished life made humankind possible. A journey to the place of our origin.
lead: In the verdant wilderness of Mexico lies a museum. No sign points the way. An asteroid struck here 66 million years ago. What it left behind changed the Earth forever.
body:
# Swimming in the crater that killed the dinosaurs: What extinguished life made humankind possible. A journey to the place of our origin.

*In the verdant wilderness of Mexico lies a museum. No sign points the way. An asteroid struck here 66 million years ago. What it left behind changed the Earth forever.*

**Alexandra von Ascheraden** · Reisen · 2025-12-13 · 2383 words · [ld.1915019](https://www.nzz.ch/reisen/was-drei-viertel-des-lebens-ausloeschte-machte-den-menschen-erst-moeglich-eine-reise-an-den-ort-unserer-entstehung-ld.1915019)

An hour south of Mérida, the capital of Yucatán, the Chicxulub Science Museum lies hidden on a university campus. Only in the final stretch do life-size plastic dinosaurs dispel any doubts about whether this is the right place. The drive had led kilometer after kilometer along lonely roads lined with impenetrable thickets of green vegetation, without a single signpost. The taxi driver drove stoically and with a slight grumble, perhaps accustomed to unusual requests. None of his passengers had ever asked to come here before; he wasn't at all sure the destination even existed.

Finally: a solitary guardhouse, its barrier stretching across the street. The guard glances impassively at the driver's ID, exchanges it for a laminated slip of paper, and keeps it. This ensures that visitors leave the university grounds again in the evening. Then he opens the barrier. The taxi rolls along bumpy concrete roads across the university grounds, which are completely deserted on Sunday. And this particular museum is only open on Sundays.

Here, right here in this no-man's-land, an asteroid struck the limestone at a steep angle 66 million years ago, traveling at 72,000 kilometers per hour and wiping out three-quarters of all life on Earth. For a long time, researchers searched for the reasons behind what happened to the Earth and for the traces of this global annihilation

![Over 2400 freshwater sinkholes (cenotes) crisscross the Yucatán Peninsula; their circular arrangement follows the fault zones of the Chicxulub impact: Cenote near Muna from a bird's-eye view.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/1da30c8a-8a62-473b-b834-270e3fa1f378.jpg?width=1024)
*Over 2400 freshwater sinkholes (cenotes) crisscross the Yucatán Peninsula; their circular arrangement follows the fault zones of the Chicxulub impact: Cenote near Muna from a bird's-eye view.* (Hector Vivas / Getty)

![The Maya climbed long ladders into the cenotes to collect drinking water, because Yucatán has no rivers; the karst soil allows rainwater to seep away immediately: Divers in the Cenote Dos Ojos near Tulum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/3e2fc6d7-c4ff-45f4-a660-4ba6fd428f18.jpg?width=1024)
*The Maya climbed long ladders into the cenotes to collect drinking water, because Yucatán has no rivers; the karst soil allows rainwater to seep away immediately: Divers in the Cenote Dos Ojos near Tulum.* (Christophe Geyres / Imago)

## Impact winter and mass extinction

What is currently believed is that the impact in the shallow sea triggered massive earthquakes and waves up to 100 meters high, which developed into tsunamis. The asteroid's impact was so massive that the rock melted kilometers deep, partially vaporizing along with the impacting celestial body and leaving behind a crater 200 kilometers in diameter. Glowing rock dust was hurled into the stratosphere, and the heat ignited wildfires. Within a few days, such dense masses of soot and dust particles entered the atmosphere that sunlight could no longer penetrate it. A prolonged cold gripped the Earth, the so-called impact winter.

Three-quarters of life was extinguished. The majority of plants disappeared, including the enormous tree ferns, of which impressive fossils bear witness, and the giant clubmosses. The enormous herbivorous dinosaurs could no longer find food, and soon the carnivorous ones followed suit. In the sea, the gigantic ichthyosaurs died out, as did the ammonites. On land, no animal larger than a rat survived.

The triumph of mammals only began with this cataclysmic event from space. And so did the rise of humble organisms like fungi, mosses, and lichens, and later ferns and flowering plants. Without this impact, there might be no humans. Had the dinosaurs survived, mammals might have remained marginal. And perhaps we humans would have too. Our existence may owe itself to a cosmic accident. And today, tourists unknowingly bathe in the crater it left behind.

That's why life-size plastic Velociraptors lurk at the museum's entrance. Behind the glass wall facing the courtyard, the Brachiosaurus towers over the ten-meter-high building and easily over the Tyrannosaurus Rex and all the other plastic dinosaurs that populate the courtyard with it.

![The cenotes follow the fracture zones of the asteroid impact in concentric rings, a pattern that can only be seen from space: aerial view of the Yucatán Peninsula.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/6289b30c-1f82-41f1-8ed7-dc8f6c29606e.jpg?width=1024)
*The cenotes follow the fracture zones of the asteroid impact in concentric rings, a pattern that can only be seen from space: aerial view of the Yucatán Peninsula.* (Pascal Kobeh / Imago)

![For day trips from Cancún, it's a time-saving destination: sixty meters in diameter, azure water, Instagram-worthy – the Cenote Ik Kil, three minutes from the Mayan pyramids of Chichén Itzá.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/9cde1c8e-9487-4f29-b768-6c34a198c19a.jpg?width=1024)
*For day trips from Cancún, it's a time-saving destination: sixty meters in diameter, azure water, Instagram-worthy – the Cenote Ik Kil, three minutes from the Mayan pyramids of Chichén Itzá.* (Hector Vivas / Getty)

## The search for the crater

As difficult as the museum was to find, it was well worth the effort. Visitors aren't accompanied by ordinary museum guides, but by staff from the university's affiliated research departments. The floor-to-ceiling projections of maps, graphics, and models vividly illustrate the sheer scale of the event that melted the Earth's crust here. Geophysicists display drill cores and rock samples from the depths of the crater, presenting the geological evidence of what once so abruptly transformed everything in this area.

For a very long time, scientists searched for the impact crater of the asteroid whose impact was suspected to have wiped out the dinosaurs. The goal was to prove this theory. It was assumed to be located somewhere on the ocean floor. And indeed it is. It lies approximately halfway beneath the Gulf of Mexico, in the area where tourists now throng the coral-white beaches.

It was precisely here that the Mexican oil company Pemex began large-scale exploratory drilling for oil in 1958. They found none. But at a depth of 1,300 meters, they encountered something remarkable: volcanic rock. Such a thing had never been found anywhere else in the region. Today, we know that a lava dome formed at this location due to the heat and force of the impact.

The large crater ring is not visible, although it is still detectable. Neither are the two smaller rings that formed closer to the impact center. The museum stands not far from the center of the crater left behind by the impacting asteroid. Leaving, one's steps hesitate, one's gaze sweeping across the landscape. Here, right here, in this seemingly peaceful region, languidly resting in the heat, it happened.

![All cenotes close no later than 5 pm; the modern tourism industry respects what was considered a divine law a thousand years ago: Divers in the Cenote Ponderosa near Tulum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/214e8b39-4928-4d5c-96c8-1101e82b5f22.jpg?width=1024)
*All cenotes close no later than 5 pm; the modern tourism industry respects what was considered a divine law a thousand years ago: Divers in the Cenote Ponderosa near Tulum.* (Christophe Geyres / Getty)

![The dripstone formations grow over millions of years, visible traces of time in the underground cave systems: stalactites in the Gran Cenote near Tulum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/5571fe51-aab0-459f-a1b6-05ae40a7eab5.jpg?width=1024)
*The dripstone formations grow over millions of years, visible traces of time in the underground cave systems: stalactites in the Gran Cenote near Tulum.* (Ullstein/Getty)

## The gift of disaster

One of the seemingly minor consequences of the impact was the formation of concentric fissures over millions of years through geological processes. When the vast coral reefs in the shallow sea later exposed the ground, forming the limestone formation we now call Yucatán, a massive cave system, following the circular crater rim, was created by the constant seepage of water. These cavities in the porous karst extend down to the groundwater level. The cenotes, with their vibrant turquoise freshwater that now feature in impressive tourist brochures, were formed where the ceilings of these subterranean caverns collapsed.

The cenotes follow the crater ring in concentric concentric rings, a pattern visible only from space. Those who bathe here move within the invisible imprint of the catastrophe.

![Without the underground karst cave systems, there would have been no Mayan civilization; the cities were built where access to groundwater was guaranteed: the house of the cenote in the ruins of Tulum.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/3bcd20a3-a6a5-4b8c-8a20-cf71f0ae072a.jpg?width=1024)
*Without the underground karst cave systems, there would have been no Mayan civilization; the cities were built where access to groundwater was guaranteed: the house of the cenote in the ruins of Tulum.* (Jon G. Fuller Jr. / UIG / Getty)

![After sunset, the Maya no longer dared to enter the caves. They were convinced that the water serpent Tsukán lived in the cenotes: offerings at the Santa María cenote after a Mayan ceremony in Homún.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/f59a4e74-197d-474d-a0f6-64d7d02dba3e.jpg?width=1024)
*After sunset, the Maya no longer dared to enter the caves. They were convinced that the water serpent Tsukán lived in the cenotes: offerings at the Santa María cenote after a Mayan ceremony in Homún.* (Rodrigo Abd / AP)

## Sacred springs of the Maya

Some cenotes are dozens of meters deep and lie exposed because the ceiling above them has collapsed due to erosion. Very often, however, only a roughly arm-length, more or less round hole in the ground hints at the presence of a cenote below, into which a tiny piece of its cave ceiling has fallen, discreetly revealing its location.

The Maya descended long ladders to draw drinking water from the riverbeds. Without them, the Mayan cities would not have existed. There are no rivers in Yucatán. The calcareous karst soil allows water to seep away quickly. Rainwater had to be stored in cisterns. The majority of the vital water supply came from the underground karst cave systems that provided access to groundwater.

The natural sinkholes were sacred. The Maya referred to the water-filled dolines as holy springs. No one would ever have dared to approach them after dusk. For, at sunset at the latest, one had to expect to encounter the water serpent Tsukán, the mythical guardian of the cenotes, in the cenotes.

Even today, all cenotes close by 5 p.m. at the latest. Respect remains: no swimming under floodlights for paying tourists. Only the catfish, which during the day curiously swim around the feet of bathers, remain.

## Instagram and mass tourism

Today, cenotes are primarily tourist attractions. One of the most frequently visited is Cenote Ik Kil, a three-minute drive from the famous Mayan pyramids at Chichén Itzá, for which it was an important source of drinking water. This makes it a time-saving destination for the numerous day-trip operators who bring busloads of tourists from Cancún to the Mayan highlights. Sixty meters in diameter, azure-blue water. You bathe two dozen meters below the surface in water that is sometimes fifty meters deep, surrounded by a packed wooden floating platform from which the aerial roots of the surrounding jungle hang. Many manage to take Instagram-worthy photos here. Then on to the next attraction, the next photo shoot.

For those who don't just want to efficiently tick «swimming in a cenote» off their bucket list, the many small cenotes off the beaten tourist track are worth a visit. With a bit of luck, you'll have the place almost entirely to yourself. Always wear a brightly colored life jacket in pink, red, blue, or yellow. You're not allowed in without one. The life jacket is your substitute for a lifeguard.

On the main roads leading out of the towns, leaflet distributors wave self-designed flyers for the cenotes, which can be reached via dirt roads branching off from the main roads.

Not far from Acanceh lies the Santa Rosa cenote. Wearing a bright pink life jacket, you can experience both here: swimming in an open cenote beneath aerial roots, or descending into the underworld, into a cenote where only a little light filters in through a small hole in the cave ceiling. Here, far from the hustle and bustle of Ik Kil, the meaning of cenotes for the Maya returns: sacred places that demanded respect.

A narrow wooden spiral staircase leads through a hole in the floor into the damp depths. With each step, the air grows cooler and more humid, the cave's twilight thickening. Only a distant drip breaks the silence. Just when the darkness threatens to become too great, the surface of the water below can be glimpsed. Blue and violet light from hidden spotlights colors the walls and water. The dripping becomes more audible. It comes from the stalactites on the cave ceiling. They form stalagmites in the water like pointed islands, visible millions of years of time. A small staircase leads from the wooden platform into the water, which is soft, cool, and inviting to swim.

![The stalactites in the Aktun Chen cave grow about one centimeter per century; the monumental formations here bear witness to millions of years of history: cave system in the Aktun Chen Natural Park, Riviera Maya.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/1179e8da-3631-4450-adf8-70d930533a22.jpg?width=1024)
*The stalactites in the Aktun Chen cave grow about one centimeter per century; the monumental formations here bear witness to millions of years of history: cave system in the Aktun Chen Natural Park, Riviera Maya.* (Greg Vaughn / Imago)

![The rainwater in the underground cavities creates its own ecosystems: Water lilies in the «Car Wash» cenote Aktun Ha near Tulum in an underwater photograph.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2025/12/08/58152283-af76-419d-b4d9-22ac81c9e672.jpg?width=1024)
*The rainwater in the underground cavities creates its own ecosystems: Water lilies in the «Car Wash» cenote Aktun Ha near Tulum in an underwater photograph.* (Imago)

## The Mayan belief system persists

Down here, where the darkness of the cave envelops you and only the dripping of the stalactites breaks the silence, you can sense why the Maya both feared and revered these places. After sunset, they believed, Tsukán, the water serpent, dwells here. To this day, all cenotes close at 5 p.m. The modern tourism industry respects what was considered divine law a thousand years ago. It is one of the few continuities that bridge the gap between the pre-Columbian past and the tourist present. Mayan beliefs persist, not as folkloric decoration, but as a practiced boundary.

Of the roughly one hundred cenotes that have been opened to tourists here, ten percent are managed by the local population. Only in these cases does the money collected go directly to the village community. These cenotes can be identified by a painted board on which someone from the village has neatly painted «turismo comunitario» (community tourism).

One of these is the Yokdzonot cenote, just twenty minutes from Ik Kil. It was once used as a source of drinking water by railway workers who settled there. When water pipes were laid in 1958, the cenote became a garbage dump. Ten years ago, the locals rediscovered what the asteroid had created 66 million years ago. Fifty villagers joined forces to remove the trash and attract tourists.

María, who sells tickets at the entrance, explains: «It was hard work that initially brought no income, so many dropped out. In the end, only sixteen people remained. They are still involved today.» They cleared the uphill paths, planted flowers in walled beds, built a restaurant up there, and secured the descent to the cenote, which is bordered by steep walls, with retaining walls, stairs, and railings.

The water's vibrant blue expanse measures forty meters in diameter. Those who descend the steps and, clad in a bright yellow life jacket, float in the soft freshwater—less chilly than expected—find themselves almost alone. Thick bundles of aerial roots dance on the surface, jungle leaves drift by. Catfish glide leisurely past. Birds sing. The voices of the few other bathers drift softly over. The fascination that the cenotes held for the Maya remains palpable.

The road to get here wasn't easy for the village cooperative. Once everything was finished, nobody came for a year. The frustration was immense. They persevered. Word slowly began to spread. The government finally agreed to subsidies. Today, the cooperative members earn their living from the business. Ten percent of the profits go towards other local community projects. «It wasn't easy. But we've built a future for ourselves here.»

It's a remarkable turn of events: what began as a cosmic catastrophe became the foundation of a high culture, degenerated into the garbage dump of modernity, and is now becoming the economic basis of a village community. The cenotes are undergoing a cultural metamorphosis, progressing from reverence to neglect to commercial exploitation. That some of the money flows back into the community is a form of justice that tourism in this region can offer.

All these fascinating cenotes may look similar, yet each one is unique. No one knows how many there are. The vegetation here in Yucatán is so lush that most are overgrown and hidden from view.

Those who bathe here immerse themselves in a twofold wonder: the cosmic catastrophe that wiped out three-quarters of life 66 million years ago, thus paving the way for the triumph of mammals and ultimately humankind; and the millennia-old Mayan culture, which made its livelihood from this catastrophe, elevating the cenotes to sacred springs and surrounding them with myths that resonate to this day.

Time operates on a different scale here. Above, on the surface, tourists pose in neon pink life jackets for Instagram photos. Below, in the cool blue of the water, stalactites have been dripping for millions of years. The crater reveals its secrets only reluctantly.

headline: Dario and Daniela Amodei: the siblings who defy the Pentagon
lead: Anthropic is one of the most successful AI companies. Behind it are a brother and sister from San Francisco who initially had no interest in the tech world.
body:
# Dario and Daniela Amodei: the siblings who defy the Pentagon

*Anthropic is one of the most successful AI companies. Behind it are a brother and sister from San Francisco who initially had no interest in the tech world.*

**Ruth Fulterer** · Technologie · 2026-03-12 · 1472 words · [ld.1928134](https://www.nzz.ch/technologie/dario-und-daniela-amodei-die-geschwister-die-dem-pentagon-die-stirn-bieten-ld.1928134)

![The Amodei siblings did not give in to the Pentagon in the dispute over the use of AI.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/11/696d710a-0aab-46c7-8d05-b97044984556.jpg?crop=2188,2917,x0,y0)
*The Amodei siblings did not give in to the Pentagon in the dispute over the use of AI.* (PD; Editing NZZ)

The most striking thing about Dario and Daniela Amodei is their unassuming nature. Unlike most tech CEOs, you could easily picture them doing their weekly grocery shopping. He is an easygoing type, looks more like he is settled in for a night in front of the TV than a gym member, and often has a broad grin on his face. She always looks her conversation partners in the eye and places her other hand on top when shaking hands. They could not be further removed from the personas of a Sam Altman, a Mark Zuckerberg, or a Jeff Bezos. And yet, these siblings are now in the spotlight as tough figures.

In the dispute over their company Anthropic, the Amodeis stood up to the Pentagon. They wanted to have a say in how the government used the chatbot Claude and refused to budge on their red lines, even under pressure.

As a result, Anthropic not only lost its status as the primary supplier of artificial intelligence (AI) to the U.S. government, but the company was also effectively declared an enemy of the state: It is now considered a supply chain risk. Anyone doing business with the U.S. government is prohibited from using Anthropic. Dario Amodei filed a lawsuit against this decision on Monday.

Few expected the tech company to fight this battle to the bitter end. But it's typical of the Amodeis. Of Dario, but also of his sister Daniela. Because it's not just in their demeanor that they differ from other AI founders.

## Dario became politically active as a physics student

The Amodeis grew up in the Mission District, a working-class neighborhood in San Francisco shaped by its Latino and queer communities. According to media reports, their father, Riccardo, was a trained leatherworker who had come to the U.S. from the Tuscan town of Massa Marittima. Their mother, Elena Engel, a Jewish American from Chicago, managed renovation projects at libraries in the area. They were said to be a close couple with idealistic values, which they also passed on to their children.

Dario was born in 1983, Daniela in 1987. They were teenagers during the dot-com boom. But Silicon Valley, although very close, didn't interest either of them.

Dario was a math nerd, took part in the Physics Olympiad with the American team in 2000, and subsequently studied physics. However, he was also interested in world politics. At 20, he urged his fellow students in his university's campus newspaper to take a stand against the Iraq War instead of passively accepting it: «We, who have so much power to influence the future, astonishingly forfeit our right to do so,» he wrote. He continued, almost prophetically: «We should never allow ourselves to be degraded to amoral technicians who operate the machines of war as casually as we operate our computers.»

His switch from physics to AI was also due to the death of his father. Riccardo died of a rare disease, for which the chances of a cure improved significantly just a few years later. For Amodei, this was the motivation to move more towards biology – and then to turn to AI as a tool that could accelerate all kinds of research. At least, that's how he tells it in interviews.

He began his career at a research lab of the Chinese company Baidu at Stanford and moved to Google's AI research lab, Google Brain, in 2015. During this time, Dario was invited to a prestigious dinner that would go down in tech history. There, Elon Musk and Sam Altman presented their plan: an AI research lab dedicated to serving humanity. This became OpenAI.

Amodei was not impressed: «It felt like it was more about famous tech investors and entrepreneurs than about AI researchers,» Wired magazine quoted him as saying. But a few months later, he joined OpenAI after all, because the company had attracted some very well-known AI researchers. Two years later, he brought his sister on board.

![Dario Amodei laid one of the foundations for Chat-GPT at OpenAI.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/06/18751425-5f02-42b8-bf23-643aec011ccc.jpg?width=1024)
*Dario Amodei laid one of the foundations for Chat-GPT at OpenAI.* (Denis Balibouse / Reuters)

## Daniela is interested in literature, music and people

Daniela Amodei studied literature and flute, then worked in development aid and politics – including as a campaign manager for a Democratic congressman. In 2013, she moved to Silicon Valley. She was an early employee at the fintech company Stripe, initially working as a recruiter, later in risk management.

She explained how literature, music, politics and technology fit together in an interview with an investment firm: Playing music in an orchestra teaches you how to assemble a team where roles are clearly defined and the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Studying literature made her more empathetic and enabled her to consider problems from different perspectives.

At OpenAI, Daniela also managed the team that developed GPT-2, a predecessor of the chatbot ChatGPT. Dario, as a researcher, played a key role in developing the technology that, years later, would usher in the AI revolution. The siblings recognized the technology's potential – and worried about its future impact.

In the fall of 2023, it became public knowledge that CEO Sam Altman was controversial at OpenAI when he lost his job and was subsequently reinstated. The board of directors had lost confidence in him. Dario and Daniela Amodei had apparently drawn their conclusions about their boss's personality years earlier. Along with five other associates, they left OpenAI at the end of 2020 to found a competing company based on their own vision: Anthropic.

In a marketing video, the seven founders sit around a table and describe their company culture. They emphasize the high level of trust among themselves at Anthropic. One says this is to Daniela's credit, as she maintains high standards: «She doesn't let any clowns in.» Daniela Amodei is now Anthropic's president and focuses primarily on the human side of the business. Dario is the CEO.

The conversation is staged, yet some aspects of it feel authentic. For example, the chemistry between the siblings and the co-founders. And the fact that they didn't simply want to «start a company,» but rather slipped into the role of founders out of a sense of duty, convinced that a better AI company is needed. All seven co-founders are now billionaires thanks to their company shares. They have pledged to donate 80% of their wealth to charity.

![«She doesn’t let any clowns in»: Daniela Amodei is responsible for shaping the company culture at Anthropic.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/06/0e7b019e-c5ac-4928-9dea-fc90d92d8591.jpg?width=1024)
*«She doesn’t let any clowns in»: Daniela Amodei is responsible for shaping the company culture at Anthropic.* (Steve Marcus / Reuters)

## The Amodeis are close to effective altruists

Dario and Daniela Amodei are close to the effective altruist movement , an ethical school whose adherents strive to increase good in the world in the most rational way possible. Daniela's husband, Holden Karnofsky, has founded several philanthropic organizations with this orientation. Today he works at Anthropic.

Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the crypto exchange FTX and formerly a leading figure in effective altruism, invested half a billion dollars in Anthropic in 2022. FTX has since collapsed, and Bankman-Fried has been imprisoned for fraud. This is likely one reason why the Amodeis are downplaying their connection to the movement .

But Anthropic's corporate philosophy aligns well with effective altruism: they want to do good while utilizing modern technology, and they are particularly concerned about future dangers, especially an overpowered AI that could spiral out of control or be used for nefarious purposes. Dario Amodei published a detailed blog post on this topic just this past January. Which brings us back to the debate with the Pentagon.

At its core, this debate revolves around who sets the limits on the use of artificial intelligence. Anthropic is attempting to mitigate the potential harm of its creation by giving its chatbot Claude a kind of «character.» This is intended to ensure that Claude refuses to perform any problematic tasks. The Pentagon, on the other hand, wants to decide for itself how it uses AI.

The main points of contention were reportedly autonomous weapons and the mass surveillance of Americans. Anthropic argues that the technology is not yet ready for autonomous weapons, and that the mass surveillance of its own citizens violates its principles.

## Anthropic has already made ethical compromises

Despite the idealism now on display, Anthropic has already made compromises. It is collaborating with Palantir, the most prominent provider of AI services for warfare and surveillance.

An internal memo leaked to Wired magazine this summer also revealed that Dario Amodei was considering attracting Gulf state funds as investors, after having previously condemned doing so. Contradictory? Amodei does not see it that way. The «media / Twitter / the outside world,» he wrote, are always looking for hypocrisy and are «also very stupid.» He added: «It's perfectly consistent to advocate for rules that say, 'No one may do X,' but when those rules fail and everyone else does X, to reluctantly do X yourself.»

The Amodeis' idealism is therefore flexible. Their steadfastness towards the Trump administration may have less to do with their own beliefs than with the reputation they have to lose, especially among their employees.

Being seen as «the good guys» in the AI race helps Anthropic hold its own in the fierce competition for talent from Google, OpenAI and Meta. Having a CEO and a president who seem genuinely nice and down-to-earth is a unique selling point in Silicon Valley.

---

- They emphasize ethical principles and safety, particularly against autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, while pragmatically making compromises despite their idealistic values.
- Their reputation as an ethically driven company gives them a competitive edge in talent-focused Silicon Valley.
author: Ruth Fulterer
summaryBullets: Dario and Daniela Amodei, founders of Anthropic, defied the Pentagon over the use of their AI technology Claude, leading to them being classified as a supply chain risk.
They emphasize ethical principles and safety, particularly against autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, while pragmatically making compromises despite their idealistic values.
Their reputation as an ethically driven company gives them a competitive edge in talent-focused Silicon Valley.

headline: An evening in Berlin's most dangerous park: Dealers whisper, «Do you want marijuana?»
lead: Since March, Görlitzer Park in Kreuzberg has been closed off at night. Politicians hope this will make the park safer, but some residents are resisting.
body:
# An evening in Berlin's most dangerous park: Dealers whisper, «Do you want marijuana?»

*Since March, Görlitzer Park in Kreuzberg has been closed off at night. Politicians hope this will make the park safer, but some residents are resisting.*

**Kathrin Klette, Berlin** · Panorama · 2026-04-05 · 1921 words · [ld.1927432](https://www.nzz.ch/panorama/goerlitzer-park-in-berlin-dealer-proteste-und-ein-umstrittener-zaun-ld.1927432)

![On the evening of March 1st, local residents protested against the nightly closure of Görlitzer Park.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/04/02/c7d4a36c-6cb7-4abd-91f0-f68853433be2.jpg?width=1024)
*On the evening of March 1st, local residents protested against the nightly closure of Görlitzer Park.* (Maryam Majd / Getty)

Görlitzer Park in Berlin-Kreuzberg is considered one of the most dangerous in Germany, but on this late Monday evening in March, it initially appears calm and peaceful. Cyclists and pedestrians crisscross the park. A man walks his dog, which wears a neon green collar. Soccer players train on a brightly lit sports field. It's a crisp evening. Only occasionally is there a faint whiff of cannabis in the air.

The dealers, however, are everywhere. They wear down jackets and baseball caps with the Louis Vuitton logo; they stand at the park entrances, lean against walls, or squat on huge rocks. «Hello. Everything alright?» they ask. «Do you want marijuana?» They are young men from Africa, and they also sell crack.

The residents don't seem to mind. They simply walk by. Some of them have gathered in the park this evening. They want their beloved «Görli» to remain open to everyone, especially at night.

Most are young, wearing black jeans and black hoodies. Some have pulled their hoods up. Grilled cheese sizzles over a fire, beer bottles clink together.

## «Pig cops, get out of Görli!»

Since the beginning of March, a security service has been locking all entrances to the park at 10 p.m., as was the case today; in the summer, the locks will be at 11 p.m. The aim of this measure is to curb drug dealing and crime in the park. In February, Senator Ute Bonde of the CDU party used drastic language to describe the measure. She said the park was no longer a place of recreation for «large segments of the population.» From now on, it will no longer be possible to enter the park at night; however, exiting through the turnstiles will always be permitted.

A few police officers walk past the demonstrators, shining their flashlights into the bushes. A beam of light flashes briefly, then disappears again. Then they position themselves at a safe distance from the young people. One of the officers shines his flashlight on the group. The people cheer, a man raises his arms. «Pig cops, get out of Görlitzer Park!» someone shouts, and the others join in. Someone throws a bottle at the police, which shatters on the asphalt path. In the darkness, it's impossible to see who threw it. The officers don't move.

A heated debate is raging over Görlitzer Park, affectionately known as «Görli» in Kreuzberg. Residents and activists have been protesting ever since the decision was made three years ago to close the park at night. A key argument is that the measure will only drive more drug dealers, addicts, and homeless people into the neighborhood. Several initiatives have formed, including «Görli 24/7,» «Rave against the Zaun,» and «Görli zaunfrei» (Görli Fence-Free). They consider the measure purely symbolic, if not an outright expression of authoritarian arbitrariness. Many don't believe the park is as dangerous as politicians claim. Are they right?

![Görlitzer Park in October 2024. No other green space in Berlin sees as many crimes committed as this one.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/04/02/cb041bb6-e3e4-4a84-b3af-b21e3ffbe142.jpg?width=1024)
*Görlitzer Park in October 2024. No other green space in Berlin sees as many crimes committed as this one.* (Emmanuele Contini / Imago)

## In Kreuzberg, the heart beats left-green

The area around Görlitzer Park is one of the most vibrant parts of Kreuzberg. Many buildings date back to the Gründerzeit (late 19th-century boom period); their richly decorated stucco windows still bear witness to the heavy elegance of the German Empire. Today, nothing of that remains.

This district is the heart of a left-leaning, green lifestyle; the Green Party has held the mayor's office for 20 years. Restaurant menus feature vegan bento boxes, falafel, and spinach smoothies. Here, no one has to explain themselves if they receive welfare or wear shabby trousers. The Social Democratic Party (SPD) advertises «Housing without rip-offs» on posters, and the mosque on Falckensteinstrasse wishes everyone a blessed Ramadan. Walls and doors are covered in graffiti, and old clothes and a sink lie scattered beside the park.

In the late 1980s, local residents successfully campaigned to have the derelict site of the former Görlitz train station transformed into a park. Now it features playgrounds, barbecue areas, and a children's farm. But it also suffers from drug problems, neglect, and violence.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 29e6c092df6c9cfb83e383a1b043a0d2]

A few days after the protests, a young man with light blond hair stands in front of an Indian restaurant near the park one evening. His face is covered in red blotches and wounds. He speaks energetically at the chalkboard listing the daily specials. Then he walks away. On a street corner, a man smokes crack. The pipe glows in the darkness. The dealer who sold him the drug burns a paper bag next to a tree a little later. In the park, a group of men stagger past, beer bottles in hand; several addicts squeeze into a toilet block and lock the door. A confused, thin man stumbles alone along the sidewalk.

A local resident recounts how drug addicts repeatedly shoot up between parked cars or sleep off their intoxication on the roadside. Homeless people sleep in doorways and relieve themselves there. Cars and basements are broken into, and syringes are thrown into bushes or next to playgrounds.

## Crack leads to rapid impoverishment

For about three years, crack cocaine, cooked with sodium bicarbonate, has flooded Berlin. It's a highly addictive drug that leads to rapid destitution. Since then, the situation has become particularly dire around Görlitzer Park. Not everyone can bear the misery. Some residents, especially those with children, have moved away.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) e182b63b2bd9fc0fd8e9cb783bbced54]

According to police crime statistics, in 2025 there were 550 assaults, 139 robberies, and 10 rapes or sexual assaults in the park and surrounding neighborhood. No other park in Berlin has such a high crime rate. Most of these incidents don't happen at night, but in broad daylight.

In the summer of 2023, a particularly horrific case shocked the city. Several men allegedly raped a woman in the park in front of her partner early one morning in June. The incident was reported by media outlets nationwide.

Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner subsequently convened a so-called security summit, at which the nighttime closure of the park was proposed. The Senate then implemented the plans despite resistance from the district.

Today, doubts exist as to whether the rape actually occurred as described. A video suggests that the sex may have been consensual; the court proceedings have been suspended. However, the politicians stuck to their plan: now, sixteen steel gates and eight turnstiles block the park entrances in the darkness, and sections of fencing fill the gaps.

![Many Kreuzberg residents believe that closing the park at night will not solve the problems. They fear that drug-related crime will simply shift to the neighborhood.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/04/02/1f965aa8-ac12-4e82-b8b4-8cc245557ee7.jpg?width=1024)
*Many Kreuzberg residents believe that closing the park at night will not solve the problems. They fear that drug-related crime will simply shift to the neighborhood.* (Maryam Majd / Getty)

## Residents: The fence is a complete waste of money

The city has indeed been trying to get the problems at Görlitzer Park under control for a long time. Zero-tolerance policies, park attendants and managers, a supervised injection site for addicts, designated areas for drug dealers, community caretakers, and weapons- and knife-free zones have all been tried. Many things have been attempted; nothing has worked.

If you listen to the conversations in the neighborhood, you'll find hardly any support for the new plan for the park. «Waste of money» is a word that comes up frequently, along with «nonsense» and «outrageous.» Aside from that, many in the neighborhood seem unfazed by the current situation. Of course, as a woman in the area, you have to be careful, says one young woman, but that's no different in other big cities. And what about the dealers? «They'd probably like to have a different job,» says a young man. How does he feel in the neighborhood? «Great.»

Only one woman seems exhausted by the situation. Jutta, 60 years old, has lived in the neighborhood for 40 years. She can be found near the park on a sunny afternoon. She points to a gas cartridge lying on the cobblestones. «Nitrous oxide, that's a huge thing here,» she says. Young people, in particular, inhale the gas from balloons. They become euphoric, almost in a trance.

Jutta says she feels safe during the day but sometimes has an uneasy feeling in the evening. She has experienced firsthand how the neighborhood has changed over the years. She recounts being attacked by an addict in April 2019. Shortly after she had unlocked her front door, she says, the man came up from behind and pushed her against the wall in the hallway. He ripped the necklace from her neck and fled, Jutta says, but neighbors caught him.

«How much more social work are we supposed to do?» Jutta asks. She loves city life but also needs security. Moving is out of the question for her because of her small pension.

![Police were present at the protests on March 1st. However, no incidents occurred.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/04/02/a1001ca3-2565-4f85-9690-f9e0fa1c75e7.jpg?width=1024)
*Police were present at the protests on March 1st. However, no incidents occurred.* (Tony Linke / Getty)

## Activists file lawsuit

Meanwhile, the activists are serious about their protest. One morning, a man in dirty gray trousers and baggy shoes lounges in the sun amidst the ruins of the Pamukkale Well, a vast landscape of stone. Across the way, in front of a warehouse, activists from the «Görli zaunfrei» (Görli Fence-Free) alliance have set up parasols, beer tables, and wooden chairs. They have called a press conference to announce that they have filed a lawsuit and an urgent application against the park plans with the Berlin Administrative Court. Almost twenty residents have come.

David Werdermann is also there, the lawyer representing five plaintiffs. He's wearing a black turtleneck, an anthracite suit, black shoes, and horn-rimmed glasses. Werdermann sits behind a beer table and explains the residents' arguments into a microphone. Ultimately, he says, it's about defending public space against senseless bans and government intervention. «It's also a question of justice,» he says. After all, many Kreuzberg residents live in cramped conditions.

Next to Werdermann sit four of the plaintiffs; most have lived here for more than 25 years. Among them are Jürgen, who is blind and says that because the park closes at night, he has to take a detour in the evenings. Anna-Maria, who uses the park to escape from everyday life and emphasizes that many young people meet there. Mathias, for whom the park is an important place to cool off, especially in the summer, where he can have a beer with friends at night. And then there's Philipp, in black pants and a black hoodie. He lives in a dark building at the back without a balcony and uses the park for barbecues, birthday parties, and sports. «Without the park, something's just missing at night,» he says. He's sure there will be protests in the summer. «Then civil disobedience will take over.» Some of the residents applaud.

Kreuzberg is where you feel restricted in your freedom because you can't go to a park at night.

## Drug deals within seconds

Meanwhile, an alternative proposal to the nighttime park closures has been developed by the «Görli zaunfrei» (Görli fence-free) initiative. It is based on the so-called Zurich model , which considers the needs of the general public as well as those of drug users. In the 1990s, Zurich successfully used this model to largely eliminate the open drug scene in the city. Today, the model is considered a best practice example.

The plan for Kreuzberg includes another supervised consumption room for addicts, a crisis intervention team, more sanitary facilities and teams that are also on site at night. It is scheduled to be presented in May. What is missing, however, is the consistent criminal prosecution of drug trafficking that is part of the Zurich model.

But the dealers are experienced. If a police car approaches in the distance, they hop on a bicycle and ride off. The deals are also completed in the blink of an eye. On a broad daylight, three dealers are standing at the park entrance when two young men approach them. Words are exchanged, then one dealer goes to the trash can by the wall and takes out a package, while another stands watch. The seller fumbles with the package, the goods and the money change hands, and the two young men are off. A transaction in seconds, as if nothing had happened.

![View from the bridge at the end of Görlitzer Park in October 2024. Whether the nighttime closure has the desired effect will be investigated later.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/04/02/7d130399-294e-4e87-8aa4-03ca13081b45.jpg?width=1024)
*View from the bridge at the end of Görlitzer Park in October 2024. Whether the nighttime closure has the desired effect will be investigated later.* (Emmanuele Contini / Imago)

---

- Activists argue the measures are symbolic politics and propose a solution inspired by the Zurich model, including consumption rooms and intervention teams.
- The conflict between freedom and security highlights social tensions in Kreuzberg's vibrant district.
