headline: Athens' fight against the shadow economy: Investigators hunt for tax evaders
lead: Greek tax morale long had a bad reputation. With the digitalization of the tax system, the government is now taking rigorous action against fraudsters – with considerable progress.
body:
# Athens' fight against the shadow economy: Investigators hunt for tax evaders

*Greek tax morale long had a bad reputation. With the digitalization of the tax system, the government is now taking rigorous action against fraudsters – with considerable progress.*

**Nicole Anliker, Athen** · Wirtschaft · 2026-04-14 · 1616 words · [ld.1925441](https://www.nzz.ch/wirtschaft/athens-kampf-gegen-die-schattenwirtschaft-mit-fahndern-auf-der-jagd-nach-steuersuendern-ld.1925441)

![A photograph of a private yacht, a map showing the current locations of the investigation teams, satellite images with «suspicious targets.» Data analysts evaluate risk profiles in the control room.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/03/c59b1e1f-f6bb-4381-886f-1c1b53152b19.jpg?crop=3518,2386,x0,y215)
*A photograph of a private yacht, a map showing the current locations of the investigation teams, satellite images with «suspicious targets.» Data analysts evaluate risk profiles in the control room.* (NZZ)

Panagiotis Kintzios knows that no one is happy to see him cross their threshold. Being a tax inspector in a country with a low tax morale isn't always fun. «We're not exactly welcome,» he says drily, with a smile. Nevertheless, the random check he's conducting with his colleague Panagiota Stasi doesn't make him nervous. This morning, their destination is a traditional coffeehouse that seems to have been frozen in time: heavy curtains, upholstered chairs, plastic tables, yellowed pictures, large TV screens – a mismatched collection. On the terrace sit old regulars – bespectacled men with thinning hair, smoking and drinking coffee, marveling at the visit from the tax authorities. Kintzios and Stasi introduce themselves to the waitress, showing their official identification and the inspection order. This is important, Stasi explains: «There are fraudsters who impersonate tax inspectors.»

A guest immediately interjects. «Why do you come here? Why don't you check the big fish?» Kintzios politely points out the duty of his job. «We're also psychologists in this role,» he had said earlier. He added that guests complain about their presence more often and provoke unpleasant situations more than the staff – especially when alcohol is involved.

Kintzios and Stasi access the coffee shop's tax data on a tablet; in just a few clicks, they have an overview. They sift through the transactions, checking the receipts issued at each individual table. Because cash register systems in Greece are now required to be networked with the tax authorities, any misuse is quickly detected. This digitalization has led to less tax evasion, Stasi explains.

![Panagiota Stasi and Panagiotis Kintzios examine the tax profile of the coffee house.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/03/b182ff57-cce2-4420-89d8-b5e0b46eef2f.jpg?width=1024)
*Panagiota Stasi and Panagiotis Kintzios examine the tax profile of the coffee house.* (NZZ)

## Replica fuel pump for training purposes

That was also the government's goal. Tax evasion and the shadow economy were considered one of the causes of the Greek financial crisis. At its peak in 2013, the informal economy was estimated to account for between 23 and 30 percent of GDP, depending on the study and methodology. «The crisis forced us to reform the tax system,» explains Giorgos Pitsilis, head of the tax authority AADE. He has been in the business for years and has overhauled the tax administration, notorious for its inefficiency. He has led the agency since it was separated from the Ministry of Finance in 2017 and began operating independently – a demand of the international creditors.

Pitsilis has digitized the tax system. By introducing a digital accounting system, transactions are monitored in real time by the tax authorities, and bank data is linked to the administration. In addition to developing digital tools, controls have been tightened, a cash limit has been introduced, and electronic payments have been promoted.

The progress is impressive. According to the government, the measures generated an additional €2.2 billion in revenue for the state last year, contributing to the country's economic recovery, with total net government revenues reaching €77 billion. While the size of the shadow economy, at 21.9 percent of GDP, remains high by European standards, it is declining. This is also reflected in the shrinking VAT gap, the difference between the theoretically owed and the actual amount of VAT paid: According to the European Commission, it has decreased by two-thirds since 2017 and stood at 10.5 percent in 2023. The EU average is 7 percent.

Pitsilis explains how digitalization enables more targeted inspections across the country. In small teams, a total of 2,000 inspectors like Kintzios and Stasi conduct random checks of restaurants, law offices, supermarkets, and gas stations, primarily when there is concrete evidence of abuse. They receive such evidence from the «boarding room» of the modern AADE operations center in Athens.

In the sparsely furnished control room – everything is bright and white – eight large screens hang on the wall. They display: real-time images from a drone inspecting a tanker truck on a highway, footage of a private yacht, a map showing the current locations of the investigation teams, and satellite images of «suspicious targets.» Half a dozen data analysts sit at rows of tables behind computers in front of them.

One of them is evaluating the latest risk profiles generated by the artificial intelligence. The focus is on several gas stations whose data on delivered, stored, and sold fuel quantities shows discrepancies. AADE monitors these automatically and in real time. Using a color-coded cluster diagram, the analyst examines the network of gas stations: owners, accountants, lawyers, and other companies involved. «If the indications of misuse become more concrete, we dispatch several investigation teams with the support of other authorities, coordinating and monitoring their operations,» explains Konstantia Tachtsidou, head of the control room.

![Konstantia Tachtsidou, head of the control room at the AADE operations center in Athens.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/03/29886a18-83e0-4cf6-b5db-e3d5e01bacc7.jpg?width=1024)
*Konstantia Tachtsidou, head of the control room at the AADE operations center in Athens.* (NZZ)

The current suspected case is said to be typical: The gasoline trade reportedly has the largest shadow economy in Greece. In light of this, the AADE has built a replica of a gas pump specifically for training purposes. They practice using it to detect technical tampering. A tanker truck is currently being replicated for the same purpose. The responsible official proudly displays the plans.

## Houses under constant construction and dwindling living space

Pitsilis, the head of the tax authority, has no illusions. Digitalization, which offers the state new possibilities in the fight against tax evasion, also benefits fraudsters. «We're in a constant race,» he says. He notes that the state has now seen through many old tricks, but new ones are sure to follow, and they have to be prepared for that.

The «old tricks» are still talked about in Greece. Particularly in the restaurant and service sectors, cash payments were long the norm, and receipts were avoided to evade VAT and keep declared income low. Until a few years ago, 70 percent of self-employed individuals also behaved conspicuously, declaring income below the legal minimum wage. Creativity was also evident in the real estate sector: houses officially remained «under construction,» facades unplastered, roofs unfinished, all to pay less tax. For the same reason, living space was reduced by a few square meters on paper, and some swimming pools existed in the garden but were not registered in the land registry.

Electronic cash register systems, house mapping, a minimum tax for the self-employed, and digital reporting systems limit the scope for such maneuvers. Nevertheless, their ingenuity is astonishing. Where does this low tax morale come from? «Perhaps it's in our DNA,» says Tachtsidou, the head of the tax office, with self-deprecating humor. Her agency's task, she explains, is to make the public understand that paying taxes is an obligation. «Many think it's optional.»

Tachtsidou used to conduct inspections herself, experiencing bribery attempts and unpleasant incidents. Even today, she notices how people avoid her in private as soon as they learn about her profession. «They become suspicious,» she says with a laugh. She adds that while the tax morale of Greeks has improved, there is still room for improvement. In her opinion, the root cause is the Greeks' distrust of their government. According to a Eurobarometer survey, 79% of the population distrusts the state. Pitsilis has an explanation for this, which he phrases diplomatically: «It's related to how people perceive the state's handling of their money.»

Yannis Marinos is a good example. The 46-year-old sits on the terrace of his restaurant in Athens' Plaka district, enjoying a coffee and a cigarette, and says: «You get the feeling you're not getting anything back.» It's a statement that resonates. Marinos makes it in connection with a recent hospital visit. He accompanied a friend there. The dilapidated infrastructure shocked the friendly man so much that he says he would rather die than have to be treated there.

Marinos implemented the electronic cash register system in his restaurant in 2024, as required by law. He supports the government's approach. He admits that the problem of undeclared income hasn't disappeared, but it has decreased. Nevertheless, he's annoyed. Unprompted, he brings up the massive embezzlement of EU subsidies: For years, the state has been evading billions, he fumes. «Then these same people come to me, checking the receipt for every single coffee, as if I were a thief.» It's not about the checks themselves, but about the principle.

He believes the 24 percent value-added tax is excessive. How the government calculates it is a mystery to him. He calls it «Greek mathematics.» This makes survival difficult, he says. He has to absorb costs somewhere, but at the same time, he can't afford to drive away customers. In his view, an even stricter control system with a lower tax rate would be fairer.

![All information converges in the control room of the AADE headquarters.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/03/03/9b22faa9-43f0-4778-afef-a4353a396caa.jpg?crop=2688,3584,x0,y136)
*All information converges in the control room of the AADE headquarters.* (NZZ)

## Lottery and amateur tax investigators

Marinos is not the only one complaining about the high VAT. Small businesses, especially mechanics and hair salons, are struggling with it. It is whispered that tradespeople are still reluctant to issue receipts. Pitsilis knows this too. «We can't just barge into a house and check if the plumber has issued an invoice.» He adds jokingly, «Unfortunately, we're not invited to doctor's appointments either. People go alone.» He therefore appeals to the common good, adding that the fight against tax evasion requires everyone's cooperation.

The government is also actively involving the population, for example with a «tax lottery.» This aims to encourage people to pay without cash. For every bill paid digitally, there's a ticket that automatically participates in a monthly drawing. 556 prizes are up for grabs each month.

He's also turning the population into amateur tax inspectors. To this end, he launched the app «appodixi,» whose name combines «app» and the Greek word for receipt. Using this app, any citizen can scan the receipt they receive and check whether the full amount has been reported to the tax office. In 2024, 75,000 reports were received. More than half of these indicated tax evasion.

Kintzios and Stasi spend a little more time in the coffee shop than planned. The digital cash register system refuses to issue a receipt due to connection problems with the server. The waitress tries to reason with the machine: «Come on, don't do this to me, I don't want to be led away in handcuffs.» Slightly flustered, she compliments Stasi's smile as she waits patiently. The most important thing, Stasi says, is to always treat people kindly and respectfully – even if they cheat. In the case of the coffee shop, that's not the case. The cash register system eventually issues the receipt, and there's nothing to complain about.

---

- Greece has reformed and digitized its tax system to combat tax evasion. Electronic cash systems and real-time monitoring show initial success, though the shadow economy remains a major issue.
- The AADE conducts targeted inspections using modern technologies such as drones and data cluster analyses. A tax lottery and the 'appodixi' app aim to encourage citizens to pay digitally and report abuse.
- Despite progress, distrust in the government remains high. Many Greeks view paying taxes more as an option than a duty, influenced by inadequate state returns and deteriorating infrastructure.
author: Nicole Anliker, Athen

The AADE conducts targeted inspections using modern technologies such as drones and data cluster analyses. A tax lottery and the 'appodixi' app aim to encourage citizens to pay digitally and report abuse.

headline: Thanks to this valley in the middle of the provinces, America rose to superpower status – today the place has an image problem. Billy Joel is partly to blame
lead: A visit to the Lehigh Valley, whose success story began with the defrauding of its Indigenous inhabitants.
body:
# Thanks to this valley in the middle of the provinces, America rose to superpower status – today the place has an image problem. Billy Joel is partly to blame

*A visit to the Lehigh Valley, whose success story began with the defrauding of its Indigenous inhabitants.*

**Ivo Mijnssen, Bethlehem, Simon Tanner** · Gesellschaft · 2026-06-13 · 3652 words · [ld.10004841](https://www.nzz.ch/gesellschaft/american-dream-aus-stahl-wie-die-usa-zur-supermacht-wurden-ld.10004841)

This is the story of a promise: Those who work hard can achieve anything. In Allentown and Bethlehem, the twin cities in Pennsylvania, the American Dream became reality. Here, European adventurers found a valley brimming with legendary riches. The steel mill enabled ordinary workers to rise in society. They built skyscrapers and bridges that became world-famous, and the warships that transformed America into a superpower. The American bard Billy Joel sings in «Allentown» about what really mattered here, «what was real»: «Iron and coke, chromium steel.»

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 76390dfeff744e20efaeb8c57d98b107]

But the dream was shattered. Since then, the Lehigh Valley has come to symbolize the decline of American power and the end of a golden era. Joel sang of a gray, impoverished city where the unemployed kill time, without prospects, without hope. The image of the dying industrial city has stuck to Allentown to this day. Mayor Matt Tuerk can no longer bear to hear it. «Billy Joel should really pay our city compensation,» he says.

This is the story of a valley at the heart of the American dream. It represents the U.S. in microcosm: its rise, fall and reinvention. In the pioneer land of Pennsylvania, change always manifested itself particularly early and clearly. The new order here began with a fraud.

**I**Expansion

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/11/251052fa-1229-492e-832b-a68bf22d5ce1.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
** (Illustration by Simon Tanner / NZZ)

When entrepreneur William Allen first entered Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, it was clear to him that if he wanted to develop the fertile land, the Indigenous people would have to go. The Lenape had lived there for millennia. But Allen, who had made a fortune as a shipowner trading rum, slaves and flour, saw the valley only as a «dense wilderness where the primitive red man roams and hunts, without the slightest sign of civilization.» In 1737, he sensed an opportunity to become even richer through a land deal. To do so, he had to defraud and expel the Lenape.

Allen was also chief justice of the colony of Pennsylvania. He summarily invented a purchase agreement: Decades earlier, the Native Americans had supposedly promised to sell the white settlers as much land as they could walk in 18 hours. Allen took the chiefs on leisurely walks to show them that no one could get very far in that time. They were familiar with the tradition of hostile parties meeting for a walk to reach an agreement. They agreed to the «Walking Purchase.»

But Allen sent not walkers but the fastest runners in Pennsylvania. «You’re running! That’s unfair, you were supposed to walk!» the Lenape shouted angrily from the path’s edge. They could only watch as the three athletes ran without a break, to the point of exhaustion. One runner gave up. Another collapsed and died shortly thereafter. Only Edward Marshall persevered, for 113 kilometers. He secured an area for the land speculator as large as the Swiss canton of Valais.

The settlers then forcibly drove out the Lenape. As payment, they received weapons and clothing, including 45 cannons, 2,000 needles and 40 mirrors. For decades, the Native Americans fought desperately for their homeland, even allying themselves with the French. «The land under my feet is the reason we are waging war against you,» said their chief, Teedyuscung. Chaos and violence reigned in Allen's promised land. Two decades after the Walking Purchase, he was still bitterly complaining about the poor security situation. His promise that this was «the best land in the world for the poor man, that very well suits the British character,» sounded like a mockery.

Larger settlements such as Bethlehem and Allentown developed slowly. They were subject to Lenape attacks until 1762. Just 15 years later, they became front-line towns in a new conflict: the American Revolutionary War. Allen's son James described how the army marched into present-day Allentown. «Thousands of wagons have passed my door, the hospitals are full.» With the armed forces came gunsmiths and transport entrepreneurs. The valley's primitive transport routes collapsed under the onslaught.

The Lehigh River could have solved the transportation problems. But it was a wild waterway full of sharp rocks and rapids. In the spring, it flooded large areas. For this reason, Americans began building a canal in 1818. Soon, timber and ore from the mountains could be shipped on it, tied together on rafts and boats, all the way to Philadelphia. Halfway there lay Bethlehem and Allentown. Refugees, German immigrants and adventurers settled here. Many were enterprising and well-educated. There were enough raw materials for the factories, and laborers as well. In 1857, the Saucona Iron Company built its first plant. This would become the Bethlehem Steel Corporation in the 20th century.

The company made a single product that shaped American modernity like no other: steel. And at its helm was an adventurer who realized his vision at great risk: Charles M. Schwab. The Pennsylvania native had worked his way up from engineer to director in Andrew Carnegie's steel mills. He believed in the American dream, in the ability of every person to fulfill their potential. «There are no limits to our personal development,» he was fond of saying. Schwab was a gifted salesman and made deals with major New York banks. When he had a falling out with J. P. Morgan, he left Carnegie's steel empire. In 1904, Schwab took over a small steel company in Bethlehem. It quickly became the second-largest producer in the U.S. Between the turn of the century and World War II, its production increased a hundredfold.

At Bethlehem Steel, Schwab staked everything on a novel, largely untested technology. When his secretary asked him if it was wise to risk the entire company on it, he said: «I have thought the whole thing through, and if we go broke, we'll go broke in a big way.» Bethlehem Steel began producing novel steel beams that were cheap and versatile, for use in skyscrapers, for example. Schwab's steel beams formed the skeletons of the most famous buildings on the New York skyline – including the Empire State Building. The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco was built with 44,000 tons of Bethlehem steel. Schwab's slogan was: «Steel built the world. Bethlehem built the steel.»

It was the age of American ascendancy, when cities grew into the sky and capitalism created unimaginable wealth. In his books, Schwab praised the morale of his workers: «I love to appeal to the American spirit in my men, the spirit of doing things better than anyone has done them before.»

The reality was considerably grimmer.

While workers received bonuses for exceeding their production targets, Schwab had them toil seven days a week, for 84 hours. Every year there were dozens of serious accidents: Workers were injured by glowing steel and inhaled toxic gases without protective equipment. Schwab did not tolerate unions. When workers went on strike in 1910 to demand Sundays off, he had mounted police fire into the crowd. People were killed and injured.

**II**War

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/6e742d8a-e03f-42e5-b061-a88a299927ec.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
** (Illustration by Simon Tanner / NZZ)

The first half of the 20th century was also a time of wars and crises. After the First World War, orders for the steel industry collapsed, and between 1929 and 1933 the Great Depression swept across the U.S. Building legendary bridges and luxurious skyscrapers was no longer a viable business model. Schwab recognized this early on: he reoriented Bethlehem Steel toward armaments production during wartime. In the First World War, the company not only supplied 100 ships and shipboard cannons, but also almost half of the artillery for the American army.

Schwab paid only limited attention to American laws. Although the U.S. was still neutral at the start of World War I, he negotiated a secret deal with the British to supply munitions and submarines. In the first months of the war, Bethlehem Steel delivered more than all British producers combined. Schwab was proud of this. «I can deliver anything if I get the money,» he reportedly said in London.

Schwab's deals caused controversy. Congressional committees accused him of exploiting his dominant position and charging Americans exorbitant prices. He was called a «merchant of death.» Schwab saw himself as being in the right. «I never had the feeling that we were doing anything other than our duty to the country and the world: to provide the means of defense.»

Schwab died in 1939, shortly after the start of World War II, an impoverished visionary. He had squandered his vast fortune on gambling, women and luxurious villas. And his shares in Bethlehem Steel were almost worthless: After 10 years of economic crisis, the company was on the verge of ruin. But with the U.S. entry into the war after Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, the company again became a central arms supplier. President Franklin D. Roosevelt called his country «the great arsenal of democracy.» Without steel from Pennsylvania, it could not have been filled. The industrial might of America stood on the front lines of a world war.

Bethlehem Steel expanded production and hired new workers. By 1943, the giant corporation had 300,000 employees working across America. They produced 73,000 tons of steel for the military and built more than 1,100 warships in the coastal shipyards. Among them was the aircraft carrier USS «Lexington,» which the Japanese destroyed in 1942 during the Battle of the Coral Sea. It sank with 200 men and 35 aircraft on board.

The enormous demand pushed the American steel industry to its limits. Because the men were in the army, there was an acute labor shortage. So women followed them into the factories. This was also true at Bethlehem Steel, where 25,000 women were suddenly soldering, welding and casting. For a conservative society, this was a shock that challenged gender roles. For the women, a new world opened up.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 40396f2820ca104c491ebe9889e07e82]

«The pay was very good for the time,» says former worker Doris M. Mann. «That’s why the women did it.» She was interviewed in 1975 for the «Women of Steel» research project. The Bethlehem native came from a poor family and had sick relatives. She needed the money. Mann initially tested the hardness of the steel that was to be used in fighter planes. Then she trained to be a crane operator. She liked the pressure, the responsibility: «Man, when you operate a crane, you have to be all there,» she said. The men watched her very closely.

The female workers also met with rejection. In Bethlehem, they underwent painful initiation rites. Men would leave hot pieces of metal on the welding torches and watch to see if the women cried when they removed them by hand. Sexual harassment also occurred. When Doris Mann was walking home from a night shift, a man exposed himself to her. «After that, my father walked with me.» She said workers regularly whistled at her. For her, that was normal.

In the U.S., wartime propaganda glorified the women in the factories. Fictional characters like Rosie the Riveter or Winnie the Welder appeared on large posters in Bethlehem and all over the country to recruit women. Rosie joined large pieces of steel with rivets; Winnie welded them together. The posters proclaiming «We Can Do It!» while Rosie flexed her muscles became world-famous. «She’s making history, working for victory. Watching out for sabotage,» a contemporary song says. The lyrics state that her boyfriend is fighting in the army, while «she’s doing overtime on the riveting machine.»

For worker Doris Mann, the job in the factory was a patriotic duty. But she also knew it could not last forever. «We went during the war because they needed women,» she says in the interview. «I think it showed that men and women can work together. I never thought of making a career out of it. Otherwise I wouldn’t have left.» She and the six million women in the arms industry were quickly laid off to make way for the returning soldiers.

**III**Decline

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/11/595e5b9b-6580-454f-b469-051474f9d145.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
** (Illustration by Simon Tanner / NZZ)

In 1945, the United States stood at the zenith of its power. It had made great sacrifices in World War II, but the country was not a landscape of ruins like Germany, Japan or the Soviet Union. The industries of its competitors were destroyed. In steel, the Americans had a virtual monopoly after the war. Their plants produced 90 tons a year. That was more than 60% of global production. An eighth of that came from Bethlehem.

Donald Young's career began in this golden age. «I come from the age of steam engines,» Young says on the phone. The 88-year-old belongs to the generation of Americans who secured their social mobility through hard work after the war. He joined Bethlehem Steel in 1956 and stayed for 56 years.Young was smart and ambitious. He took evening classes to continue his education, learning a great deal about metals and their processing. As a foreman, his pay increased. And the unions, which had become very influential in the factories since the war, secured him additional benefits. Young calls them «bennies»: health insurance, life insurance and a generous pension.

The man from Baltimore witnessed how rapidly technology developed. «When I started, we calculated the steel composition with a pen and paper,» he says. Now, he explains, computers do everything. And when he started, he adds, there was almost no safety equipment. «Now you have to wear an astronaut suit just to be allowed near liquid steel.» Young has little use for digitalization. He describes himself as an «old curmudgeon» who thinks back nostalgically to the old days. But he knows the steel industry perished because it did not change. And he remembers the exact day the decline began.

On July 15, 1959, a strike by 500,000 workers began that lasted four months. They demanded higher wages. Suddenly, supplies from the factories ceased – a shock for the construction sector, automakers and shipyards. The American government therefore allowed foreign steel into the country. The Europeans and Japanese were ready. «Suddenly, all the floodgates were open,» says Young. Overnight, the U.S. became a major steel importer.

The new competition hit Bethlehem Steel hard because its plants were outdated. «The technology was stuck at the level of the 1920s. For a long time, there was simply no reason to modernize,» says Don Young. The factories in Europe and Asia, on the other hand, were brand new. They produced more cheaply and efficiently, partly thanks to subsidies. Ironically, the Americans themselves had laid the groundwork for this: The first loans came from the Marshall Plan.

Bethlehem recovered once more. The global economy grew, and steel production reached a record high in 1973. Then came the oil price shock. Energy prices rose rapidly, making everything more expensive. At the same time, the auto industry, a key customer, collapsed. And because the government imposed new environmental regulations, the old plants now cost twice as much: They required more energy and had to be made cleaner at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. Bethlehem Steel incurred debt – just as interest rates were rising sharply. It was the perfect storm.

In 1977, the company reported a deficit of almost half a billion dollars. Five years later, this was followed by another $1.5 billion. At the time, it was the fourth-largest loss in American corporate history. The reasons lay in past mistakes, not least the generous pension benefits from the golden years. Bethlehem Steel laid off tens of thousands of workers and closed plants. The «Rust Belt» was born, a vast belt of shuttered, rusting industrial sites from Pennsylvania to the Midwest.

The steel industry was now in free fall. In Bethlehem itself, the wave of layoffs was spread out over a quarter of a century, as the company was hesitant to touch its most important plant. But in 1995, steel production ended in the Lehigh Valley as well. «The guys were crying when they shut down the blast furnaces. Me too,» says Don Young. «But I kept going.» When Bethlehem Steel went bankrupt in 2001, Young went on to work for another steel company. «I only retired when they forced me out at 75.» Today, he gives tours of the former plant grounds in Pennsylvania. In spirit, he remains a steelworker.

**IV**Emptiness

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/11/87af6907-ff39-4fa8-a3e8-1bf0dc55d931.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
** (Illustration by Simon Tanner / NZZ)

The deep crisis in the steel industry, a symbol of national strength, shook the entire country. Desolate landscapes and impoverished towns were left behind in the Rust Belt. In 1982, moved by the daily headlines about plant closures, Billy Joel wrote his song «Allentown.» It was actually about Bethlehem, but Joel felt that sounded too religious. Besides, Allentown rhymed better. «We’re living here in Allentown, and they’re closing all the factories down,» the New Yorker sang. «Out in Bethlehem they’re killing time. Filling out forms, standing in line.»

Joel wrote his requiem for the American dream. He meant the whole country when he spoke of Allentown, he says in a documentary. For the new generation, the promise of upward mobility and prosperity faded in the economic crisis of the 1980s. «Every kid had a pretty good shot to get at least as far as their old man got,» went another verse. But, the song continued, the children never made it.

> [embed: youtube ]

In December 1982, at the height of the layoffs, Billy Joel performed in Bethlehem. The mayor of Allentown welcomed him and symbolically handed him the key to the city. «It's a raw song about a raw city,» he said during the ceremony . And: «Sure, we have unemployment and unfulfilled dreams, but who doesn't?» When Joel took to the stage that evening, the audience was agitated. A local journalist described the performance as a mixture of rock concert, workers' demonstration, and therapy session. «They took all the coal out of the ground. And the union men slunk away,» Joel sang. The workers cheered. «Don't take any shit from anybody,» he shouted to them. He played «Allentown» twice : at the beginning and at the end.

The decline of the steel industry changed the U.S. far beyond the Lehigh Valley, and politically as well. Ronald Reagan won the 1980 presidential election with the slogan «Make America Great Again.» He lamented the weakness of the U.S. – and idealized the postwar years as an era with a stable set of values, full of industrial potential.

In 2020, Donald Trump appeared in Allentown with the same message . He railed against «globalists» in Washington and the parasites in Europe who were merely exploiting America. Together, he claimed, they had destroyed industry. «Steel created the middle class, built our great skyscrapers, and won two world wars,» Trump said. He promised to revive industry with tariffs. The results of this policy were modest, but it resonated with many who felt overwhelmed by constant change and sought refuge in the past.

The abandoned factory site in Bethlehem today appears at first glance to be a typical industrial wasteland: an emptiness the size of Gibraltar. It's a depressing landscape with long halls full of shattered windows, a lost place. Rusting railway tracks covered in graffiti snake through former loading facilities. Behind them loom the disused blast furnaces.

**V** Reinvention

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/3ab13d39-fc81-4508-9f28-49f45fe8544f.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
** (Illustration by Simon Tanner / NZZ)

Only at second glance, on this cold winter day in late 2025, does it become apparent that there is life in the old walls. In a former workshop, the National Museum of Industrial History recounts the past. In the summer, concerts and festivals are held regularly next to it. One and a half million people visit the brownfield site every year. The television broadcaster PBS has moved into a new building, and a stadium is home to the local hockey team. Behind it stands a casino with a hotel and shopping center. Culture, shopping and entertainment: Bethlehem has reinvented itself for the American consumer society. Where workers once toiled, tourists now stand at slot machines or buy handmade jewelry at the Christmas market.

Industry hasn't disappeared from the Lehigh Valley. Allentown and the former Bethlehem Steel plant are part of a cluster of factories, warehouses, and shipping terminals. Companies like Amazon, FedEx, UPS, and Walmart have significantly expanded their presence. Brands like Olympus, Fender, and Crayola have remained. The transportation sector employs 40,000 people, almost the same number as Bethlehem Steel once did. While steel production is gone, the valley's proximity to the metropolises of New York and Philadelphia, its excellent transportation system, and the expertise of its residents remain its trump cards. This has changed little in the last 300 years.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 2462d02280533220c4068a087a455e68]

Matt Tuerk, the mayor of Allentown, therefore dislikes hearing the term «Rust Belt.» «Billy Joel really ought to give back the key to the city,» he says in an interview. Tuerk is only half-joking when he demands compensation. As a former economic development officer, he says he had trouble attracting investors because they so strongly associated Allentown with industrial decline. The Democrat therefore prefers to emphasize the many new jobs and the large influx of people from other parts of the country.

The fact that Matt Tuerk became mayor at all shows how much the valley has changed. The 51-year-old is the first Latino in this position. His grandmother came to the US from Cuba after the war, and he grew up near the Lehigh Valley. Its inhabitants, including the steelworkers, were almost exclusively white back then. Now Allentown is a city with a Latino majority. Sixty percent of the residents have moved there since 2010. «They don't even know the steel era anymore. Because they weren't here,» says Tuerk.

But demographic change also creates uncertainty, Tuerk says. «There’s a segment of the long-established population that mourns the 1970s.» Politically, the Lehigh Valley is deeply divided. White suburban residents vote Republican, while Allentown and Bethlehem are in Democratic hands. In 2008, Obama won a majority in the valley. In 2024, it was Donald Trump. This too is related to demographic shifts: A portion of the Latino population is receptive to the conservative values of the American right. Added to this was dissatisfaction with the high cost of living and relatively low wages. This is a political development representative of the entire United States.

«There’s a lot of frustration in the city among those who aren’t benefiting from the growth,» says Mayor Matt Tuerk. This is closely linked to the changing economy: Many of the newcomers are leaving New York and other major cities because life has become too expensive for them. In Allentown, they find affordable housing because white residents left the city in the 1980s. The city centers became deserted.

But this development, too, is not permanent. Downtown Allentown is experiencing a tremendous boom. While simple stores with barred windows still stand in many places, one office tower after another is shooting up on the main street. Next to them are newly opened hotels and restaurants for a high-spending clientele. There is a modern technology museum for children, and the art museum is about to move into a new building. In the last five years, house prices have risen by two-thirds. Poor families fear they will be displaced.

The Lehigh Valley is thus on the verge of another transformation. What was once an undeveloped valley became the heart of American modernity, and a new economy was forged from an industrial wasteland. Indigenous tribes were followed by white Europeans and, more recently, Latinos. A multilayered and polarized society has emerged from this rich history. What still connects it is becoming increasingly uncertain. It is an emblem of the entire country, which is searching for a new place for itself in the world.

As Billy Joel sings: «Well we’re waiting here in Allentown. For the Pennsylvania we never found.» The valley and its people are reinventing themselves once again. What will come of it remains to be seen.

headline: Uzbekistan: A country discovers its future in art
lead: A center for contemporary art in Tashkent, a biennial in Bukhara and a pavilion in Venice: uzbekistan's move into modernity is taking place between craftsmanship and conceptual art.
body:
# Uzbekistan: A country discovers its future in art

*A center for contemporary art in Tashkent, a biennial in Bukhara and a pavilion in Venice: uzbekistan's move into modernity is taking place between craftsmanship and conceptual art.*

**Sabine B. Vogel** · Feuilleton · 2026-06-15 · 1725 words · [ld.10011305](https://www.nzz.ch/feuilleton/usbekistan-und-die-kunst-wie-ein-land-seine-zukunft-gestaltet-ld.10011305)

The room feels like a hiding place. Dark, crammed to the ceiling. Canvases lean against the wall, paintings are stacked under the suspended ceiling, and books are everywhere. This is where Vyacheslav Akhunov, born in 1948, works. When he moved here in the 1980s, Uzbekistan was still part of the USSR. His studio, along with an apartment next door in the prefabricated building, was rent-free – a privilege. The price: painting in the style of Soviet Realism, true to the party line.

Akhunov smiles when he tells the story. «Nobody in Moscow knew that,» he says, «but I've always been a conceptual artist» – not just one of the pioneers, but the very first in Uzbekistan, adds Gayane Umerova. «Contemporary art in Uzbekistan begins with Akhunov.»

![A view into the studio of Vyacheslav Akhunov in Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/14/00b50ab3-4a52-4a43-84c7-4fa64cf33d71.jpg?crop=1701,2268,x0,y0)

![Installationsansicht «Instrument of Minds» während der 61. Biennale di Venezia im Palazzo Franchetti: Vyacheslav Akhunov, «Triumphal Arch», 1979/2026.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/14/4db5f827-29c0-456b-ae7d-834971603775.jpg?crop=1406,1875,x547,y0)

Umerova has headed the state-run Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) since 2017. 2017 is no coincidence. It is a pivotal year for the Central Asian country, which, after gaining independence in 1991, was long ruled by the dictator Islam Karimov. In 2016, Shavkat Mirziyoyev came to power and opened up the previously highly isolated nation. He abolished the exit visa, reformed the administration, and relaxed state controls – including in cultural policy. While the focus had previously been on a «positive» national history, a fresh wind is now blowing through the country under the slogan «Brücke zwischen Tradition und Moderne».

## Messengers of a new era

Uzbekistan is home to 38 million people today, almost half of whom are under 25. The aim is to create jobs for them in the creative industries. But culture also serves as soft power, helping to give the country a new image and elevate it to the global art world map. The starting point for this lies in the past: craftsmanship, ornamentation, materials, and architecture – specifically, the «Tashkent-Moderne».

After the devastating earthquake of 1966, the Russian central government decided to rebuild Tashkent as a «showcase of the Soviet Orient.» Modern architecture, but with white concrete arabesques and blue ceramic cladding. Thus, the facades became harbingers of a new era.

Later, much of it disappeared behind advertising spaces. These are now banned. Iconic buildings like the Palace of Peoples' Friendship and the former Stalin Museum are being renovated, while new museums are planned: the Universal Museum designed by Tadao Ando and the CCA (Center for Contemporary Art) in Tashkent. It was originally supposed to open in March, but that would be «inappropriate in times of the Iran war,» according to the Iranian-born artistic director, Sara Reza.

Architect Olivier Marty of the French studio KO, who is converting the former coach house built in 1912, reveals in an interview that some details still need to be finalized before the exhibition and residency program starts in September. However, the true heart of Uzbekistan's new cultural policy lies further west, in the former oasis state of Bukhara: In November 2025, the biennial there will open for the first time, and it is far more than just an exhibition.

Rather, it serves as a gateway to bringing contemporary art closer to the public. And it's a school where a new generation of curators is being trained – some of whom will even be allowed to curate the Uzbekistan Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale.

![Installation «Blue Room» in Bukhara: Abdulvahid Bukhoriy in collaboration with Jurabek Siddikov, 2024–2025.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/14/432db47e-dfb2-4e49-be1e-d5c4d588b26a.jpg?crop=1653,2204,x1,y0)
*Installation «Blue Room» in Bukhara: Abdulvahid Bukhoriy in collaboration with Jurabek Siddikov, 2024–2025.* (Felix Odell / zVg ACDF, Bukhara Biennial 2025)

And at the same time, the Bukhara Biennale is also a manifesto: «Our aim is not to emphasize Uzbek nationality through cultural projects,» says Umerova, «but to preserve traditional craftsmanship and combine it with contemporary art.» Seventy works, distributed throughout the restored old town, were created in close cooperation with national artisans in the fields of ceramics, textiles, and carpets – craftsmanship is being rediscovered.

In a caravanserai, one of those early inns along trade routes with its many small rooms arranged around an open courtyard, Egyptian superstar Wael Shawky displayed brass reliefs, gleaming in the sun and carved with intricate pictorial motifs. «My work explores the nostalgia of Islamic memories,» he explained. He said the motifs were derived from miniature painting and that the material was reminiscent of the gold leaf typical of this Persian art.

Marina Perez Simão transformed the entire courtyard into a colorful field of ceramic patterns. «We want to establish international cultural diplomacy and build new infrastructure within the country,» Umerova summarizes the strategy. «But we are being cautious. We don't want to provide too much support, but rather inspire the development of an independent art scene.» However, something essential is still lacking. Collectors? Hardly any. An art market? Not really. When asked where the conceptual artist Akhunov has sold his work, he replies succinctly: «Nowhere!»

During the Soviet era, only the state bought art – and he didn't even offer his works to them. «My art was forbidden.» Too subversive: From the thick, state-published catalog «Soviet Art,» he removed all the pages and refilled the book with his collages. Page after page of silhouettes of Lenin, filled with newspaper clippings and images ranging from nude women to art historical details.

His canvases are also strictly conceptual; one he densely inscribed with the words «breathe slowly and quietly.» The words refer to mantras, to the power of endless repetition. He explains that he had to exist quietly and invisibly back then. Today, the political situation for artists has clearly improved. Nothing is forbidden anymore, neither tapestries nor «Muslim Magic,» as Akhunov calls the practices based on shamanic traditions.

Freedom alone doesn't create infrastructure. While there are some galleries, such as «Regeneration Art» and «Bon Factum» in Tashkent, and «Art Station» in Samarkand, the fact remains: «Art is not yet part of society,» explains Zi Kakhramonova. She is one of the seven artists whose work is featured in the Uzbekistan pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. The pavilion's focus is on the Aral Sea. Once the fourth-largest inland sea in the world, it is now a desert.

![View of the Uzbekistan Pavilion at the 61st Biennale di Venezia: (back) A.A. Murakami, «The Sun Sets in a Shell», 2026 (hergestellt mit Unterstützung von Mandarin Knitting Technology und Zegna Baruffa Lane Borgosesia), (vorne) Zi Kakhramonova’s Archive of Lost Forms, «The Aural Sea» (Installationsansicht), 2026.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/14/a869c4cd-9bb2-4aee-a519-24a16b1c516c.jpg?crop=2500,1875,x0,y0)
*View of the Uzbekistan Pavilion at the 61st Biennale di Venezia: (back) A.A. Murakami, «The Sun Sets in a Shell», 2026 (hergestellt mit Unterstützung von Mandarin Knitting Technology und Zegna Baruffa Lane Borgosesia), (vorne) Zi Kakhramonova’s Archive of Lost Forms, «The Aural Sea» (Installationsansicht), 2026.* (PD)

## The vanished lake

«Welcome to the heart of the environmental disaster,» our guide Jussuf sums it up. In 1985, the water level in Moynak, a once-thriving port city in the autonomous but heavily integrated Republic of Karakalpakstan, receded by five kilometers, he explains. This was no accident. The lake's demise was deliberately engineered in the 1960s by the Soviet Union diverting its feeder rivers to irrigate fields and create new cotton-growing areas on the lakebed – a fatal plan.

Today, 90% of the part of the lake located in Uzbekistan is steppe. Only 12,000 inhabitants still live there, the airport is almost never in operation, and the high fence was blown down by strong winds and never repaired. These winds relentlessly drive the pollutants, salt, and sand particles deposited in the dried-up lakebed onto the fields. Twice a year, the fields must be flooded with water to be cultivated at all. On the former shore, a few rusted ships rot in the steppe. Two brand-new ships were placed on the sand in 2010 during the U.N. secretary-general's visit to dramatically illustrate the situation. Later, more were added, which lie like skeletons in a harbor between the systematically planted saxaul bushes. These plants are extremely salt- and drought-resistant and are intended to stabilize the Aralkum Desert.

This lake is the central focus of Uzbekistan's contribution to this year's Venice Biennale. Among the participants is 21-year-old Aigul Sarsen. She lives in Nukus, the capital of Karkalpakstan, about a three-hour drive from the Aral Sea. Her studio is in an empty house, shared with «more than ten other artists,» she says – she doesn't know the exact number. «We hardly ever meet; everyone works independently.» She only had a few months for Venice, and she sees her sketches and expressive paintings as a sign of «hope that the lake will return.» She imagines the lake, which she has never experienced, as a goddess, a hybrid female being.

## Forbidden art

Nukus is also home to the fascinating Savitsky Museum, founded in 1966 and named after the collector Igor Savitsky, who amassed over 100,000 works, primarily from the 1920s. It is also known as the «Museum of Forbidden Art,» as works by Aleksandr Sardan, Sergey Shigolev, and Vasiliy Lilsenko were banned at the time. Here, they are grouped under the heading «Avanguardia Orientalis.» These paintings do not rely on exoticism but are rooted in the region – the desert, the caravan routes depicted in vibrant bursts of color, and the oases.

The museum shop sells faded posters. In our hotel in Nukus, acrylic paintings are even for sale, unlabeled, leaning against each other, for 600,000 som each, which is about 43 euros. Uzbekistan is still at the beginning of its journey toward a functioning art scene. But thanks in large part to the Venice Biennale, the global market has already been reached. Some artists from the last Biennale already have exhibitions worldwide, such as Saodat Ismailova at the Swiss Institute in New York.

![Installation during the first Biennale in Bukhara, scheduled for September 5 to November 23, 2025: Marina Perez Simão in collaboration with Bakhtiyar Babamuradov, 2024–2025.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/14/42972bc8-6239-4c81-8fbb-3a0d2c1c933d.jpg?crop=2362,1772,x0,y0)
*Installation during the first Biennale in Bukhara, scheduled for September 5 to November 23, 2025: Marina Perez Simão in collaboration with Bakhtiyar Babamuradov, 2024–2025.* (Felix Odell / zVg ACDF, Bukhara Biennial 2025)

Akhunov, who is prominently featured in the parallel program of the Venice Biennale, also hopes for this. He did participate in Documenta in 2012, where «1 m²» was exhibited: 400 empty matchboxes, their inner surfaces painted, covered, and inscribed – a micro-exhibition that could be hidden again at any time. But only now, with the major retrospective in the magnificent Palazzo Franchetti, can he show his entire oeuvre. Right at the entrance, we pass through the four-meter-high «Triumphal Arch» (1979/2026) with 365 metal scissors embedded in the walls – the scissors as a symbol of censorship and state control.

In «Mantras of the USSR,» Akhunov dissects the ideological language of the USSR. In «Instrument of Minds,» as the work is titled, he says it's not about the past, but about «how thoughts survive.» His ideas are now inspiring a new, young generation for whom conceptual art is second nature, like Zi Kakhramonova. She emphasizes that she doesn't want to portray the lost Aral Sea as a catastrophe. Her «Archive of Lost Forms» stands in the middle of the room, filled with salt, from which ceramic creatures emerge as if from another time. She counters the loss of the Aral Sea's biodiversity with imagined forms. Uzbekistan, as these projects make clear, is discovering art not only as cultural heritage but also as a possibility for the future.

---

- Challenges include developing a local art scene and infrastructure, including markets and collectors, as projects like the Venice Pavilion highlight environmental crises such as the Aral Sea's disappearance.

headline: The Indians triumphed at the Little Bighorn River – but their downfall was nonetheless inevitable
lead: 150 years ago, US troops suffered a crushing defeat against the Sioux and Cheyenne. Under the leadership of Sitting Bull, these tribes fought to survive their nomadic way of life. Their descendants have still not overcome the trauma of subjugation.
body:
# The Indians triumphed at the Little Bighorn River – but their downfall was nonetheless inevitable

*150 years ago, US troops suffered a crushing defeat against the Sioux and Cheyenne. Under the leadership of Sitting Bull, these tribes fought to survive their nomadic way of life. Their descendants have still not overcome the trauma of subjugation.*

**Werner J. Marti (text), Andrea Mittelholzer (photo editing)** · International · 2026-06-23 · 2178 words · [ld.10003586](https://www.nzz.ch/international/custers-letzte-schlacht-vor-150-jahren-wurde-die-us-armee-am-little-bighorn-river-von-den-indianern-vernichtend-geschlagen-deren-untergang-war-trotzdem-unaufhaltsam-ld.10003586)

On June 27, 1876, General Philip Sheridan in Chicago received a disturbing report from his subordinate, General Alfred Terry, in Montana. Sheridan was the commander-in-chief in the war against the last free Plains Indians. Terry wrote: «It is my painful duty to report that on the 25th of this month, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer and the troops under his command were struck by a great disaster.»

Terry further wrote that Custer's 7th U.S. Cavalry Regiment had attacked a large Sioux and Cheyenne encampment on the Little Bighorn River from two sides. Three companies launched a surprise attack on the village from the south across the river in the early afternoon. Five more companies, under Custer's command, were to bypass the encampment and then launch the main attack from the north. While attempting to cross the river, Custer was repulsed by the Native Americans and forced to retreat to a nearby hill. His troops were then surrounded. Custer and 209 men were killed by the Native Americans.

![Oldest known depiction of the Battle of Little Bighorn from 1876. Custer (center of image on black horse) is portrayed in a heroic light.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/22/9b0013c0-20f6-4f9e-82d5-7c740cc05c22.jpg?crop=3094,2498,x0,y0)
*Oldest known depiction of the Battle of Little Bighorn from 1876. Custer (center of image on black horse) is portrayed in a heroic light.* (De Agostini / Getty)

The attackers in the south were also driven back across the river by a counterattack and forced to entrench themselves. The Native Americans besieged them until noon the following day. Afterward, they broke camp and allowed the survivors to withdraw. General Terry reached the battlefield shortly afterward. A total of 263 men from the 7th Cavalry Regiment were killed and at least 50 seriously wounded in the fighting. On the Native American side, 40 to 60 were killed and an unknown number were wounded.

![George Armstrong Custer, 1839–1876, commander of the 7th U.S. Cavalry Regiment.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/eb35e54e-9a9b-45a9-bf77-f5dc7324bf3d.jpg?crop=2500,3750,x0,y0)
*George Armstrong Custer, 1839–1876, commander of the 7th U.S. Cavalry Regiment.* (Buyenlarge / Archive Photos / Getty)

## Fight against white land seizure

General Sheridan's adversary was the Hunkpapa Sioux leader Sitting Bull, who was born around 1831 near the Missouri River in South Dakota. The western Sioux tribes – also known as Lakota after their language – and the Cheyenne lived as nomads on the northern American prairie at that time. They were warrior peoples who constantly fought with their neighbors for the best hunting grounds. At the heart of their lives was the bison, of which there were once 40 to 60 million in North America. It not only provided them with their primary food source in the form of meat, but they also utilized virtually every part of the animal for their daily lives.

![Sitting Bull, chief of the Hunkpapa Sioux and leader of the Sioux and Cheyenne in their last war with the U.S. Army in 1876/77.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/5d3813d6-c16a-4e65-9a61-cd9f681df844.jpg?crop=2415,4084,x0,y0)
*Sitting Bull, chief of the Hunkpapa Sioux and leader of the Sioux and Cheyenne in their last war with the U.S. Army in 1876/77.* (Library of Congress / Corbis Historical / Getty)

Even in his early youth, Sitting Bull distinguished himself as an excellent warrior and in 1857 became war chief of the Hunkpapa Sioux. At this time, white settlers began migrating into Lakota territory, a development he resisted with raids. After a two-year war with the U.S. Army, a majority of the Lakota and their Cheyenne allies finally signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868. This treaty established the Great Sioux Reservation, which essentially encompassed present-day South Dakota west of the Missouri River. They were granted exclusive rights to this territory.

![The signing of the Treaty of Laramie in 1868. It created the Great Sioux Reservation, where the Plains Indians were to become sedentary.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/950a1eb3-aa29-4780-8edb-0d84f92c1b9f.jpg?crop=3732,2680,x0,y0)
*The signing of the Treaty of Laramie in 1868. It created the Great Sioux Reservation, where the Plains Indians were to become sedentary.* (Bettmann / Getty)

In return, the Native Americans had to settle on the reservation under the agency responsible for their tribe and henceforth live on government food rations. The bison was deliberately exterminated to deprive the nomadic Native Americans of their livelihood and to clear the prairie for settlement by white settlers.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) 574d521c98a8f1819e0fba789f830e0c]

Sitting Bull and numerous so-called Traditionals refused to sign the Laramie Treaty. They continued their traditional nomadic lifestyle in what is now North Dakota and Montana, where white immigration had not yet begun to the same extent.

![The Sioux led a nomadic life and lived by hunting bison. Photograph of a traditional camp on the prairie.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/23b754d4-b265-4c2c-b637-d1852325793e.jpg?crop=4507,3422,x4,y9)
*The Sioux led a nomadic life and lived by hunting bison. Photograph of a traditional camp on the prairie.* (HUM Images/Universal Images Group/Getty)

![From 1850 onward, increasing numbers of white people moved into the territory of the Sioux and Cheyenne. Settlers in Nebraska in front of their simple dwellings.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/e3b09e4a-e44d-4087-af83-412d1c10c517.jpg?crop=3240,2391,x0,y0)
*From 1850 onward, increasing numbers of white people moved into the territory of the Sioux and Cheyenne. Settlers in Nebraska in front of their simple dwellings.* (Imago)

## Sitting Bull's War

In the summer of 1874, an expedition under Lieutenant Colonel Custer discovered gold in the Black Hills within the reservation. This led to an invasion of gold prospectors into the territory reserved for Native Americans and to renewed conflict with the Lakota and Cheyenne. In November 1875, U.S. President Ulysses Grant decided to force the remaining Traditionals onto the reservation. He issued them an ultimatum to report to the agencies responsible for them there by January 31, 1876.

The ultimatum was a thinly veiled declaration of war. The Native Americans were in their winter camps in Montana, and many children and elderly people would have been unlikely to survive a march to their agencies in South Dakota through the freezing weather and deep snow.

After the ultimatum expired unheeded, General Sheridan ordered a campaign against the Traditionals in their strongholds south of the Yellowstone River in early February. Three troop contingents advanced into the area from the south, east and west. They were reinforced by Native American scouts from tribes hostile to the Sioux. On March 17, the vanguard of the southern contingent, under the command of General George Crook, attacked a Cheyenne camp on the Powder River in the early morning. The attack came as a complete surprise to the approximately 500 inhabitants. Although they managed to escape, the soldiers burned the tipis and destroyed their food supplies and belongings.

![General Philip Henry Sheridan, 1831–1888, commander-in-chief in the last war against the Plains Indians of 1876/77.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/39d73911-de22-4e8e-b161-56e6a80406ff.jpg?crop=3679,2731,x82,y72)
*General Philip Henry Sheridan, 1831–1888, commander-in-chief in the last war against the Plains Indians of 1876/77.* (Hulton-Deutsch Collection / Corbis / Getty)

Thus began the last great war against the Plains Indians. Sitting Bull sent messengers urging the nomadic groups of Traditionals, as well as the warriors on the reservations, to join him at a large summer camp on the Rosebud River. With the unification of several thousand Native Americans, he hoped to be able to resist the U.S. Army.

On June 17, the first major battle took place outside the Rosebud camp between General Crook's troops and the united Traditionals. Although outnumbered, the latter managed to halt Crook's forces. After the six-hour battle, the general returned to his base camp in Wyoming to tend to the wounded and replenish depleted supplies, where he waited for reinforcements for seven weeks.

The Traditionals moved on to the Little Bighorn River. The camp had by then grown to around 7,000 people, among them an estimated 1,800 warriors. Despite General Crook's withdrawal, the danger was not over, as General Terry's troops were approaching from the east. Thus, in the early afternoon of June 25, Custer's 7th Cavalry Regiment launched a surprise attack, which ended in a catastrophic defeat for the U.S. Army.

![George Armstrong Custer with Native American scouts. Warriors from tribes hostile to the Sioux and Cheyenne supported the U.S. Army in reconnaissance and combat.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/3591aee7-8379-4c24-8d47-fc47d7168ff9.jpg?crop=2927,3634,x0,y0)
*George Armstrong Custer with Native American scouts. Warriors from tribes hostile to the Sioux and Cheyenne supported the U.S. Army in reconnaissance and combat.* (Bettmann / Getty)

## Campaign of annihilation

But the victory over Custer did little good for the Native Americans. Sitting Bull knew that the U.S. Army would now seek revenge with new troops. He could not maintain the enormous camp much longer. Providing for so many people and ponies in one place for an extended period was impossible. Furthermore, the camp, with its many children, women and elderly people, was too immobile to defend itself against or evade attacks from new American troops. It therefore dispersed into numerous groups. Many warriors from the reservations returned to their families.

At his headquarters in Chicago, General Sheridan now planned a total war against the last nomadic Lakota and Cheyenne. He had a series of new forts built in Montana, from which he launched relentless attacks against the camps of the remaining Traditionals. He imposed military control on the Native Americans on the reservations, forcing them to surrender the weapons and ponies they had retained to exercise their hunting rights under the 1868 treaty.

![Photo taken in Sitting Bull's camp in 1875.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/26/db7038ed-4a0c-4024-a82e-7d2d93cb758e.jpg?crop=4073,5500,x0,y0)
*Photo taken in Sitting Bull's camp in 1875.* (Smith Collection / Gado / Archive Photos / Getty)

The situation became increasingly difficult for the Traditionals. White bison hunters were now decimating the remaining herds in Montana as well. The Native Americans lost their livelihoods and began to suffer from hunger. Furthermore, their camps were repeatedly destroyed by the U.S. Army. The inhabitants were forced to flee without supplies or belongings. Twice, in October and December 1876, this also happened to Sitting Bull's camp. The winter of 1876/77 became a struggle for survival. In the new year, the last Traditionals had only two options: surrender on the reservation or flee to Canada, where they would be safe from the U.S. Army.

## Exile in Canada

At the end of April 1877, Sitting Bull crossed the border into Canada with around 900 followers. The refugees were greeted kindly by the Royal Mounted Police. However, it was made clear to them that they were now subject to local laws and would not receive food rations from Canada. The latter was not necessary at the moment. In the border region with the U.S., where Sitting Bull's followers found a new home, a large herd of bison provided sufficient food for the time being.

Within months, however, the number of refugees from the U.S. swelled to several thousand. They became serious competition for the Canadian First Nations. The bison herds were overexploited. The following year, bison became rare even in southern Canada. Hunger returned. Fearing a conflict with the U.S., Canada now pressed for the refugees to return to its southern neighbor. In the following years, more and more Traditionals returned there and surrendered.

On July 19, 1881, Sitting Bull finally surrendered with a last group of nearly 200 people at Fort Buford on the Missouri River. It was a sad sight, a local journalist wrote: people in rags, some almost naked, with the harrowing expressions of those who had not eaten enough for months. Upon surrendering his weapon, Sitting Bull wished only to be remembered as the last of his tribe to give up his rifle.

![Sitting Bull's camp in the Standing Rock Reservation after arrival from Canada. Meat is being dried between the tipis.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/26/eb6d7049-63ba-4d53-ad6f-e0355096ab21.jpg?crop=4332,3353,x0,y0)
*Sitting Bull's camp in the Standing Rock Reservation after arrival from Canada. Meat is being dried between the tipis.* (Bettmann / Getty)

It was a humiliating scene for the Native American leader. All his life he had been his own master. Now he and his people were taken to the Standing Rock Agency, which was responsible for them. He and his followers had to abandon their traditional way of life and submit to the white administrator and the army.

## Last years on the reservation

The bison was on the brink of extinction. Its numbers plummeted from 40 to 60 million around 1800 to just a few thousand by the mid-1880s. Paradoxically, it was none other than General Sheridan who contributed to the species' survival. One of the last small herds survived in Yellowstone National Park, established in 1872. It became the starting point for building a new population. In 1886, Sheridan sent the army into the park to keep out intruders. The army managed the park for 30 years, ensuring the species' survival. Today, there are once again half a million animals.

![Millions of bison were killed by white settlers on the prairie and often simply left for dead. Their bones were later collected and processed into glue or fertilizer. The 1892 image shows a huge pile of bison skulls in front of a processing plant in Rogueville, near Detroit.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/441b4212-bf44-415b-a74c-0a53702d93fa.jpg?crop=5689,4448,x0,y0)
*Millions of bison were killed by white settlers on the prairie and often simply left for dead. Their bones were later collected and processed into glue or fertilizer. The 1892 image shows a huge pile of bison skulls in front of a processing plant in Rogueville, near Detroit.* (Burton Historical Collection/Detroit Public Library)

After his surrender, Sitting Bull and 172 followers were held as prisoners of war for 19 months. The Americans thus broke a promise they had previously made to him. Six smaller reservations were carved out of the Great Sioux Reservation, and the rest was opened up for settlement by white settlers. After his release, Sitting Bull lived with his followers on the Standing Rock Reservation of the Hunkpapa Sioux. He engaged in some farming and, as a legendary war hero, toured the United States with a Wild West show.

He never adapted to a settled life. He once told a missionary that he would rather die as a Native American than live as a white man. On December 15, 1890, he was shot and killed by Native American police officers during an attempt to arrest him. The white administrator of the reservation had feared that Sitting Bull might incite a rebellion as part of a Native American religious revival movement.

![Sitting Bull's log cabin with family members in the Standing Rock Reservation.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/c97a443f-ef93-4a97-89e2-e3315e5feb73.jpg?crop=3325,2293,x106,y128)
*Sitting Bull's log cabin with family members in the Standing Rock Reservation.* (Library of Congress / Corbis Historical / Getty)

![Traditional Native American tipis in front of a school built by white people in the Pine Ridge Reservation of the Oglala Sioux in South Dakota.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/22/5feaf38a-7348-46b3-9820-3453ffcc988b.jpg?crop=3244,2163,x0,y311)
*Traditional Native American tipis in front of a school built by white people in the Pine Ridge Reservation of the Oglala Sioux in South Dakota.* (Library of Congress / Corbis Historical / Getty)

## Unresolved trauma

The descendants of Sitting Bull's Hunkpapa Sioux have still not overcome the trauma of losing their traditional way of life. Many continue to live on the Standing Rock Reservation. Nearly 80% are unemployed. Alcoholism and high suicide rates are rampant. The poverty rate is around 50%, almost four times the national average. The healthcare system is chronically underfunded, contributing to a low life expectancy.

Outside of reservation administration and local education and healthcare, there are few jobs. The Sioux lack sufficient fertile land and access to credit for successful agriculture. Those with better education can hope for advancement in American cities, but if they leave the reservation, they risk losing their connection to their people and their cultural roots.

![Desolate situation on the Pine Ridge Reservation of the Oglala Sioux. Photo from 1970.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/05/12/9f2e68f6-66cd-4386-9ab6-25f34ec6fb7f.jpg?crop=4961,3297,x0,y0)
*Desolate situation on the Pine Ridge Reservation of the Oglala Sioux. Photo from 1970.* (Michelle Vignes / Gamma Rapho / Getty)
