headline: The cradle of evil: Adolf Hitler's birthplace becomes a police station. Can a house be decontaminated?
lead: A police command has moved into the city where Adolf Hitler was born. «So what?» some say, life goes on. «Are you kidding me?» others cry, memories are being erased here. A city in Austria is grappling with its toxic legacy.
body:
# The cradle of evil: Adolf Hitler's birthplace becomes a police station. Can a house be decontaminated?

*A police command has moved into the city where Adolf Hitler was born. «So what?» some say, life goes on. «Are you kidding me?» others cry, memories are being erased here. A city in Austria is grappling with its toxic legacy.*

**Sacha Batthyany (text), Roderick Aichinger (photos)** · NZZ am Sonntag Magazin · 2026-06-28 · 3070 words · [ld.10012889](https://www.nzz.ch/nzz-am-sonntag-magazin/hitlers-geburtshaus-in-braunau-wird-zur-polizeiwache-geht-das-ld.10012889)

It's a street like countless others in the provinces. A boutique selling Italian menswear. An organic bakery with watery coffee. A gun shop. A barbershop. A kebab shop.

Someone who knew nothing about it would drive by, quickly wolf down a kebab, and buy some bread. Maybe new shoes?

Nothing earth-shattering happened here. At least, no crime. A child was born 137 years ago. The son of customs officer Alois, an amateur beekeeper, and Klara, née Pölzl. The midwife assigned to the family on that April 20, 1889, was named Franziska Pointecker, according to the city archives. A few days after his birth, the child was baptized Adolf in the nearby parish church of St. Stephen, known for its imposing bell tower.

That complicates things.

It casts a shadow over this high-gabled house, over this small town on the Austrian-German border, which is called Braunau of all places.

It changes the way we look at the gun shop and at the faces of people who have done nothing except grow up in the same place as the presumably greatest mass murderer in history: What is it like to grow up with this shadow?

How much do the places where we live shape us?

![In the barbershop: «Nazi tourists raise their arms and grin.»](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/4432ccda-64ac-45e1-b098-2f29b83fd61b.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)
*In the barbershop: «Nazi tourists raise their arms and grin.»* (NZZAS – Magazine NZZaS)

«Oh, come on!» says Rotraud Steiger in her cozy living room. She has lived on this street for sixty years and recently had her cataracts removed by laser surgery.

When she pulls back the curtains, she has a direct view of Adolf Hitler's birthplace. «That was all so long ago,» she says. People are also dying in Ukraine, she adds, and the same thing is supposedly happening there as it did here back then. «Why dredge up the past?»

«Every day the bald guys and the guys in bomber jackets come,» says one of the boys from the barbershop, showing photos.

Some of these Nazi tourists lay down candles; others raise their right arm and grin. «Once, I was approached by a stranger in Cologne while driving my car with a Braunau license plate,» he says. «He told me I was always welcome and offered me his private parking space.»

«Braunau is a projection surface,» says the current mayor Johannes Waidbacher on the balcony of the town hall, squinting in the sun.

«Our city will forever be in the history books and attract media attention. We have to deal with that.»

The house that makes this town world-famous and attracts visitors from all over the world, because Hitler spent his first months here, Salzburger Vorstadt 15, has a white facade and small mullioned windows.

After the war, it was first a school, later a library, and for a long time served as a workshop for people with disabilities. It has been empty since 2011, has undergone renovations costing 20 million euros in recent years and will reopen at the end of July.

The district police headquarters will move into the building where Hitler was born in a few weeks. Interrogation rooms. Training rooms. Cells. This is either the bitterest irony or the most astute appropriation imaginable.

Some wanted to tear it down instead. Others called for a museum, a House of Responsibility. The disability rights organization felt the Hitler House wasn't wheelchair accessible enough. Local residents were upset that they hadn't been consulted.

«Why not a café?» asks the owner of the men’s fashion store.

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/74920729-5396-47e1-9065-9d79c0e91aeb.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/ba15201b-ab34-468e-a00c-de836b5ccc88.jpg?crop=4587,5734,x0,y0)

The architectural competition that preceded the renovation stated: «The external redesign of the existing building should eliminate the memory of the Nazi era.»

Then-Interior Minister Wolfgang Peschorn spoke of stripping Hitler's birthplace of its «memory.» There was also talk of a «complete neutralization.»

Should memories be erased? Should history be allowed to disappear? Will this small town on the Inn River, with its 18,000 inhabitants, lose its shadow if the most famous house in the area receives a gleaming white facade?

![View from the city gate into the street where the birthplace is located.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/d999945f-60a0-4dde-b47a-0d6aa71b4a37.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)
*View from the city gate into the street where the birthplace is located.*

The debate about the future of the building coincides with a widespread desire to «draw a line under the Nazi era.» In the so-called Memo study series conducted by Bielefeld University, a representative opinion poll on the culture of remembrance in Germany, a majority has for the first time expressed support for letting the commemoration of the Holocaust rest. Eighty years is enough, they argue.

Willi Mernyi from Austria, chairman of the Mauthausen Committee, an association that advocates for the victims of the Nazi regime, reports a similar situation and speaks of an «indifference towards history.» He increasingly hears what the neighbor Rotraud Steiger also says: It's all ancient history! Always these accusations! Why constantly dwell on the past?

What is happening in Braunau is «typical for this country,» says Mernyi. «Ideally, they would have torn the house down and swept history under the rug. But since that’s not possible, they just set up a police station.» That way, he adds, they can immediately book the Nazis who take pictures of themselves on the street. «Passt schon,» people say, which he calls the most Austrian of all phrases.

Mernyi admits that dealing with this house properly is not easy. «There is no normality in Braunau,» he says, just as there is reportedly no normality in Mauthausen, the site of the largest concentration camp on Austrian soil, where hundreds of thousands were shot and gassed.

For a long time in Austria, he says, people tried to suppress history and remained silent because the generation of perpetrators was supposedly still alive and former Nazis held high office.

«Today, when all the criminals are dead, we are fighting against something much worse,» laments Willi Mernyi, «this historical apathy,» a numbness to the events of National Socialism.

And when antisemitism increases, as it has recently, when autocrats are celebrated and there is talk of remigration, he says, «the outcry becomes quieter, the outrage less intense.» People no longer care, or they simply wave it away. «Passt schon.»

![Auschwitz survivor Eva Umlauf: «You cannot separate yourself from your history.»](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/6a88465c-92e0-4f33-ae6a-f0b1a61c3e53.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)
*Auschwitz survivor Eva Umlauf: «You cannot separate yourself from your history.»*

Some 130 kilometers from Braunau, Austria, Eva Umlauf sits on the beige sofa of her penthouse apartment in Munich, in a villa district on the Isar River. Umlauf is a psychotherapist. The 83-year-old works with people's memories and has grappled with her own her entire life.

She pulls up the sleeve of her bottle-green sweater, which matches her eyes, and points to faded prisoner numbers on her forearm, distorted by all the years since they were tattooed under her skin in Auschwitz when she was a baby.

A26959.

When she goes to the doctor and offers her forearm for a blood draw, she says young nurses ask her: «What have you got smeared there?» For them, she notes, it was all so long ago. Some make jokes: «A tattoo at your age?»

«You can’t undo history, you can’t run away from it,» says Umlauf. She lives with these numbers and confronts them daily. «You can’t separate yourself from your history.»

She has several patients, descendants of perpetrators, who come to her for therapy, knowing that she survived Auschwitz, and tell her their family histories: Grandfathers who murdered, grandmothers who worshiped the Führer, fathers who remained silent their entire lives and drowned their war trauma in alcohol.

«They expect absolution from me,» Umlauf says, «but I do not grant it. I only listen.»

Confronting our memories is fundamental, Umlauf says. «It makes us human.» We must reflect on our history, she adds, and know what happened in the past to prevent similar things from happening again.

When she looks around today, it gives her a chill. «I see parallels to the rise of the Nazi Party in the 1930s.» Like Willi Mernyi, she warns against autocrats everywhere who are flirting with dictatorship. Strangers write to her after television appearances, like a recent one on the Markus Lanz talk show, saying, «The Jews are killing children in Gaza.» «Many are glad that the Jews are as bad as the Germans were back then,» she says. «They need a justification.»

That's why she visits schools and talks to teenagers about the Holocaust. «I doubt I can achieve much. But I want to prevent young people from voting for the AfD.»

Eva Umlauf has written a book, an appeal entitled «This Is Exactly How It Begins.» «The fear is back. Jews are being threatened again, synagogues are being attacked again,» she writes. «And with the AfD, a party that the Office for the Protection of the Constitution considers a confirmed right-wing extremist group is reaching for power.»

«Never again?» Umlauf asks in her book. She quotes the famous oath of the liberated inmates of the Buchenwald concentration camp and immediately provides the answer: «It’s happening again!»

Last autumn, Eva Umlauf traveled to Braunau for the first time and told her life story at the «Contemporary History Days,» an annual congress: Of the 232,000 children deported to Auschwitz, around 600 survived. Eva was one of them.

She was on one of the last trains to Auschwitz in 1944. The day before, children from the ramp had still been sent directly «to the gas.» But her transport was delayed, and selection was no longer taking place, as Umlauf recounted in a trembling voice at the Braunau event center: «That is the only reason I am alive.»

The morning after her presentation, she visited Hitler's house, which at that time was still covered with scaffolding and tarpaulins. Cameras guarded the construction site because strangers had traveled from afar to chisel stones out of Hitler's birthplace, just as they had once done with the Berlin Wall.

Umlauf stands in her kitchen, making coffee. «A police station in Hitler's birthplace?» She pauses and looks out the window. «Wouldn't something more harmless and less symbolic be better? A beverage store?»

People like Eva Umlauf are called eyewitnesses, but is she really one? She was two years old when she and her mother were deported from the Sered transit camp in Slovakia to the Auschwitz extermination camp. She lost her father and most of her family. She is a victim of the Shoah, but she has no memory of the war.

When the last eyewitnesses are gone and soon there is no one left to tell of the horrors, what will remain?

Places like Braunau.

![Idyllic Braunau.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/eef0be35-fc2f-4e9e-9142-434c82385b35.jpg?crop=5798,3865,x0,y0)
*Idyllic Braunau.*

It's unclear on which floor the Hitler family lived. What is known is that the father, Alois, a customs officer in the Innviertel region on the edge of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, who oversaw the animal transports from Braunau to Munich, wanted to live as close as possible to his beehives and therefore moved twice within the town. This is how Florian Kotanko, the local historian who knows the story of every cobblestone here, tells it during a walk through the old town.

Adolf Hitler returned to Braunau only once more. On his triumphant journey to Vienna in 1938, where he announced the «Anschluss» of Austria, he stopped in the town square. He also mentioned his birthplace in his inflammatory book «Mein Kampf.» During the war, the house was purchased by Martin Bormann, the Reich Leader of the Nazi Party , on behalf of the party, and transformed into a gallery in honor of the Führer.

«There’s a rumor that Hitler was born in a stable behind the house,» says Kotanko. It was a myth, he explains, meant to turn Braunau into the Bethlehem of the Third Reich, «but that’s all nonsense. Just like the legend that he was born in a precipitate birth right in the middle of the Inn Bridge.»

The fact is that after 1945 the building first housed a school, and later a higher technical college. For a long time it was rented to Lebenshilfe, an organization for the care of people with physical and mental disabilities.

Well into the 1980s, it was just one house among many on a street like countless others in the province. Braunau was Braunau – and not «Hitlertown,» as international media call the town today, because the name guarantees attention.

«The residents didn’t care at all who was born in this house,» says Kotanko. «They went to school here, not to Hitler’s house.» What we now call a culture of remembrance only emerged later, and with it, the place acquired a symbolic significance.

The process of coming to terms with Nazi crimes was slower in Austria than in Germany. Denazification was also less rigorous, with the result that many perpetrators returned to high-ranking positions after the war.

Braunau's mayor from 1967 to 1989, a certain Hermann Fuchs, was allegedly a member of the local Hitler Youth and reportedly felt personally attacked whenever the town's history was mentioned. No wonder everyone remained silent.

And so, not only in Braunau but throughout the entire country, people wrapped themselves in a comfortable blanket of silence, making themselves at ease in the deeply rooted victim myth that Austria became the first victim of Nazi Germany through «the Anschluss» in March 1938.

And they concealed the fact that Hitler had been cheered by 250,000 people on Vienna's Heldenplatz: a country in a Führer frenzy.

> [embed: oembed ]

Unlike in Germany, there was no significant 1968 movement in the country that raised uncomfortable questions about guilt and responsibility. That is, until the so-called Waldheim affair shook the nation from the mid-1980s onwards.

Former UN Secretary-General and later Austrian President Kurt Waldheim was suspected of having been involved in war crimes in the Balkans as an officer in the Wehrmacht. «Everything came to light with Waldheim,» says historian Florian Kotanko.

On the occasion of Hitler's 100th birthday in 1989, Mayor Gerhard Skiba, Fuchs' successor, not only issued a ban on weddings for April 20 but also had a granite block from the quarry of the former Mauthausen concentration camp placed in front of the birthplace.

From that moment on, this house at Salzburger Vorstadt 15, which everyone had silently walked past for years, could no longer be overlooked. It had become a memorial. The media wrote about it and turned sleepy Braunau into «Hitlertown.» Suddenly, Nazis and other misguided individuals were making pilgrimages to their Führer's temple in this small town on the matcha-green Inn and lighting candles. Recently, a drunken Swiss man with the Waffen-SS honorary ring on his finger was among them.

A once-forgotten place becomes a projection, as the mayor put it. A symbol against its will. And it pops up on the map of dark places, like Predappio, Mussolini's birthplace, where Duce supporters still salute with the Roman salute, or Stalin's Gori northwest of Tbilisi.

Simultaneously with this dubious fame, the Association for Contemporary History was founded, which continues to grapple with this toxic legacy , organizing events and initiating debates. In 2011, Adolf Hitler was stripped of his honorary citizenship of the city, 66 years after the war.

And just a few months ago, the last street names that commemorated Nazi figures disappeared after fierce resistance from the right-wing conservative FPÖ, for whom «the administrative effort» was too high.

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/397b21d2-02a3-4bc8-ba9a-c8ab2fea5556.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/e2afc903-fe6a-43be-960e-62be29a0f749.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)

«There is such a commotion about this house,» says her neighbor, Rotraud Steiger, who has been looking at this facade from across the street for 60 years and who, when she complains in her Innviertel dialect, immediately sounds like Thomas Bernhard.

A few years ago, during a skiing holiday, she was insulted by a Dutch stranger at the ski lift, simply because she was from Braunau. «One more word and you'll end up in the snow,» she barked back.

«Enough is enough,» she says calmly on her sofa. She has nothing against confronting the past. Her father, she says, regretted being a member of the Nazi Party his entire life. She just thinks «everything has gotten out of hand.» She’s had enough of the Hitler tourists, the TV crews, the same old memorial concerts and «all this theater.»

Hence the police station. It's supposed to maintain order, decontaminate the poisoned house, keep «Hitlertown» out of the headlines, and drive out the Nazis. But this place is like a sauce stain on your pants: the harder you rub and scrub, the more determined you are to make it disappear, the bigger it gets.

«Braunau forces you to take a stand,» says Stefan Schlögl, who grew up here and now lives in Vienna. He recounts how he once sent strange old men, who had somewhat surreptitiously asked him as a child for directions to «that Hitler house,» to the garbage dump.

It all started in 1991, says Schlögl. News reports showed images of Nazi marches and burning asylum seeker accommodations in Hoyerswerda, Germany.

«That's when the young right-wingers in Braunau became active. Guys in bomber jackets, whom I knew from the sandbox, intercepted me on my way to the cinema and pushed me against the wall.»

But he is not traumatized by it, says Schlögl, a freelance journalist who returned to his roots and has been heading the Association for Contemporary History in Braunau for a year. «Fights in the countryside were nothing unusual back then.»

They have since apologized to him, he says. «Nonsense back then,» they reportedly whispered to him. And he, in true Austrian fashion, replied: «Passt schon.»

For a long time, he says, he has wondered from afar what the media made of his birthplace. The narrative of this «dark place» that refuses to confront its past, he says in an ice cream parlor café, has long been «part of journalistic folklore» in Austria.

Braunau and this house are «like that one crisis relationship in the family,» about which everyone talks and has something to say, Schlögl recently wrote about his hometown in the newspaper «Die Zeit.»

Considering the three years Hitler lived here, Braunau's significance is grossly exaggerated, Schlögl says. «If some crackpot runs around in a Hitler uniform, international newspapers report on it.» Elsewhere, he notes, the same story would be worth only a brief mention.

Regarding the changing of street names, he adds, everyone was outraged. How could it be, people asked, that until a few months ago, alleys and stairways were still named after committed Nazis?

What gets forgotten in all this, Schlögl says, is how much the town contributes to the culture of remembrance in Austria with its events, discussion evenings and films. «Braunau is much more progressive than other Austrian cities, like Salzburg, where more streets are still named after Nazi Party members than after women.»

![Hitler? «That only interests old people.»](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/06/25/38c92a9c-7da0-415b-a71f-f99ed5dbec35.jpg?crop=4000,6000,x0,y0)
*Hitler? «That only interests old people.»*

It's getting late in Hitler's birthplace; the mobile phone shops, bank branches and shoe stores around the cobbled town square have long since closed.

The local youth gather in the parking lot of a shopping center outside the old town. They cruise around McDonald's in souped-up cars, listening to German rap and eating greasy pizza from cardboard boxes on the hood of their cars. It's a balmy early summer evening in May.

They heard about the Hitler house in school, says one of them as döner sauce runs down his hand. Others shrug. That only interests the old people.

«Nothing happening today,» they say. The «Herzog,» the local nightclub, is closed. They seem like they want to get away, out of Braunau, to somewhere that life is happening and time hasn't stood still.

Later, three young Romanian women in tight dresses pass by. They haven't lived in the area long; they stayed because they found work at the register of a furniture store. They have their own stories.

«Hitler was born here?» asks one woman as indifferently as possible, sounding neither surprised nor shocked, smoking slim cigarettes with a white filter.

«I didn't know that.»

---

- Some see this as a clever repurposing, while others fear it erases history, especially since places like Braunau retain symbolic significance.
- Witnesses and historians stress the importance of confronting history, even as historical apathy increasingly takes hold.

headline: The quiet giant: how China's Geely Group conquered Europe's car market from within
lead: Volvo, Lotus, and now Geely itself, alongside many lesser-known brands: The Hangzhou-based company is aiming for maximum diversity. Its market share is growing steadily, but it risks European customers losing track in the jungle of names and positioning.
body:
# The quiet giant: how China's Geely Group conquered Europe's car market from within

*Volvo, Lotus, and now Geely itself, alongside many lesser-known brands: The Hangzhou-based company is aiming for maximum diversity. Its market share is growing steadily, but it risks European customers losing track in the jungle of names and positioning.*

**Herbie Schmidt** · Mobilität · 2026-08-07 · 1450 words · [ld.10018163](https://www.nzz.ch/mobilitaet/der-leise-gigant-wie-chinas-geely-konzern-europas-automarkt-von-innen-heraus-erobert-ld.10018163)

![The Chinese group Geely established itself in Europe starting in 2010. Hardly anyone noticed.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/ffa844eb-22e6-45cb-bdaa-88edf7ed0c63.jpg?crop=6000,4000,x0,y0)
*The Chinese group Geely established itself in Europe starting in 2010. Hardly anyone noticed.* (Stephanie Lecocq / Reuters)

Peter Z. had just bought a Volvo EX30, a compact electric car from the Swedish brand, known for its image of safety and solidity. He felt comfortable from the start thanks to its Scandinavian design and secure driving experience. When he happened to learn that while the car was developed in Sweden, Volvo had been a subsidiary of China’s Geely group since 2010, he was shocked. He now believed he had bought a Chinese car, one that suddenly seemed less safe and solid to him. But he can continue driving reassured, as both the technical basis of the Swedish EV and its design were created in Gothenburg.

Now, however, it gets interesting: it was not Volvo that developed the vehicle platform used for the EX30 — called Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA) — but another Geely brand named Zeekr. This indicates how the Hangzhou-based group operates. The port city of Hangzhou lies a good two hours’ drive southwest of Shanghai. It is considered one of China’s technological strongholds; IT companies like Alibaba Group are headquartered there.

Geely is one of the Chinese automotive groups coping with declining domestic sales because the government no longer prioritizes electric vehicle promotion. Since 2022, there have been no more EV subsidies in China, and the tax exemption will also be abolished starting in 2027. Geely, therefore — like BYD, Chery, Leapmotor, and Great Wall — must seek salvation by exporting its vehicles. Europe is one suitable market, as its automotive industry lags technologically behind China and currently cannot keep pace with Chinese groups.

![The Volvo EX30 is a Swedish car, but it has only recently begun production in Europe. Previously, production took place at Geely in China.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/c2fe35e0-93b7-4efe-aa29-bc4f985322eb.jpg?crop=1587,893,x223,y357)
*The Volvo EX30 is a Swedish car, but it has only recently begun production in Europe. Previously, production took place at Geely in China.* (PD)

## Long-planned

However, unlike BYD, for example, Geely does not try to boast as an almighty technology leader in Europe. It takes a more differentiated approach. Its strategy, reminiscent of the Greek myth of the Trojan Horse, is designed for the long term:

![Geely is developing hybrid engines together with Renault in a joint venture called Horse Powertrain.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/aaecdc78-7f2e-42bd-9202-23e2f93040e7.jpg?crop=617,497,x0,y0)
*Geely is developing hybrid engines together with Renault in a joint venture called Horse Powertrain.* (PD)

This structure created a multi-brand system blending European and Chinese brands. The four brands — Volvo, Polestar, Lynk & Co, and Zeekr — form a cluster for electric and hybrid cars, all developed together under one roof in Gothenburg but positioned differently. Volvo is positioned as the solid premium brand with high safety and quality standards. Polestar and Zeekr offer electric cars with the latest technology and high performance. And Lynk & Co, like Smart, primarily targets urban lifestyle groups.

The advantage of this Swedish quartet is that all brands are developed for European customers or at least strongly tailored to them. Even the Geely design department is led by an experienced European, whose office is also located in the Gothenburg complex: German Stefan Sielaff, who came as chief designer from Bentley, brings extensive experience from Audi and Mercedes.

Geely is now also expanding its namesake brand into European markets — Spain, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg. Geely also aims to offer a competitor to Citroën or Dacia in the European mass market for particularly affordable cars. Geely is also entering the market as a car brand in Switzerland these days.

## Technologically broadly positioned

One advantage of Geely’s group strategy is its ability to leverage far-reaching synergies. Not only is the Volvo EX30 based on the SEA architecture, but its modular chassis also forms the basis for the Smart #1 and the luxury sports car Lotus Eletre. European manufacturers can only dream of such economies of scale.

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/609e7a07-1895-4be5-97a8-a16dbb1d083a.jpg?crop=1920,1080,x0,y180)

![](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/6c7dac7e-8814-47e4-9ea7-e548027e2532.jpg?crop=3005,1690,x846,y1387)

At the same time, Geely does not focus solely on electric cars but remains open to various technologies for Europe. Since manufacturers outside China possess extensive technological know-how in building internal combustion engines and hybrid systems, Geely benefits from its joint venture agreements: with Renault for powertrain development and with Ford for building cars with various powertrains, the so-called Multi-Energy Vehicles. Two electric Geely SUVs, a new Ford Bronco, and the next Ford Kuga are slated for production at the Ford plant in Valencia.

Here, the Hangzhou-based group has clear advantages, for example, over Tesla, but also over its Chinese competitors in Europe such as Chery and Great Wall. Only BYD and Leapmotor also rely on European production. Leapmotor benefits from a cooperation with the Stellantis group, gaining insights into technologies where China is not yet at the forefront.

## European protectionism: Limited impact

To protect the European automotive industry from rising imports of Chinese cars, the EU imposed punitive tariffs on electric cars manufactured in the People’s Republic. Manufacturers like BYD and Chery quickly adjusted their export portfolios and are currently launching more plug-in hybrid vehicles in Europe.

Geely also reacted differently in this case. The group pursues a balanced strategy with multiple brands and various powertrains. For example, to retain European customers for the aforementioned Volvo EX30, manufactured in China, and to avoid price increases, the group began building the EV at Volvo’s Belgian plant as well. This way, punitive tariffs do not apply.

For its other brands and vehicles, the company remains unfazed by the tariffs. Lothar Schupet, the German head of Europe for Geely’s subsidiary brand Zeekr, told the NZZ, «We will not pass punitive tariffs on to customers.» Geely prefers to accept selective margin losses as long as it gains European market share. And even with Zeekr, he added, it would be possible to switch to hybrid vehicles if necessary, as the technology already exists within the group. Moreover, the company learns daily through partnerships with Renault and Ford.

Thus, the Geely group is also likely to soon possess sufficient technological competence to build vehicles for Europe in Europe, either under already known brands or those that can boast particularly attractive prices. And this with powertrains that the market and regulations demand. Geely CEO Li Shufu skillfully orchestrated this.

![Vehicles from the Geely group, such as the Lynk & Co 02, are interesting products, but nobody in Europe knows the brands and models.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/05/0c14190a-5250-43c9-ae44-6b8e003dc88e.jpg?crop=3491,1964,x273,y638)
*Vehicles from the Geely group, such as the Lynk & Co 02, are interesting products, but nobody in Europe knows the brands and models.* (PD)

However, Geely did not sufficiently consider one thing in its planned triumphant advance in Europe: Some of the group’s brands are unfamiliar to European customers, with names and complicated model designations that no one can remember. This also applies to the Geely group itself, apart from Volvo, Lotus, the London taxi, and Smart.

Unlike European brands such as VW, Fiat, and Peugeot, Zeekr and Lynk & Co cannot benefit from a long tradition and success stories of previous models. Anyone who buys a Polestar initially knows nothing about the brand. They buy because they like the technology, the design, and especially the price. This must suffice for now until Geely brands have established themselves in Europe, become part of the streetscape, and written their first success story.

Chinese multi-brand groups face another problem with the positioning of individual brands. Which European buyer today can clearly name the difference between Lynk & Co and Volvo? This requires further investment from parent company Geely. However, the group currently seems less concerned with which of its subsidiary brands is more successful than others. Customers can quickly lose track. It is much easier to focus on established European brands. They are easier to categorize and thus still have a real advantage over the flood of Chinese automakers.

---
**Auto summary (NZZ, GPT-generated):**
- China's Geely Group continues its steady expansion into the European car market, leveraging a multi-faceted strategy that includes acquisitions and joint ventures with European brands like Volvo, Lotus, and Renault.
- European customers may find the brand diversity and complex positioning confusing, despite Geely maintaining design and development hubs in Gothenburg.
- Through joint ventures and the SEA platform, Geely capitalizes on synergies to stay competitive, though struggles with the acceptance of its less established brands in Europe.
author: Herbie Schmidt
summaryBullets: China's Geely Group continues its steady expansion into the European car market, leveraging a multi-faceted strategy that includes acquisitions and joint ventures with European brands like Volvo, Lotus, and Renault.
European customers may find the brand diversity and complex positioning confusing, despite Geely maintaining design and development hubs in Gothenburg.
Through joint ventures and the SEA platform, Geely capitalizes on synergies to stay competitive, though struggles with the acceptance of its less established brands in Europe.

headline: When crude oil enters the sea off Oman, it is always an ecological catastrophe – what research has learned from past disasters
lead: Seabirds stuck together in oil, fish belly up – the immediate consequences of an oil spill are obvious. In the long term, however, life proves to be surprisingly resilient.
body:
# When crude oil enters the sea off Oman, it is always an ecological catastrophe – what research has learned from past disasters

*Seabirds stuck together in oil, fish belly up – the immediate consequences of an oil spill are obvious. In the long term, however, life proves to be surprisingly resilient.*

**Georg Rüschemeyer** · Wissenschaft · 2026-08-22 · 1497 words · [ld.10019954](https://www.nzz.ch/wissenschaft/wenn-wie-jetzt-vor-oman-rohoel-ins-meer-gelangt-ist-das-immer-eine-oekologische-katastrophe-was-die-forschung-aus-vergangenen-ungluecken-gelernt-hat-ld.10019954)

![Pelican in the Gulf of Mexico, shortly after the Deepwater Horizon oil rig blowout in 2010. Contaminated seabirds often only become poisoned by the oil during desperate attempts to clean it up.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/18/b3a105c9-a6f6-4fdd-bff6-296ec8774790.jpg?crop=3000,2029,x0,y0)
*Pelican in the Gulf of Mexico, shortly after the Deepwater Horizon oil rig blowout in 2010. Contaminated seabirds often only become poisoned by the oil during desperate attempts to clean it up.* (Win McNamee / Getty)

For weeks, a largely unnoticed ecological drama has been unfolding in the Arabian Sea off the coast of Oman. The damaged supertanker «Caroline Bezengi» lies aground off the island of al-Kibliya. Huge quantities of crude oil are flowing into the sea from the ship, which is considered part of Russia's so-called shadow fleet. Experts estimate the cargo at more than 100,000 tons. It is difficult to say how much of it has already leaked. The resulting oil slick now covers an area of many hundreds of square kilometers, as can be clearly seen in satellite images. In mid-August, it reached the Omani coast.

The oil spill is unfolding in the midst of the Al Hallaniyyat Islands Nature Reserve, a strictly protected marine sanctuary. The islands are important breeding grounds for rare sea turtles and seabirds, and the waters boast coral reefs famous among dive tourists and a unique subspecies of humpback whale.

It is still too early to assess the potential damage to the ecosystem. What is clear is that crude oil is pure poison for all marine habitats, from the deep sea to the beach. «How severe the ecological consequences are in individual cases depends heavily on the abiotic conditions at the respective accident site,» says oceanographer Marcus Dengler from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel. There, the physicist primarily focuses on ocean currents.

## Release point: crucial factors

First, the point of release. Crude oil that escapes at the seafloor, as in the Deepwater Horizon drilling platform blowout, can disperse significantly even in the water column. In shallow-water accidents near the coast, most of it quickly floats as an oil slick on the surface. There, the surf often whips it into a suspension of oil and water, similar to what you get when shaking a vinaigrette. Researchers affectionately call the result «Chocolate Mousse»: a viscous mass floating on the sea surface with many times the volume of the oil it contains. It is transported particularly far by ocean currents and makes it difficult to contain the oil's spread.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) eba29ab8b3563c62c88b5868e0ae6622]

Whether moussed or not: «The further fate of the oil on the surface depends on large ocean currents and local wind conditions,» says Dengler. These can drive the oil out to the open sea, as was the case with the tanker «Castillo de Bellver» accident in 1983 off the coast of South Africa, which, despite more than 100,000 tons of oil released, had comparatively mild ecological consequences. This is because, when dispersed in the vast ocean, the hydrocarbon mixture is relatively quickly broken down by the influence of light and finally degraded by bacteria.

## Crude oil: a complex mixture

Wherever the journey takes it, light components of the crude oil evaporate along the way, while the remaining long-chain components clump together. «If these clumps become denser than seawater, they sink into the depths, and the oil slick continues to lose mass,» Dengler explains.

However, it is not a case of «out of sight, out of mind,» because in the depths, microbial degradation heavily consumes the often already scarce oxygen, thereby burdening the less obvious ecosystems, Dengler maintains. «In the current case in the Arabian Sea, this will be particularly interesting, as there are naturally large oxygen-free zones in the depths due to the lack of connection to cold, oxygen-rich ocean areas,» he adds.

Another effect also contributes to the oxygen deficiency, severely impairing the teeming life below the oil slick even on the open sea: it blocks the penetration of sunlight. The microalgae of the phytoplankton thus lack their basis for life, and additionally, because they live near the surface, they are also poisoned by soluble oil components. The consequence: the base of the entire food web collapses over large areas.

## Oil disasters: no fixed rules

Despite all degradation processes, the slick usually still contains more than enough oil when it finally reaches a coast. How severely it affects the local communities and how long it takes for them to overcome this damage depends on many factors: exposed rocky coasts suffer less than species-rich estuaries, and in polar seas, the microbial degradation of oil takes significantly longer due to low temperatures than in the tropics. «Every accident is different,» summarizes Marcus Dengler.

> [embed: q-tool (chart/map) eba29ab8b3563c62c88b5868e0aab2e7]

An exemplary look at five notorious oil disasters of the past illustrates some of the lessons that science has been able to draw so far:

## «Deepwater Horizon»: Gulf of Mexico (2010)

![The oil slick on the beach of Grand Isle, Louisiana, on May 22, 2010. The catastrophe also threatened the existence of many fishermen.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/18/b9850c09-a0c8-4eb1-9e78-fa8bd41856fa.jpg?crop=3000,1897,x0,y0)
*The oil slick on the beach of Grand Isle, Louisiana, on May 22, 2010. The catastrophe also threatened the existence of many fishermen.* (John Moore / Getty)

On April 20, 2010, the Deepwater Horizon drilling platform exploded in the Gulf of Mexico off New Orleans. By the time the well was temporarily sealed in July, at least half a million tons of crude oil had leaked out. «This accident differed in some important characteristics from typical tanker accidents,» says oceanographer Marcus Dengler. For example, the oil escaped at great depths, along with huge amounts of methane gas. It dispersed over large areas at a water depth of more than 1,000 meters, and a significant portion sank to the bottom.

But what rose to the surface was enough to contaminate more than 2,000 kilometers of the American coastline, including the Mississippi Delta and sensitive salt marshes. An overview study concluded six years after the accident that many communities had, however, recovered surprisingly well.

However, the consequences are not yet over for longer-lived animals at the top of the food pyramid, including large fish, dolphins, and sea turtles. A follow-up study published in 2020 found the tilefish to be particularly contaminated with harmful hydrocarbons: the fish dig extensive burrows into the sediment and thus regularly encounter submerged oil, the residues of which damage their internal organs.

## «Amoco Cadiz»: Brittany (1978)

![The bow of the «Amoco Cadiz» shortly after the accident in 1978. Today, all parts of the ship lie underwater and are a popular destination for divers.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/20/5c9c3e66-0f6c-455e-b389-1cc2b2e4c4d3.jpg?crop=3893,2576,x0,y0)
*The bow of the «Amoco Cadiz» shortly after the accident in 1978. Today, all parts of the ship lie underwater and are a popular destination for divers.* (Imago)

Today, the wreck of the supertanker «Amoco Cadiz» lies at a depth of 30 meters off the coast of Brittany. It ran aground on rocks on March 16, 1978, after a rudder failure, broke apart, and with its cargo of a good 220,000 tons of crude oil, caused one of the most serious oil disasters, directly off a European coast. The oil killed seabirds and marine animals along 360 kilometers of coastline, including thousands of tons of oysters. The recovery of the affected area followed the typical pattern of ecological succession: initially, a few species largely insensitive to the toxic hydrocarbons colonized the newly available space on rocks and sediments. Over the years, more and more species were added until, by the mid-1980s, biodiversity largely corresponded to what it had been before the accident.

## «Exxon Valdez»: Alaska (1989)

![After the «Exxon Valdez» accident, helpers cleaned the beach with hot steam – a serious mistake, as it turned out.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/18/74007f4b-d0e0-4b8d-8baa-32be6a72a050.jpg?crop=5315,3543,x0,y0)
*After the «Exxon Valdez» accident, helpers cleaned the beach with hot steam – a serious mistake, as it turned out.* (Jean-Louis Atlan / Sygma)

Hardly any oil spill has been the subject of as many ecological impact studies as the accident of the tanker «Exxon Valdez,» which ran aground on a reef off the coast of South Alaska on March 24, 1989. Approximately 40,000 tons of leaked crude oil covered about 2,000 kilometers of pristine coastline with a brown slick.

Seabirds, but also sea otters and other marine mammals, died by the thousands. Some holes in the ecological network closed quickly on their own, while others remained open for decades. For example, the bladderwrack, which had previously served as habitat and food for countless animals, was only able to re-establish itself very slowly over large areas: its place on the rocks had in the meantime been occupied by other algae and barnacles.

In many places, the bladderwrack was less a victim of the oil than of the cleaning measures. After the accident, attempts were made to remove the oil from the coast using steam cleaners. This was successful, but it also successfully removed all life from the rocks and pebble beaches. Since then, cleaning operations have been carried out with considerably more restraint.

## Oil Spill in the Second Gulf War: Kuwait (1991)

![Beach in Kuwait shortly after Iraqi forces caused the largest oil spill of all time. Burning oil wells blaze in the background.](https://img-msp-prod.nzz.ch/2026/08/18/4296bc64-c0bf-490e-b0b3-02cb283d4c32.jpg?crop=4748,3300,x0,y0)
*Beach in Kuwait shortly after Iraqi forces caused the largest oil spill of all time. Burning oil wells blaze in the background.* (Allan Tannenbaum / Archive Photos / Getty)

To hinder the landing of coalition forces, the Iraqi army channeled an estimated over one million tons of oil into the Persian Gulf during the Second Gulf War – the largest oil spill of all time. Salt marshes and mangrove belts died off over large areas – and with them their typical animal communities. At first glance, many of the affected ecosystems quickly recovered from the acute damage. But even here, the oil remains deep in the sediment to this day. Moreover, the Persian Gulf never truly recovers: large quantities of crude oil also entered the tropical sea during recent hostilities.

## Oil Spill in Bahia las Minas: Panama 1986

A scientific peculiarity is the oil spill of just 8,000 tons of oil that flowed from a ruptured storage tank into Bahia las Minas on the Caribbean side of Panama on April 27, 1986. Affected areas included coral reefs, sensitive seagrass beds, and mangrove forests, which died off over approximately 70 hectares. What is special is that the Galeta Marine Laboratory of the Smithsonian Institution is located in the middle of the affected region, from which biologists have been studying life in and around the surrounding sea since the 1960s.

For this reason, researchers were immediately on site and could draw on extensive datasets about the state of the ecosystem before the accident – a unique scientific opportunity that led to numerous publications. For example, a study recently published in the «Bulletin of Marine Science» shows that the mangrove stands regenerating in the areas affected in 1986 thrived less well for up to 20 years than those in unaffected areas.

---
**Auto summary (NZZ, GPT-generated):**
- A supertanker is leaking oil off the coast of Oman, causing a massive oil spill in a strictly protected marine reserve.
- The ecological impact affects both surface habitats and oxygen-deprived deep-sea areas.
- Scientific studies of past oil disasters highlight the ongoing challenges in the recovery of affected ecosystems.
author: Georg Rüschemeyer

The ecological impact affects both surface habitats and oxygen-deprived deep-sea areas.
Scientific studies of past oil disasters highlight the ongoing challenges in the recovery of affected ecosystems.

headline: Porsche 911 GT3 RS: Aerodynamic Extremism and Mechanical Purity on the Sustenpass
lead: With 525 horsepower, active DRS wing architecture, and 860 kilograms of downforce, the GT3 RS transforms the high alpine Sustenpass into an uncompromised masterclass of German motorsport engineering.
body:
## Atmospheric High RPM and Alpine Elevation

At 2,224 meters above sea level, thin alpine air chokes forced-induction engines, but the 4.0-liter naturally aspirated flat-six in the 911 GT3 RS screams with unfiltered clarity up to its 9,000 RPM redline. Developing 525 horsepower without turbos, its mechanical throttle response on the ascent from Innertkirchen provides millimetric traction control across damp asphalt switchbacks.

«This is not a touring vehicle disguised as a racer. It is a homologated motorsport chassis engineered specifically for high-speed lateral compression,» explains Porsche motorsport director Andreas Preuninger.

## Dynamic Aerodynamics and Chassis Telemetry

The defining leap in this generation lies in Formula 1-derived active aerodynamics:
- Active front diffusers and a two-tier rear carbon wing generate 860 kg of downforce at 285 km/h.
- Steering wheel rotary dials allow independent adjustment of front and rear rebound and compression damping across four stages.
- Electronically controlled differential lock can be fine-tuned mid-corner to manipulate vehicle yaw on tight alpine hairpins.

## The NZZ Verdict: Mechanical Sovereignty in an Electric Era

In an automotive landscape increasingly dominated by heavy, sanitized electric luxury barges, the GT3 RS represents an unapologetic monument to analogue mechanical precision. Its lightweight carbon construction (1,450 kg DIN) and carbon-ceramic brakes deliver deceleration forces that demand physical resilience. It is an uncompromising triumph of specialized German mechanical engineering.
author: Christian Eichberger

headline: Porsche 911 GT3 Touring Review: The Driver’s Car That Refuses to Shout
lead: The Porsche 911 GT3 Touring takes one of the world's most capable performance cars and removes the obvious visual theatre. There is no enormous fixed rear wing, no attempt to look like a race car parked outside a supermarket—just a naturally aspirated flat-six, a superb chassis and a manual gearbox that make the Touring one of the purest modern sports cars you can buy.
body:
There is something almost deliberately understated about the Porsche 911 GT3 Touring.
Park one next to a typical modern supercar and it can look strangely ordinary. There are no extravagant doors, no enormous air intakes and no rear wing rising above the roof. Its silhouette is familiar enough that someone who knows little about cars could mistake it for an ordinary 911.
That is precisely the point.
The GT3 Touring is Porsche's answer to a question that modern performance cars increasingly struggle to answer: how much performance do you actually need to advertise?
Underneath the restrained bodywork is a car that remains fundamentally extreme.
The current-generation 911 GT3 Touring combines rear-wheel drive with a naturally aspirated 4.0-liter flat-six producing 502 horsepower. It can be ordered with either a seven-speed dual-clutch PDK transmission or, more importantly for purists, a six-speed manual gearbox.
The numbers are impressive, but they are not really what defines the car.
The engine does.
In an era where turbocharging, hybridization and increasingly sophisticated electronic systems have become the norm, the GT3's naturally aspirated engine feels almost rebellious. There is no giant wave of torque arriving at low revs and no electric motor filling in the gaps. Instead, the engine rewards commitment.
The harder you push it, the better it becomes.
The engine's character changes as the revs rise. Low in the range, it is perfectly usable and relatively calm. Higher up, the throttle becomes more responsive, the exhaust note intensifies and the entire car seems to become increasingly impatient.
Keep going and the engine climbs toward its 9,000-rpm redline.
That final stretch of the rev range is the reason this car exists.
Modern performance cars are often extraordinarily fast but surprisingly easy to drive quickly. Turbocharged engines can produce enormous torque with minimal effort, while sophisticated automatic transmissions can select the perfect gear before the driver has even considered what to do.
The GT3 Touring is different.
It still has enormous capability, but it encourages the driver to participate.
That becomes particularly obvious with the manual transmission.
The six-speed gearbox is not the quickest way to extract every possible tenth of a second from the car. The PDK is faster. It can shift with near-instantaneous precision and makes the car devastatingly effective on a circuit.
But the manual introduces something the stopwatch cannot measure.
Interaction.
Selecting a gear, matching the revs and deciding when to shift become part of the experience. You are no longer simply requesting acceleration. You are managing the engine.
For some buyers, that will be enough reason to choose the manual.
For others, the PDK makes more sense. The GT3 is sufficiently capable that its performance can quickly become overwhelming on public roads, and the dual-clutch gearbox allows the driver to concentrate on steering and braking while the transmission handles the ratios.
Either way, the chassis is the real star.
The 911 GT3 has been engineered around the idea that cornering speed matters just as much as straight-line acceleration. The suspension is extraordinarily sophisticated, and Porsche has managed to give the car tremendous body control without making it feel completely intolerable on normal roads.
That balance is difficult.
A track-focused car needs stiff suspension, aggressive geometry and minimal body movement. A road car needs enough compliance to deal with potholes, broken surfaces and poorly maintained roads.
The GT3 manages to operate in both environments.
It can feel almost excessively serious when driven gently. There is a sense that the chassis is constantly waiting for something more interesting to happen.
Then the road opens.
The steering is immediate without feeling nervous. The front end responds to small inputs, while the rear remains planted and predictable. Rather than simply generating grip, the car communicates what the tires are doing.
That communication is increasingly rare.
Modern performance cars have become extraordinarily good at hiding mistakes. Stability systems, active differentials, torque-vectoring systems and sophisticated suspension electronics can intervene before the driver even realizes the car is approaching its limits.
The GT3 uses electronics too, but the overall experience still feels mechanical.
You can feel the weight transfer.
You can feel the front tires load up.
You can sense when the rear begins to rotate.
And because the car communicates these changes so clearly, the driver can exploit them rather than simply react to them.
The Touring package does not fundamentally transform the GT3's mechanical character. Instead, it changes the way the car presents itself.
The enormous fixed rear wing is gone.
In its place is a manually or electronically deployable rear spoiler integrated into the normal 911 bodywork. The result is considerably more discreet.
This creates one of the most appealing contradictions in the entire car.
The GT3 Touring looks relatively civilized.
It absolutely is not.
It can accelerate from a standstill with the violence expected from a serious performance machine, carry extraordinary speed through corners and stop with enormous confidence. Yet from the outside, much of that capability remains hidden.
That discretion is valuable.
There is a growing tendency in the performance-car market toward increasingly aggressive styling. Cars are covered in aerodynamic devices, enormous wheels, carbon-fiber panels and vents whose visual importance sometimes exceeds their functional importance.
The GT3 Touring does not need to prove anything.
Its proportions are enough.
Inside, the philosophy continues.
The cabin is unmistakably 911, which means the driving position is excellent and the controls are arranged around the driver. It does not attempt to turn the cockpit into a nightclub of screens and animations.
That is not to say the GT3 is technologically primitive. It is not.
But the technology is subordinate to the driving experience.
That distinction is important.
There is a temptation in modern luxury cars to treat the interior as the primary product and the mechanical components as supporting hardware. The GT3 reverses that hierarchy.
You are sitting inside the car because you intend to drive it.
The seats hold you securely without making every journey feel like an endurance race. Visibility remains surprisingly good for a performance car. The driving position gives the impression that Porsche spent considerably more time thinking about where the driver should sit than about how impressive the dashboard should look in photographs.
Practicality is another unexpected strength.
The 911 is not a conventional family car, but the front luggage compartment and rear seats give it more utility than many two-seat sports cars. The rear seats are not exactly luxurious, but they can be useful for small passengers, luggage or simply creating additional storage space.
That makes the GT3 Touring unusual.
It is a genuine performance car that does not require the owner to have a second car simply to perform ordinary tasks.
You can drive it to work.
You can take it on a long road trip.
You can put luggage in it.
And then, with remarkably little preparation, you can take it to a racetrack and discover just how much engineering Porsche has hidden underneath the restrained bodywork.
There are compromises, naturally.
The ride can become harsh on poor roads, particularly with aggressive wheel and tire configurations. Road noise is not the GT3's strongest attribute. Fuel consumption is irrelevant to anyone buying one but still worth acknowledging. And the car's enormous capability can be difficult to access legally on public roads.
There is also the question of price.
A GT3 Touring is expensive before options, and Porsche's options catalogue can make an already costly car substantially more expensive. Carbon-fiber components, special paint, upgraded seats and other desirable additions can rapidly transform the purchase price.
That leads to an uncomfortable question.
Is the GT3 Touring actually worth the money?
If the objective is transportation, obviously not.
If the objective is maximum acceleration per dollar, there are cheaper cars that can embarrass it in a straight line.
If the objective is lap time alone, even Porsche offers more specialized machinery.
But if the objective is driving, the equation changes.
The GT3 Touring represents something increasingly unusual: a performance car where the engineering is designed to reward the person behind the wheel rather than simply impress the person standing beside it.
That is why the lack of a giant rear wing matters.
It is not merely a styling decision.
It communicates the philosophy of the car.
The GT3 Touring does not need to announce what it is. It assumes the driver will discover that for themselves.
And after a few kilometers of fast road, the understated bodywork starts to make perfect sense.
The car does not feel like it is performing for an audience.
It feels like it was built for one person.
The driver.
author: NZZ Redaktion

headline: Tennis Has Entered an Era Where Nobody Gets to Stay on Top Forever
lead: The modern tennis landscape is becoming increasingly difficult to dominate. The sport's established champions still possess extraordinary experience and consistency, but a younger generation is challenging them with greater athleticism, power and tactical variety. The result is a tour in which rankings can change quickly and even the biggest names are no longer guaranteed to control the biggest tournaments.
body:
Tennis has always been a sport built around individual excellence.
There is nowhere to hide on a singles court. No teammate can cover a bad afternoon, no coach can enter the match and no substitution can rescue a player whose game has fallen apart. For two or three hours, everything depends on one person making better decisions than the opponent standing across the net.
That has traditionally made sustained dominance extremely difficult.
The greatest players can win for years, but eventually the rest of the tour begins to understand them. Their patterns become familiar. Their weaknesses become targets. Younger opponents arrive with fewer expectations and greater physical reserves.
The current generation is experiencing that transition in real time.
The old model of tennis dominance was built around a small number of players who could remain at the top for an extraordinary period. They could win on hard courts, clay and grass, adapt their games and maintain an almost absurd level of consistency over an entire season.
The modern game is becoming less predictable.
One reason is physical.
Today's elite players are bigger, faster and more powerful than previous generations. The modern professional is expected to defend corners that would once have been considered winning positions, recover almost immediately and then generate enough racket-head speed to turn defense into attack.
A point that begins with one player defending the baseline can change direction in a single shot.
That makes athleticism increasingly important.
But physical ability alone does not explain the evolution of the sport.
Equipment has changed. Court conditions have changed. Sports science has improved. Players have access to more detailed information about their opponents than ever before.
A professional tennis player can arrive at a tournament with an extensive analytical profile of the opponent waiting on the other side of the net.
Where do they serve under pressure?
Which direction do they prefer on important points?
How often do they attack the second serve?
How does their performance change after long rallies?
The answers can influence tactical decisions before the match even begins.
Yet data has not eliminated improvisation.
Quite the opposite.
At the highest level, everyone knows roughly what the opponent wants to do. The challenge is preventing them from doing it while simultaneously executing your own plan.
That creates a fascinating tactical battle.
A player might spend an entire match attacking an opponent's backhand, only for that opponent to begin deliberately running around it and taking forehands from unusual positions.
Another player might return serves aggressively for the first set, then suddenly move several steps farther behind the baseline to give themselves more time.
The best players are constantly adjusting.
That is particularly important in Grand Slam tennis, where matches are longer and physical problems become increasingly difficult to hide.
A player can survive a bad set in a best-of-three match.
In a best-of-five match, the same problem can become a structural weakness.
A minor drop in serve percentage can become a break of serve. A slightly slower recovery between points can become a longer rally. A small tactical mistake can become a lost set.
Eventually, the match exposes whatever the player cannot sustain.
This is why endurance has become almost as important as explosiveness.
Modern tennis rewards players who can maintain intensity without wasting energy. The ability to win a point in four shots is useful, but so is the ability to survive a 25-shot rally without losing concentration.
The best competitors understand the difference.
They know when to accelerate and when to reset.
They know that not every point needs to be spectacular.
This is one of the less glamorous aspects of elite tennis: much of winning is about refusing to give the opponent opportunities.
A player does not necessarily need to hit the most impressive shot.
They need to make fewer damaging mistakes.
That becomes particularly important when facing an opponent with superior raw power.
The modern baseline game can sometimes resemble a controlled exchange of artillery. Both players stand several meters behind the baseline and repeatedly strike the ball at extraordinary speed.
But the most effective players rarely rely on power alone.
They manipulate space.
A cross-court forehand moves the opponent toward one corner. The next shot goes behind them. A short angle pulls them forward. A heavy ball pushes them back.
The objective is not simply to hit the ball harder.
It is to make the opponent hit it from somewhere they do not want to be.
That is why movement remains one of the most important skills in tennis.
A player with an enormous serve can still struggle if their movement breaks down. A brilliant returner can become vulnerable if they cannot generate offense after getting the ball back. A powerful forehand becomes less useful if the player cannot create enough time to use it.
The modern great therefore needs multiple solutions.
They need a serve that produces free points.
They need a return that prevents the opponent from dominating immediately.
They need a reliable baseline game.
They need enough variety to disrupt rhythm.
And, increasingly, they need the psychological resilience to continue executing when the match becomes uncomfortable.
The mental side of tennis is perhaps the hardest part to measure.
A player can lose five games in a row and still win the match.
They can be two points away from victory and suddenly find themselves facing break point.
They can dominate an opponent for an hour and then watch the entire match change because of one poor service game.
There is no clock to rescue them.
The match ends when the required number of sets has been won.
That creates an unusual form of pressure.
Tennis players must simultaneously think about the present point and the larger match.
Thinking too far ahead can be destructive. A player serving for the match cannot afford to mentally celebrate before the final point. But ignoring the score entirely is equally dangerous.
The greatest competitors learn to operate somewhere between the two.
They treat each point as important without allowing the previous point to determine the next one.
That ability may become even more valuable as the competitive field becomes deeper.
When fewer players are overwhelmingly dominant, tournaments become less predictable. A dangerous opponent can appear in the second round. A highly ranked player can face a difficult matchup before reaching the later stages.
The traditional assumption that the biggest names will inevitably meet in the semifinals becomes harder to sustain.
For fans, that uncertainty is valuable.
Tennis becomes more difficult to predict, and therefore more interesting to watch.
The sport is not losing its superstars.
It is gaining more players capable of challenging them.
That distinction matters.
The end of one era does not necessarily mean the beginning of another dominated by a single replacement.
It may mean that tennis is entering a period in which several players are capable of beating each other, depending on surface, conditions, form and matchup.
That would represent a significant change in the sport's competitive landscape.
For years, the central question at major tournaments was often straightforward:
Who can stop the champion?
Increasingly, the question may be different.
Who is going to survive everyone else?
That is a much harder question to answer.
And for a sport built around one-on-one competition, uncertainty may be exactly what tennis needs.
author: NZZ Redaktion

headline: The New Era of Formula 1 Is About to Get Very Different
lead: Formula 1 is entering another major technical transition, with new regulations set to reshape how teams approach power, aerodynamics and race strategy. The changes could disrupt the competitive order and force teams to rethink what it means to build the fastest car on the grid.
body:
Formula 1 has always been a sport of evolution.
Every few years, the rules change. Cars become faster in one area and slower in another. Engineers find loopholes. Teams copy successful ideas. Drivers adapt. Eventually, the advantage disappears and the cycle begins again.
The next major regulatory era promises to be one of the most consequential yet.
The new generation of Formula 1 cars is designed around a different balance between mechanical and aerodynamic performance. Power-unit technology is changing, active aerodynamic systems are becoming more important and the cars are being designed with greater emphasis on efficiency.
For fans, that might sound like an engineering exercise.
It is anything but.
Technical regulations determine the competitive landscape of Formula 1. A small change to the rules can transform a midfield team into a championship contender, while a dominant team can suddenly find itself fighting for podiums rather than victories.
That uncertainty is part of what makes a regulation change so fascinating.
The teams begin with incomplete information. Engineers have to predict how competitors will interpret the rules, where the greatest performance opportunities exist and which concepts will ultimately prove too complicated or inefficient.
The first challenge is the power unit.
Modern Formula 1 engines are already extraordinarily sophisticated, combining a combustion engine with electrical energy recovery and deployment. The next generation places a greater emphasis on electrical power while removing some of the complexity associated with previous hybrid systems.
That changes the engineering equation.
A team can no longer simply ask how much power the combustion engine can produce. Engineers must consider how efficiently the entire powertrain can generate, recover and deploy energy throughout a lap.
Energy management therefore becomes even more important.
A driver approaching a long straight might have a significant electrical reserve available—or might not. A team that manages its energy better could gain performance without necessarily having the most powerful engine.
That creates another layer of strategy.
The fastest car on a qualifying lap is not necessarily the fastest car over an entire race. Teams have to balance energy deployment, tire management, fuel consumption and aerodynamic efficiency.
And then there are the aerodynamics.
Formula 1 has spent much of the modern era attempting to improve racing by reducing the sensitivity of cars to following another vehicle. The goal is straightforward: if a driver can remain closer to the car ahead through corners, overtaking becomes easier.
The next generation takes the concept further by introducing greater aerodynamic adjustability.
Rather than relying entirely on fixed aerodynamic configurations, cars can alter aspects of their aerodynamic setup to optimize performance for different parts of a circuit.
In theory, this should make the cars more efficient.
In practice, the competitive consequences will depend on how successfully each team integrates the system into its overall aerodynamic philosophy.
That is where Formula 1 becomes less about individual components and more about systems engineering.
An aerodynamic gain is useless if it creates excessive tire degradation.
An engine that produces enormous peak power is less useful if it consumes energy inefficiently.
A car that is incredibly fast in qualifying may struggle if its tires overheat during a 70-lap race.
Every advantage creates another problem to solve.
This is why the opening races of a new regulatory era are often so revealing.
The stopwatch does not care about reputation.
A famous team can arrive with decades of engineering experience and still get the fundamental concept wrong. A smaller team can identify an unconventional solution and suddenly find itself fighting at the front.
Formula 1 history is full of these moments.
The introduction of radically different aerodynamic regulations has repeatedly created unexpected winners and losers. Teams that adapt quickly tend to benefit, while organizations that become attached to existing concepts can spend years attempting to recover.
The same dynamic applies to drivers.
A technically different car changes what is required behind the wheel. Braking points can move. Cornering techniques can change. Energy deployment can become another variable for drivers to manage during a race.
The best drivers will therefore need to do more than simply drive quickly.
They will need to understand the car.
They will need to know when to deploy electrical power, when to protect tires, when to attack and when to conserve. Communication with the engineers becomes increasingly important because the driver is operating within a complex strategic system.
That does not make Formula 1 less of a driving sport.
It makes the driver's role more complicated.
The most interesting question is what all of this will do to racing.
More efficient cars could theoretically make strategic decisions more important. Greater aerodynamic flexibility could create new overtaking opportunities. A more balanced technical formula could potentially reduce the advantage of the largest teams.
But regulations do not automatically produce close racing.
Teams are exceptionally good at finding performance. If one organization discovers a fundamentally better interpretation of the rules, the competitive order can become more predictable rather than less.
That is why the first year of a new technical era is so important.
It is the moment when the theoretical possibilities of the regulations meet reality.
Wind tunnels, computational simulations and dyno testing can only predict so much. Eventually, the cars have to run at racing speeds, on real circuits, with real tires and real drivers.
Then the stopwatch delivers its verdict.
For fans, the uncertainty is the attraction.
Nobody knows exactly which concept will win before the cars hit the track. A team that has looked mediocre for years could suddenly become a title contender. A championship favorite could discover that its technical philosophy has reached a dead end.
And that is the enduring appeal of Formula 1.
It is simultaneously a driving competition, an engineering competition and a strategic competition.
The regulations provide the boundaries.
The teams decide how far they can push them.
The drivers ultimately have to turn those ideas into lap time.
When the next generation of cars takes to the track, the most important question will not simply be which driver is fastest.
It will be which team understood the future first.
author: NZZ Redaktion

headline: The Arctic Is Becoming a New Front in Global Power Politics
lead: As the Arctic becomes more accessible because of a warming climate, its strategic importance is growing. Russia, the United States, Canada and other powers are competing for influence over a region containing valuable resources, emerging shipping routes and increasingly important military positions.
body:
For centuries, the Arctic was largely defined by its isolation. Extreme cold, sea ice and enormous distances made the region difficult to access and expensive to operate in.
That calculation is changing.
As Arctic sea ice declines, previously inaccessible areas are becoming easier to reach for longer periods of the year. This is creating new possibilities for shipping, energy extraction and military activity.
Russia has perhaps the greatest strategic interest in the region. Its northern coastline stretches across thousands of kilometers, and Moscow has invested heavily in Arctic infrastructure, ports and military capabilities. The Northern Sea Route could eventually provide a shorter maritime connection between Europe and Asia, although difficult conditions and infrastructure limitations remain significant obstacles.
The United States and its allies are increasingly focused on the same geography.
The Arctic connects North America, Europe and Russia, making it strategically important for missile warning, submarines and military logistics. As tensions between Russia and Western countries have increased, the region has become less of a peripheral concern and more of a component of broader security planning.
Economic interests add another layer.
The Arctic contains significant deposits of oil, gas and minerals, while demand for critical minerals has increased because of the global transition toward electric vehicles, renewable energy and advanced technologies.
But exploiting those resources is difficult.
Extreme weather, fragile ecosystems, limited infrastructure and enormous operating costs make Arctic projects considerably more complicated than comparable projects elsewhere.
The central irony is that climate change is simultaneously making the region more accessible and more strategically valuable.
The Arctic may therefore become one of the defining geopolitical arenas of the coming decades—not because the region is becoming less remote, but because the world is becoming increasingly interested in what lies beyond the ice.
author: NZZ Redaktion

headline: Your Smartphone Is Becoming a Computer You Wear in Your Pocket
lead: Smartphones have gradually evolved from communication devices into the central computing platforms of modern life. Cameras, payments, navigation, authentication, entertainment and increasingly sophisticated AI tools now live inside a device that rarely leaves its owner's side. The next stage may be less about making phones more powerful and more about making them disappear into the background.
body:
*Smartphones have gradually evolved from communication devices into the central computing platforms of modern life. Cameras, payments, navigation, authentication, entertainment and increasingly sophisticated AI tools now live inside a device that rarely leaves its owner's side. The next stage may be less about making phones more powerful and more about making them disappear into the background.*

The smartphone was once an accessory.
Today, it is infrastructure.
A single device can replace a camera, map, music player, television remote, wallet, boarding pass, notebook and increasingly even a computer. For billions of people, losing a phone is no longer an inconvenience. It can mean temporarily losing access to their money, accounts, contacts and digital identity.
The interesting question is what comes next.
Smartphones are already powerful enough for most everyday tasks. Processor improvements continue, but the average user rarely needs dramatically more performance simply to send messages or browse the internet.
The next major change may therefore come from artificial intelligence.
Instead of opening an application and telling it what to do, users could increasingly describe the outcome they want. An AI assistant might search through documents, compare information, schedule appointments or complete a sequence of tasks across multiple applications.
That changes the role of the phone.
Rather than being a collection of apps that the user operates individually, it becomes an interface through which the user interacts with a larger digital system.
But convenience creates a security problem.
An AI assistant with access to email, contacts, files and financial services could potentially do far more damage if compromised than a traditional application. The more capable the assistant becomes, the more important permissions, authentication and human oversight become.
Hardware is evolving too.
Foldable displays, improved cameras, satellite connectivity and increasingly sophisticated sensors are expanding what a smartphone can do. Meanwhile, wearable devices are taking over some functions that once required a phone to be actively used.
The eventual result may be surprisingly subtle.
The most important technology of the future may not be the device with the largest screen or fastest processor. It may be the system that allows people to interact with computing without thinking about the computer at all.
The smartphone has already transformed from a telephone into a general-purpose computer.
The next transformation may be turning that computer into something we barely notice.
author: Teofilus Shaduka
